abstract: In this paper we discuss why special purpose chips are needed for useful implementations of connectionist neural networks in such applications as pattern recognition and classification. Three chip designs are described: a hybrid digital/analog programmable connection matrix, an analog connection matrix with adjustable connection strengths, and a digital pipe lined best-match chip. The common feature of the designs is the distribution of arithmetic processing power amongst the data storage to minimize data movement.
originalAbstract: In this paper we discuss why special purpose chips are needed for useful implementations of connectionist neural networks in such applications as pattern recognition and classification. Three chip designs are described: a hybrid digital/analog programmable connection matrix, an analog connection matrix with adjustable connection strengths, and a digital pipe lined best-match chip. The common feature of the designs is the distribution of arithmetic processing power amongst the data storage to minimize data movement.

paragraphs: The paper examines special-purpose chips for implementing connectionist neural networks in tasks such as pattern recognition and classification. Its focus is the hardware organization needed to make these networks useful in practice. The authors discuss why neural computation motivates dedicated designs and present three different ways to organize the required operations.

One design is a programmable connection matrix combining digital and analog elements. Another is an analog connection matrix whose connection strengths can be adjusted. The third is a digital best-match chip with pipelined processing. These alternatives cover different hardware arrangements for representing connections and carrying out operations relevant to neural processing.

The shared design principle is to distribute arithmetic processing among the places where data is stored. This arrangement aims to reduce data movement by bringing computation closer to the information it uses. That common principle ties the three designs together despite their different analog and digital choices. The paper’s contribution is an implementation perspective in which the placement of storage and arithmetic is central to supporting neural-network applications.
summary.tldr: Three specialized chip designs reduce data movement by distributing neural-network arithmetic among data storage.

title: Microelectronic Implementations of Connectionist Neural Networks

abstract: Previous work has shown the ability of Multilayer Perceptrons (MLPs) to estimate emission probabilities for Hidden Markov Mod(cid:173) els (HMMs). The advantages of a speech recognition system incor(cid:173) porating both MLPs and HMMs are the best discrimination and the ability to incorporate multiple sources of evidence (features, temporal context) without restrictive assumptions of distributions or statistical independence. This paper presents results on the speaker-dependent portion of DARPA's English language Resource Management database. Results support the previously reported utility of MLP probability estimation for continuous speech recog(cid:173) nition. An additional approach we are pursuing is to use MLPs as nonlinear predictors for autoregressive HMMs. While this is shown to be more compatible with the HMM formalism, it still suffers from several limitations. This approach is generalized to take ac(cid:173) count of time correlation between successive observations, without any restrictive assumptions about the driving noise.

paragraphs: This paper explores combining multilayer perceptrons with hidden Markov models for speech recognition. The neural network estimates emission probabilities, which connect a model's hidden states to observed speech evidence. This arrangement combines neural discrimination with the HMM framework for sequences, while allowing features and temporal context to contribute without restrictive distributional or independence assumptions.

Experiments use the speaker-dependent portion of the English-language Resource Management database. The reported results support earlier findings that neural probability estimation is useful for continuous speech recognition. The significance is that a neural component can supply useful probability estimates within a sequence model while incorporating multiple sources of acoustic and contextual evidence.

The paper also explores using multilayer perceptrons as nonlinear predictors in autoregressive HMMs. This formulation is described as more compatible with the HMM formalism, although it retains several limitations. The authors generalize it to account for correlations between successive observations without restrictive assumptions about the driving noise. These two approaches examine different ways to make learned neural relationships part of probabilistic speech modeling.
summary.tldr: The paper supports neural probability estimation for HMM speech recognition and explores nonlinear prediction that accounts for temporal correlations.

title: Connectionist Approaches to the Use of Markov Models for Speech Recognition

abstract: The Neural Prediction Model is the speech recognition model based on pattern prediction by multilayer perceptrons. Its effectiveness was con(cid:173) firmed by the speaker-independent digit recognition experiments. This paper presents an improvement in the model and its application to large vocabulary speech recognition, based on subword units. The improvement involves an introduction of "backward prediction," which further improves the prediction accuracy of the original model with only "forward predic(cid:173) tion". In application of the model to speaker-dependent large vocabulary speech recognition, the demi-syllable unit is used as a subword recognition unit. Experimental results indicated a 95.2% recognition accuracy for a 5000 word test set and the effectiveness was confirmed for the proposed model improvement and the demi-syllable subword units.

paragraphs: This paper extends a speech recognizer based on pattern prediction by multilayer perceptrons. The earlier model had shown effectiveness in speaker-independent digit recognition. The new work improves its prediction mechanism and applies it to a larger vocabulary, using units smaller than whole words as the basis for recognition.

The model adds backward prediction to its existing forward prediction. This gives the prediction process an additional direction, and the authors report that it improves prediction accuracy. For the large-vocabulary application, the system uses demi-syllables as subword units. This choice provides intermediate speech components through which the recognizer can handle the word vocabulary.

The large-vocabulary experiment is speaker-dependent and reports 95.2% recognition accuracy on a 5,000-word test set. The results support both the added backward prediction and the use of demi-syllable units. The distinction between the earlier and current settings matters: the speaker-independent evidence concerns digits, while the stated large-vocabulary result concerns recognition adapted to a speaker.
summary.tldr: Backward prediction and demi-syllable units improve a neural speech model that achieves 95.2% accuracy on a speaker-dependent 5,000-word test set.

title: Speech Recognition Using Demi-Syllable Neural Prediction Model

abstract: We present a local learning rule in which Hebbian learning is conditional on an incorrect prediction of a reinforcement signal. We propose a biological interpretation of such a framework and display its utility through examples in which the reinforcement signal is cast as the delivery of a neuromodulator to its target. Three exam pIes are presented which illustrate how this framework can be applied to the development of the oculomotor system.
originalAbstract: We present a local learning rule in which Hebbian learning is conditional on an incorrect prediction of a reinforcement signal. We propose a biological interpretation of such a framework and display its utility through examples in which the reinforcement signal is cast as the delivery of a neuromodulator to its target. Three exam pIes are presented which illustrate how this framework can be applied to the development of the oculomotor system.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a local learning rule that combines Hebbian adaptation with prediction of a reinforcement signal. Hebbian learning links changes in a connection to the activity of the units it joins. Here, those changes are conditional: an incorrect prediction of reinforcement is what permits the Hebbian update to occur.

This condition gives the reinforcement signal a specific role in directing self-organization. Activity-dependent learning is enabled when the reinforcement prediction fails, tying local adaptation to a discrepancy in what the system expected. The proposed biological interpretation treats reinforcement as the arrival of a neuromodulator at its target, connecting the abstract learning condition to a biological signaling framework.

The authors present three examples applying the framework to development of the oculomotor system, which controls eye movements. These examples demonstrate how the same learning rule can be used in that developmental setting. The contribution is a mechanism for making local Hebbian changes depend on reinforcement prediction, together with a biological interpretation and illustrative developmental applications.
summary.tldr: A local learning rule gates Hebbian adaptation on reinforcement prediction errors, with examples from oculomotor development.

title: Using Aperiodic Reinforcement for Directed Self-Organization During Development

The MAP estimate minimizes uncertainty in all respects: cross-entropy between model and data; entropy of the model ; entropy of the data's descriptive statistics. Iterative estimation extinguishes weakly supported parameters, compressing and sparsifying the model. Trimming operators accelerate this process by removing excess parameters and, unlike most pruning schemes, guarantee an increase in posterior probability. Entropic estimation takes a overcomplete random model and simplifies it, inducing the structure of relations between hidden and observed variables. Applied to hidden Markov models (HMMs), it finds a concise finite-state machine representing the hidden structure of a signal. paragraphs: The paper tackles two learning problems together: estimating a model's probabilities and discovering which hidden relationships the model needs. It starts with an oversized random model and uses an entropy-based prior to favor informative, less ambiguous probability assignments. Learning therefore determines both the values of the parameters and the structure that survives.

The estimator balances agreement with the data against uncertainty in the model and the data's descriptive statistics. Parameters with weak support gradually disappear, making the representation smaller and sparser. Additional trimming operations speed up this simplification. Their distinctive property is that removing parameters is guaranteed to increase posterior probability, tying simplification directly to the Bayesian learning objective.

Applied to hidden Markov models, the approach produces compact state machines for music, handwriting, and video sequences. The reported surviving states align with meaningful divisions in the data, while transitions capture predictable dynamics. These findings suggest that compression can help expose interpretable temporal structure while preserving the model's ability to predict.
summary.tldr: An entropy-based learning method simplifies oversized probabilistic models into compact structures that capture meaningful temporal relationships.

title: An Entropic Estimator for Structure Discovery

abstract: The partition function for a Boltzmann machine can be bounded from above and below. We can use this to bound the means and the correlations. For networks with small weights, the values of these statistics can be restricted to non-trivial regions (i.e. a subset of [-1 , 1]). Experimental results show that reasonable bounding occurs for weight sizes where mean field expansions generally give good results.
originalAbstract: The partition function for a Boltzmann machine can be bounded from above and below. We can use this to bound the means and the correlations. For networks with small weights, the values of these statistics can be restricted to non-trivial regions (i.e. a subset of [-1 , 1]). Experimental results show that reasonable bounding occurs for weight sizes where mean field expansions generally give good results.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to constrain the possible values of means and correlations in a Boltzmann machine. These statistics describe average unit behavior and relationships between units. The approach begins with upper and lower bounds on the partition function, the quantity used to normalize the model's probabilities.

The authors use those partition-function bounds to derive bounds on the statistics themselves. For networks with small weights, the resulting intervals are nontrivial: they cover only part of the full range from minus one to one. This gives information about where the true values can lie, even without specifying them exactly.

Experiments show reasonable bounding for weight magnitudes where mean-field expansions generally perform well. This places the practical finding in a qualified regime, rather than asserting equally informative bounds at all interaction strengths. The contribution is a connection between bounds on a global model quantity and restrictions on individual statistics, with empirical evidence that the restrictions can be useful for sufficiently small weights.
summary.tldr: Partition-function bounds yield informative bounds on Boltzmann-machine means and correlations in a small-weight regime.

title: Means, Correlations and Bounds

abstract: We introduce a new type of Self-Organizing Map (SOM) to navigate in the Semantic Space of large text collections. We propose a “hyper- bolic SOM” (HSOM) based on a regular tesselation of the hyperbolic plane, which is a non-euclidean space characterized by constant negative gaussian curvature. The exponentially increasing size of a neighborhood around a point in hyperbolic space provides more freedom to map the complex information space arising from language into spatial relations. We describe experiments, showing that the HSOM can successfully be applied to text categorization tasks and yields results comparable to other state-of-the-art methods.

We propose a “hyper- bolic SOM” (HSOM) based on a regular tesselation of the hyperbolic plane, which is a non-euclidean space characterized by constant negative gaussian curvature. The exponentially increasing size of a neighborhood around a point in hyperbolic space provides more freedom to map the complex information space arising from language into spatial relations. We describe experiments, showing that the HSOM can successfully be applied to text categorization tasks and yields results comparable to other state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a self-organizing map for navigating the semantic space of large text collections. Its central design choice is to organize the map on a hyperbolic plane, giving the spatial representation a geometry different from an ordinary flat map. The aim is to express complex relationships in language through spatial relationships.

The proposed hyperbolic SOM uses a regular tessellation of a space with constant negative curvature. A neighborhood around a point grows exponentially as it extends outward. The authors argue that this growth provides more freedom for mapping the information structure of text, making the geometry an active part of the representation.

Experiments show that the method can be applied successfully to text categorization and gives results comparable to other leading methods. These findings support hyperbolic organization as a workable approach to representing text collections. The reported comparison establishes competitive categorization performance, while the broader motivation is navigation through a spatial arrangement of semantic information.
summary.tldr: A self-organizing map on a hyperbolic plane organizes text semantics and achieves competitive text categorization results.

title: Hyperbolic Self-Organizing Maps for Semantic Navigation

abstract: We describe the g-factor, which relates probability distributions on image features to distributions on the images themselves. The g-factor depends only on our choice of features and lattice quanti(cid:173) zation and is independent of the training image data. We illustrate the importance of the g-factor by analyzing how the parameters of Markov Random Field (i.e. Gibbs or log-linear) probability models of images are learned from data by maximum likelihood estimation. In particular, we study homogeneous MRF models which learn im(cid:173) age distributions in terms of clique potentials corresponding to fea(cid:173) ture histogram statistics (d. Minimax Entropy Learning (MEL) by Zhu, Wu and Mumford 1997 [11]) . We first use our analysis of the g-factor to determine when the clique potentials decouple for different features . Second, we show that clique potentials can be computed analytically by approximating the g-factor. Third, we demonstrate a connection between this approximation and the Generalized Iterative Scaling algorithm (GIS), due to Darroch and Ratcliff 1972 [2], for calculating potentials. This connection en(cid:173) ables us to use GIS to improve our multinomial approximation, using Bethe-Kikuchi[8] approximations to simplify the GIS proce(cid:173) dure. We support our analysis by computer simulations.

paragraphs: A probability distribution over image features is related to, but distinct from, a distribution over images. This paper introduces the g-factor to describe that relationship. The factor depends on the chosen features and lattice quantization, independently of the training images. It therefore captures an aspect of the representation that matters when learning image probabilities.

The authors study maximum-likelihood learning in homogeneous Markov random field models whose clique potentials correspond to feature histograms. Their analysis identifies when potentials for different features decouple. They also show that approximating the g-factor allows potentials to be calculated analytically, connecting a property of the feature representation to the computation of model parameters.

A further result links the approximation to generalized iterative scaling. The authors use that connection to improve their multinomial approximation and introduce Bethe-Kikuchi approximations to simplify the iterative-scaling procedure. Computer simulations support the analysis. The contribution is a framework that explains how feature-level distributions shape image-level learning and uses that explanation to develop parameter-computation methods.
summary.tldr: The g-factor connects feature distributions to image distributions and supports analytical and iterative methods for learning image-model potentials.

title: The g Factor: Relating Distributions on Features to Distributions on Images

abstract: Behavioral goals are achieved reliably and repeatedly with movements rarely reproducible in their detail. Here we offer an explanation: we show that not only are variability and goal achievement compatible, but indeed that allowing variability in redundant dimensions is the optimal control strategy in the face of uncertainty. The optimal feedback control laws for typical motor tasks obey a “minimal intervention” principle: deviations from the average trajectory are only corrected when they interfere with the task goals. The resulting behavior exhibits task-constrained variabil- ity, as well as synergetic coupling among actuators—which is another unexplained empirical phenomenon.
originalAbstract: Behavioral goals are achieved reliably and repeatedly with movements rarely reproducible in their detail. Here we offer an explanation: we show that not only are variability and goal achievement compatible, but indeed that allowing variability in redundant dimensions is the optimal control strategy in the face of uncertainty. The optimal feedback control laws for typical motor tasks obey a “minimal intervention” principle: deviations from the average trajectory are only corrected when they interfere with the task goals. The resulting behavior exhibits task-constrained variabil- ity, as well as synergetic coupling among actuators—which is another unexplained empirical phenomenon.

paragraphs: People can achieve the same movement goal repeatedly without reproducing every detail of the movement. This paper explains how reliable outcomes can coexist with variable trajectories. Its central claim is that, under uncertainty, allowing variation in redundant dimensions can be the optimal control strategy. These are aspects of movement that can vary without preventing success.

The authors show that optimal feedback control laws for typical motor tasks follow a minimal intervention principle. A deviation from the average trajectory calls for correction only when it interferes with the task goal. Feedback therefore depends on the consequence of a deviation, rather than treating every departure from an average movement as an error.

The resulting behavior has variability shaped by the task's requirements and coordinated coupling among actuators. These two properties emerge together from the control strategy. The explanation makes movement variability part of successful control under uncertainty: some details remain flexible while feedback protects the aspects of movement that determine whether the goal is reached.
summary.tldr: Optimal feedback control under uncertainty can allow harmless movement variation while correcting deviations that threaten the task goal.

title: A Minimal Intervention Principle for Coordinated Movement

abstract: This paper investigates a boosting approach to discriminative learning of label sequences based on a sequence rank loss function. The proposed method combines many of the advantages of boost(cid:173) ing schemes with the efficiency of dynamic programming methods and is attractive both, conceptually and computationally. In addi(cid:173) tion, we also discuss alternative approaches based on the Hamming loss for label sequences. The sequence boosting algorithm offers an interesting alternative to methods based on HMMs and the more recently proposed Conditional Random Fields. Applications areas for the presented technique range from natural language processing and information extraction to computational biology. We include experiments on named entity recognition and part-of-speech tag(cid:173) ging which demonstrate the validity and competitiveness of our approach.

The proposed method combines many of the advantages of boost(cid:173) ing schemes with the efficiency of dynamic programming methods and is attractive both, conceptually and computationally. In addi(cid:173) tion, we also discuss alternative approaches based on the Hamming loss for label sequences. We include experiments on named entity recognition and part-of-speech tag(cid:173) ging which demonstrate the validity and competitiveness of our approach.

paragraphs: The paper studies how boosting can learn to assign labels to sequences. The learning objective uses a sequence rank loss, making the ranking of candidate label sequences central to training. This focuses the method on structured predictions in which the output is an entire sequence of labels, rather than a single category.

The proposed algorithm combines boosting with the computational efficiency of dynamic programming. The authors also discuss alternatives based on Hamming loss, which assesses disagreement at individual sequence positions. Considering these losses makes the treatment of prediction errors an explicit part of the method: ranking whole label sequences and counting positionwise errors provide different training perspectives.

Experiments on named entity recognition and part-of-speech tagging demonstrate the approach's validity and competitiveness. The paper presents sequence boosting as an alternative to methods based on hidden Markov models and conditional random fields. It also identifies information extraction, natural language processing, and computational biology as application areas. The stated empirical findings support the method on the two reported language tasks without claiming universal superiority across sequence problems.
summary.tldr: Sequence boosting combines a ranking-based learning objective with dynamic programming and shows competitive results on two language-labeling tasks.

title: Discriminative Learning for Label Sequences via Boosting

abstract: The problem of learning a sparse conic combination of kernel functions or kernel matrices for classification or regression can be achieved via the regularization by a block 1-norm [1]. In this paper, we present an al- gorithm that computes the entire regularization path for these problems. The path is obtained by using numerical continuation techniques, and involves a running time complexity that is a constant times the complex- ity of solving the problem for one value of the regularization parameter. Working in the setting of kernel linear regression and kernel logistic re- gression, we show empirically that the effect of the block 1-norm reg- ularization differs notably from the (non-block) 1-norm regularization commonly used for variable selection, and that the regularization path is of particular value in the block case.
originalAbstract: The problem of learning a sparse conic combination of kernel functions or kernel matrices for classification or regression can be achieved via the regularization by a block 1-norm [1]. In this paper, we present an al- gorithm that computes the entire regularization path for these problems. The path is obtained by using numerical continuation techniques, and involves a running time complexity that is a constant times the complex- ity of solving the problem for one value of the regularization parameter. Working in the setting of kernel linear regression and kernel logistic re- gression, we show empirically that the effect of the block 1-norm reg- ularization differs notably from the (non-block) 1-norm regularization commonly used for variable selection, and that the regularization path is of particular value in the block case.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning a sparse combination of kernels for classification or regression. A block 1-norm penalty encourages sparsity across kernel components, making the strength of regularization an important part of the learning problem. Different penalty values can produce different combinations, so understanding their full progression is useful.

The authors present an algorithm for computing the entire regularization path: the sequence of solutions obtained as the penalty parameter varies. It uses numerical continuation to follow that sequence. The stated running-time complexity is a constant multiple of the complexity of solving the problem at one parameter value, making a full path computationally attractive within their analysis.

Experiments in kernel linear regression and kernel logistic regression show that block regularization behaves noticeably differently from ordinary 1-norm regularization used for selecting variables. The authors find the full path particularly valuable in the block setting. This connects the computational contribution to a practical question: how the selection and weighting of kernels change as regularization becomes stronger or weaker.
summary.tldr: A numerical-continuation algorithm efficiently computes full regularization paths for learning sparse combinations of kernels.

title: Computing regularization paths for learning multiple kernels

abstract: A good image object detection algorithm is accurate, fast, and does not require exact locations of objects in a training set. We can create such an object detector by taking the architecture of the Viola-Jones detector cascade and training it with a new variant of boosting that we call MILBoost. MILBoost uses cost functions from the Multiple Instance Learning literature combined with the AnyBoost framework. We adapt the feature selection criterion of MILBoost to optimize the performance of the Viola-Jones cascade. Experiments show that the detection rate is up to 1.6 times better using MILBoost. This increased detection rate shows the advantage of simultaneously learning the locations and scales of the objects in the training set along with the parameters of the classifier.
originalAbstract: A good image object detection algorithm is accurate, fast, and does not require exact locations of objects in a training set. We can create such an object detector by taking the architecture of the Viola-Jones detector cascade and training it with a new variant of boosting that we call MILBoost. MILBoost uses cost functions from the Multiple Instance Learning literature combined with the AnyBoost framework. We adapt the feature selection criterion of MILBoost to optimize the performance of the Viola-Jones cascade. Experiments show that the detection rate is up to 1.6 times better using MILBoost. This increased detection rate shows the advantage of simultaneously learning the locations and scales of the objects in the training set along with the parameters of the classifier.

paragraphs: Object detectors must learn what an object looks like, but training can also require knowing exactly where each example appears. This paper develops a detector that does not need precise object locations in its training images. It combines the Viola–Jones cascade architecture with a new boosting method called MILBoost.

MILBoost brings cost functions from multiple-instance learning into the AnyBoost framework. This formulation allows object location and scale to be learned together with classifier parameters, rather than requiring exact locations in advance. The authors also adapt its feature-selection criterion to optimize performance within the cascade architecture, connecting the training objective to the detector's structure.

The experiments report a detection rate up to 1.6 times better with MILBoost. That figure describes the largest reported improvement, not a uniform gain across every setting. The authors interpret the improvement as evidence for learning object placement and appearance jointly. The approach thus addresses training annotation requirements and detection performance through the same learning formulation.
summary.tldr: MILBoost jointly learns object locations, scales, and classifier parameters, with reported detection-rate improvements of up to 1.6 times.

title: Multiple Instance Boosting for Object Detection

abstract: A standard method to obtain stochastic models for symbolic time series is to train state-emitting hidden Markov models (SE-HMMs) with the Baum-Welch algorithm. Based on observable operator models (OOMs), in the last few months a number of novel learning algorithms for similar purposes have been developed: (1,2) two versions of an "efficiency sharpening" (ES) algorithm, which iteratively improves the statistical efficiency of a sequence of OOM estimators, (3) a constrained gradient descent ML estimator for transition-emitting HMMs (TE-HMMs). We give an overview on these algorithms and compare them with SE-HMM/EM learning on synthetic and real-life data.
originalAbstract: A standard method to obtain stochastic models for symbolic time series is to train state-emitting hidden Markov models (SE-HMMs) with the Baum-Welch algorithm. Based on observable operator models (OOMs), in the last few months a number of novel learning algorithms for similar purposes have been developed: (1,2) two versions of an "efficiency sharpening" (ES) algorithm, which iteratively improves the statistical efficiency of a sequence of OOM estimators, (3) a constrained gradient descent ML estimator for transition-emitting HMMs (TE-HMMs). We give an overview on these algorithms and compare them with SE-HMM/EM learning on synthetic and real-life data.

paragraphs: This paper examines algorithms for learning stochastic models of symbolic time series. The reference approach is a state-emitting hidden Markov model trained with the Baum–Welch algorithm. Against that familiar route, the authors review newer learning procedures based on observable operator models, or OOMs, for modeling similar kinds of sequence data.

Two of the procedures are versions of an efficiency-sharpening algorithm. They repeatedly improve the statistical efficiency of a sequence of OOM estimators, focusing on how effectively estimation uses the observations. Another procedure is a maximum-likelihood estimator for transition-emitting hidden Markov models, optimized through constrained gradient descent. The distinction between state-emitting and transition-emitting models is part of the comparison.

The paper brings these algorithms together and compares them with state-emitting HMM learning through expectation-maximization on synthetic and real data. Its contribution is an overview and empirical comparison of alternative estimation strategies for symbolic sequences. The abstract identifies the algorithms and evaluation settings without declaring one method a universal winner, so the findings should be understood as comparative evidence within the studied tasks.
summary.tldr: The paper reviews OOM-based sequence-learning algorithms and compares them with conventional hidden Markov model training on synthetic and real data.

title: Efficient Estimation of OOMs

abstract: Although variants of value iteration have been proposed for ﬁnding Nash or correlated equilibria in general-sum Markov games, these variants have not been shown to be effective in general. In this paper, we demon- strate by construction that existing variants of value iteration cannot ﬁnd stationary equilibrium policies in arbitrary general-sum Markov games. Instead, we propose an alternative interpretation of the output of value it- eration based on a new (non-stationary) equilibrium concept that we call “cyclic equilibria.” We prove that value iteration identiﬁes cyclic equi- libria in a class of games in which it fails to ﬁnd stationary equilibria. We also demonstrate empirically that value iteration ﬁnds cyclic equilibria in nearly all examples drawn from a random distribution of Markov games.

paragraphs: The paper examines value iteration as a tool for finding equilibria in general-sum Markov games, where players' interests need not be strictly opposed. Existing variants seek Nash or correlated equilibria, but their general effectiveness had not been established. The authors construct examples showing that these variants cannot reliably find stationary equilibrium policies across arbitrary games.

They then propose a different interpretation of the algorithm's output through cyclic equilibria. These equilibria are non-stationary: the relevant policies can vary through a cycle rather than remain fixed over time. This changes the equilibrium target and provides a way to understand behavior that does not settle into a stationary solution.

The theoretical result proves that value iteration identifies cyclic equilibria in a class of games where it fails to find stationary equilibria. Experiments additionally find cyclic equilibria in nearly all examples sampled from a random distribution of games. Together, these results establish a specific theoretical success and broader empirical support, without asserting success for every general-sum Markov game.
summary.tldr: Value iteration can find cyclic equilibria in some Markov games where it fails to find stationary equilibria.

title: Cyclic Equilibria in Markov Games

abstract: This paper explores two aspects of social network modeling. First, we generalize a successful static model of relationships into a dynamic model that accounts for friendships drifting over time. Second, we show how to make it tractable to learn such models from data, even as the number of entities n gets large. The generalized model associates each entity with a point in p-dimensional Euclidian latent space. The points can move as time progresses but large moves in latent space are improb- able. Observed links between entities are more likely if the entities are close in latent space. We show how to make such a model tractable (sub- quadratic in the number of entities) by the use of appropriate kernel func- tions for similarity in latent space; the use of low dimensional kd-trees; a new ef(cid:2)cient dynamic adaptation of multidimensional scaling for a (cid:2)rst pass of approximate projection of entities into latent space; and an ef(cid:2)- cient conjugate gradient update rule for non-linear local optimization in which amortized time per entity during an update is O(log n). We use both synthetic and real-world data on upto 11,000 entities which indicate linear scaling in computation time and improved performance over four alternative approaches. We also illustrate the system operating on twelve years of NIPS co-publication data. We present a detailed version of this work in [1].

paragraphs: The paper represents a changing social network by giving each entity a position in a hidden Euclidean space. Nearby entities are more likely to share an observed link. Positions can move over time, but large movements are unlikely, allowing relationships to drift while preserving continuity between successive network states.

A second contribution makes learning practical as the network grows. The method combines suitable similarity kernels, low-dimensional kd-trees, a dynamic version of multidimensional scaling for an initial approximate placement, and conjugate-gradient optimization for refinement. The resulting approach is subquadratic in the number of entities, with amortized update time per entity of O(log n).

The authors also illustrate the method using twelve years of NIPS co-publication data. Together, the results show how a continuous model of changing relationships can be paired with computational techniques that make sizable dynamic networks accessible.
summary.tldr: Moving latent positions model changing social relationships, while efficient geometric computations make learning practical on large networks.

title: Dynamic Social Network Analysis using Latent Space Models

abstract: The problem of obtaining the maximum a posteriori estimate of a general discrete random field (i.e. a random field defined using a finite and discrete set of labels) is known to be N P-hard. However, due to its central importance in many applications, several approximate algorithms have been proposed in the literature. In this paper, we present an analysis of three such algorithms based on convex relaxations: (i) L P - S: the linear programming (L P) relaxation proposed by Schlesinger [20] for a special case and independently in [4, 12, 23] for the general case; (ii) Q P - R L: the quadratic programming (Q P) relaxation by Ravikumar and Lafferty [18]; and (iii) S O C P - M S: the second order cone programming (S O C P) relaxation first proposed by Muramatsu and Suzuki [16] for two label problems and later extended in [14] for a general label set. We show that the S O C P - M S and the Q P - R L relaxations are equivalent. Furthermore, we prove that despite the flexibility in the form of the constraints/objective function offered by Q P and S O C P, the L P - S relaxation strictly dominates (i.e. provides a better approximation than) Q P - R L and S O C P - M S. We generalize these results by defining a large class of S O C P (and equivalent Q P) relaxations which is dominated by the L P - S relaxation. Based on these results we propose some novel S O C P relaxations which strictly dominate the previous approaches.

paragraphs: Finding the most probable labeling in a general discrete random field is computationally hard. Convex relaxations make the problem more approachable by replacing it with a related optimization problem. This paper compares three existing formulations based on linear programming, quadratic programming, and second order cone programming.

The authors show that the particular quadratic and second order cone relaxations under study are equivalent. They also prove that the linear programming relaxation strictly dominates both in approximation quality. Thus, the greater flexibility of the other optimization forms does not, by itself, make these particular formulations stronger.

The analysis extends to a large family of second order cone relaxations and equivalent quadratic relaxations, all dominated by the examined linear program. Building on these findings, the authors propose new second order cone relaxations that strictly dominate the previous approaches. The contribution is both a comparison of existing approximation strength and a basis for designing stronger relaxations; it does not claim that the optimization category alone determines quality.
summary.tldr: An analysis ranks existing MAP relaxations by approximation strength and motivates stronger second order cone formulations.

title: An Analysis of Convex Relaxations for MAP Estimation

abstract: Variational methods are frequently used to approximate or bound the partition or likelihood function of a Markov random field. Methods based on mean field theory are guaranteed to provide lower bounds, whereas certain types of convex relaxations provide upper bounds. In general, loopy belief propagation (BP) provides (often accurate) approximations, but not bounds. We prove that for a class of attractive binary models, the value specified by any fixed point of loopy BP always provides a lower bound on the true likelihood. Empirically, this bound is much better than the naive mean field bound, and requires no further work than running BP. We establish these lower bounds using a loop series expansion due to Chertkov and Chernyak, which we show can be derived as a consequence of the tree reparameterization characterization of BP fixed points.

In general, loopy belief propagation (BP) provides (often accurate) approximations, but not bounds. paragraphs: Approximate inference methods differ in whether their answers are certified bounds or simply estimates. Mean field methods provide lower bounds, while certain convex relaxations provide upper bounds. Loopy belief propagation often gives accurate approximations, but generally does not guarantee which side of the true quantity its result lies on.

This paper proves a stronger statement for a class of attractive binary graphical models. For these models, the value associated with any fixed point of loopy belief propagation is a lower bound on the true likelihood. The scope is tied to that model class and to a fixed point; the statement does not turn arbitrary belief propagation outputs into bounds.

The authors establish the result using a loop series expansion and show how that expansion follows from a tree reparameterization description of belief propagation fixed points. Empirically, the bound is much better than naive mean field and requires no additional work beyond running belief propagation. The contribution gives an existing approximation a certified interpretation within the stated setting.
summary.tldr: For a class of attractive binary models, every loopy belief propagation fixed point provides a lower bound on the true likelihood.

title: Loop Series and Bethe Variational Bounds in Attractive Graphical Models

abstract: In this paper we develop a Gaussian process (GP) framework to model a collection of reciprocal random variables defined on the \emph{edges} of a network. We show how to construct GP priors, i.e.,~covariance functions, on the edges of directed, undirected, and bipartite graphs. The model suggests an intimate connection between \emph{link prediction} and \emph{transfer learning}, which were traditionally considered two separate research topics. Though a straightforward GP inference has a very high complexity, we develop an efficient learning algorithm that can handle a large number of observations. The experimental results on several real-world data sets verify superior learning capacity.

We show how to construct GP priors, i.e.,~covariance functions, on the edges of directed, undirected, and bipartite graphs. The model suggests an intimate connection between \emph{link prediction} and \emph{transfer learning}, which were traditionally considered two separate research topics. Though a straightforward GP inference has a very high complexity, we develop an efficient learning algorithm that can handle a large number of observations. The experimental results on several real-world data sets verify superior learning capacity.

paragraphs: This paper develops a Gaussian process framework for random variables associated with network edges. Placing the modeled quantities on edges makes relationships themselves the objects of prediction. The authors construct covariance functions for directed, undirected, and bipartite graphs, allowing the framework to address several different forms of network organization.

A covariance function specifies how the modeled edge variables relate within the Gaussian process prior. Through this formulation, the authors identify a close connection between link prediction and transfer learning, two areas usually treated separately. The framework therefore offers a shared statistical perspective on predicting relationships and using information across related learning problems.

Straightforward Gaussian process inference would be computationally expensive in this setting. The paper develops an efficient learning algorithm capable of handling many observations, making the edge-based formulation more practical. Experiments on several real-world datasets report superior learning capacity. These results provide empirical support for the approach while the covariance constructions supply its broader modeling contribution across different graph types.
summary.tldr: Gaussian processes defined over network edges connect link prediction with transfer learning and support efficient learning from many observations.

title: Gaussian Process Models for Link Analysis and Transfer Learning

abstract: We propose a general method called truncated gradient to induce sparsity in the weights of online-learning algorithms with convex loss. This method has several essential properties. First, the degree of sparsity is continuous---a parameter controls the rate of sparsification from no sparsification to total sparsification. Second, the approach is theoretically motivated, and an instance of it can be regarded as an online counterpart of the popular $L_1$-regularization method in the batch setting. We prove that small rates of sparsification result in only small additional regret with respect to typical online-learning guarantees. Finally, the approach works well empirically. We apply it to several datasets and find that for datasets with large numbers of features, substantial sparsity is discoverable.
originalAbstract: We propose a general method called truncated gradient to induce sparsity in the weights of online-learning algorithms with convex loss. This method has several essential properties. First, the degree of sparsity is continuous---a parameter controls the rate of sparsification from no sparsification to total sparsification. Second, the approach is theoretically motivated, and an instance of it can be regarded as an online counterpart of the popular $L_1$-regularization method in the batch setting. We prove that small rates of sparsification result in only small additional regret with respect to typical online-learning guarantees. Finally, the approach works well empirically. We apply it to several datasets and find that for datasets with large numbers of features, substantial sparsity is discoverable.

paragraphs: Online learning updates a model as observations arrive, but the resulting weight vector need not be sparse. The paper introduces truncated gradient, a general method for encouraging zero weights in online algorithms with convex loss. This makes sparsity part of the ongoing update process rather than requiring a separate batch-fitting procedure.

A parameter controls the rate of sparsification continuously, ranging from no sparsification to total sparsification. The method also has a theoretical connection to a familiar batch approach: one instance can be understood as an online counterpart of L1 regularization. This gives the update rule an interpretation grounded in regularized learning.

The authors prove that small sparsification rates add only a small amount of regret relative to typical online-learning guarantees. This provides a qualified statement about the cost of encouraging sparsity, rather than claiming it is always free. Experiments on several datasets find substantial discoverable sparsity when the number of features is large, supporting the method's practical usefulness for producing sparse models during online learning.
summary.tldr: Truncated gradient induces adjustable sparsity in online learning, with small additional regret at small sparsification rates.

title: Sparse Online Learning via Truncated Gradient

abstract: We propose a new model for natural image statistics. Instead of minimizing dependency between components of natural images, we maximize a simple form of dependency in the form of tree-dependency. By learning filters and tree structures which are best suited for natural images we observe that the resulting filters are edge filters, similar to the famous ICA on natural images results. Calculating the likelihood of the model requires estimating the squared output of pairs of filters connected in the tree. We observe that after learning, these pairs of filters are predominantly of similar orientations but different phases, so their joint energy resembles models of complex cells.
originalAbstract: We propose a new model for natural image statistics. Instead of minimizing dependency between components of natural images, we maximize a simple form of dependency in the form of tree-dependency. By learning filters and tree structures which are best suited for natural images we observe that the resulting filters are edge filters, similar to the famous ICA on natural images results. Calculating the likelihood of the model requires estimating the squared output of pairs of filters connected in the tree. We observe that after learning, these pairs of filters are predominantly of similar orientations but different phases, so their joint energy resembles models of complex cells.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a model of natural-image statistics that actively seeks a simple form of dependence between components. The dependence has a tree structure, and the model learns both that structure and the image filters. Its aim differs from approaches that try to make the learned components statistically independent.

After learning from natural images, the resulting filters detect edges, resembling the filters associated with independent component analysis on natural images. This observation matters because a dependence-seeking model arrives at a similar kind of image feature. The learned edge structure therefore appears within this alternative statistical organization of the components.

Computing the model's likelihood requires estimating squared outputs for filter pairs joined in the tree. The authors observe that learned pairs predominantly share orientation while differing in phase. Their joint energy resembles models of complex cells. The findings connect the learned tree relationships to structured combinations of edge filters, while describing that biological connection as a resemblance rather than an identity.
summary.tldr: Learning tree-dependent natural-image components produces edge filters whose paired energies resemble complex-cell models.

title: The 'tree-dependent components' of natural scenes are edge filters

abstract: Pruning can massively accelerate the computation of feature expectations in large models. However, any single pruning mask will introduce bias. We present a novel approach which employs a randomized sequence of pruning masks. Formally, we apply auxiliary variable MCMC sampling to generate this sequence of masks, thereby gaining theoretical guarantees about convergence. Because each mask is generally able to skip large portions of an underlying dynamic program, our approach is particularly compelling for high-degree algorithms. Empirically, we demonstrate our method on bilingual parsing, showing decreasing bias as more masks are incorporated, and outperforming fixed tic-tac-toe pruning.
originalAbstract: Pruning can massively accelerate the computation of feature expectations in large models. However, any single pruning mask will introduce bias. We present a novel approach which employs a randomized sequence of pruning masks. Formally, we apply auxiliary variable MCMC sampling to generate this sequence of masks, thereby gaining theoretical guarantees about convergence. Because each mask is generally able to skip large portions of an underlying dynamic program, our approach is particularly compelling for high-degree algorithms. Empirically, we demonstrate our method on bilingual parsing, showing decreasing bias as more masks are incorporated, and outperforming fixed tic-tac-toe pruning.

paragraphs: Computing feature expectations in large models can involve expensive dynamic programs. Pruning speeds up this computation by skipping parts of the program, but using a single fixed pruning mask introduces bias. This paper proposes varying the mask through a randomized sequence so that computational savings can be combined with a principled treatment of the resulting approximation.

The masks are generated using auxiliary-variable Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling. This supplies theoretical convergence guarantees for the approach. Each mask can skip substantial portions of the underlying dynamic program, making the method especially appealing for algorithms with high computational degree. The randomization is therefore part of an inference procedure with an analysis, rather than simply an arbitrary choice of discarded computations.

Experiments on bilingual parsing show that bias decreases as more masks are incorporated. The method also outperforms fixed tic-tac-toe pruning in the reported evaluation. These findings illustrate the intended tradeoff: individual computations remain pruned, while accumulating information across masks improves the estimate. The contribution links the speed benefits of pruning with a sampling-based route toward more accurate expectations.
summary.tldr: MCMC-generated pruning masks accelerate expectation calculations, with convergence guarantees and decreasing empirical bias as more masks are used.

title: Randomized Pruning: Efficiently Calculating Expectations in Large Dynamic Programs

abstract: We present a new way of converting a reversible finite Markov chain into a nonreversible one, with a theoretical guarantee that the asymptotic variance of the MCMC estimator based on the non-reversible chain is reduced. The method is applicable to any reversible chain whose states are not connected through a tree, and can be interpreted graphically as inserting vortices into the state transition graph. Our result confirms that non-reversible chains are fundamentally better than reversible ones in terms of asymptotic performance, and suggests interesting directions for further improving MCMC.
originalAbstract: We present a new way of converting a reversible finite Markov chain into a nonreversible one, with a theoretical guarantee that the asymptotic variance of the MCMC estimator based on the non-reversible chain is reduced. The method is applicable to any reversible chain whose states are not connected through a tree, and can be interpreted graphically as inserting vortices into the state transition graph. Our result confirms that non-reversible chains are fundamentally better than reversible ones in terms of asymptotic performance, and suggests interesting directions for further improving MCMC.

paragraphs: Markov chain Monte Carlo uses a sequence of linked samples to estimate quantities of interest. This paper studies how changing the transitions of a finite Markov chain affects the long-run variance of such estimates. It begins with a reversible chain and constructs a nonreversible version with a theoretical performance guarantee.

The construction has a graphical interpretation: it inserts circulating flows, called vortices, into the state-transition graph. The method applies to reversible chains whose states are not connected through a tree. That structural condition matters because the stated transformation uses the connectivity available beyond a tree-shaped graph.

The authors prove that the transformed chain reduces the asymptotic variance of the associated MCMC estimator. The guarantee therefore concerns the variability of estimates in the long-run regime. Within the setting covered by the construction, it establishes a principled benefit from breaking reversibility and motivates further work on transition designs that exploit directed circulation to improve sampling performance.
summary.tldr: Adding directed circulation to suitable finite reversible Markov chains provably reduces the asymptotic variance of MCMC estimates.

title: Improving the Asymptotic Performance of Markov Chain Monte-Carlo by Inserting Vortices

abstract: We present a new algorithm for differentially private data release, based on a simple combination of the Exponential Mechanism with the Multiplicative Weights update rule. Our MWEM algorithm achieves what are the best known and nearly optimal theoretical guarantees, while at the same time being simple to implement and experimentally more accurate on actual data sets than existing techniques.
originalAbstract: We present a new algorithm for differentially private data release, based on a simple combination of the Exponential Mechanism with the Multiplicative Weights update rule. Our MWEM algorithm achieves what are the best known and nearly optimal theoretical guarantees, while at the same time being simple to implement and experimentally more accurate on actual data sets than existing techniques.

paragraphs: The paper introduces MWEM, an algorithm for releasing data under differential privacy. Its central contribution is to bring strong theoretical guarantees together with a procedure the authors describe as straightforward to implement. The practical question is whether a private release method can offer both rigorous assurances and useful accuracy on actual datasets.

MWEM combines two named ingredients: the Exponential Mechanism and the Multiplicative Weights update rule. The contribution is their combination in a data-release algorithm. This gives the paper a clear methodological focus: a relatively simple construction is used to obtain guarantees that the authors report as the best known and close to optimal.

The authors also report experiments in which MWEM is more accurate on real datasets than existing techniques. That is an empirical comparison for the evaluations they conducted. Together, the theoretical and experimental findings support the paper’s practical message: simplicity of implementation can coexist with strong privacy-related guarantees and competitive accuracy in released data.
summary.tldr: MWEM combines the Exponential Mechanism with Multiplicative Weights to provide nearly optimal theoretical guarantees and improved empirical accuracy for private data release.

title: A Simple and Practical Algorithm for Differentially Private Data Release

abstract: This paper addresses the problem of category-level 3D object detection. Given a monocular image, our aim is to localize the objects in 3D by enclosing them with tight oriented 3D bounding boxes. We propose a novel approach that extends the well-acclaimed deformable part-based model[Felz.] to reason in 3D. Our model represents an object class as a deformable 3D cuboid composed of faces and parts, which are both allowed to deform with respect to their anchors on the 3D box. We model the appearance of each face in fronto-parallel coordinates, thus effectively factoring out the appearance variation induced by viewpoint. Our model reasons about face visibility patters called aspects. We train the cuboid model jointly and discriminatively and share weights across all aspects to attain efficiency. Inference then entails sliding and rotating the box in 3D and scoring object hypotheses. While for inference we discretize the search space, the variables are continuous in our model. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in indoor and outdoor scenarios, and show that our approach outperforms the state-of-the-art in both 2D[Felz09] and 3D object detection[Hedau12].

paragraphs: This paper studies how to locate objects in three dimensions from a single image. The desired output is a tightly fitting, oriented 3D box around each object. This combines identifying an object category with estimating where the object lies and which way it faces.

The approach represents an object category as a deformable cuboid containing faces and parts. Both can move relative to their anchors on the box, allowing the representation to accommodate variation within a category. Each face's appearance is modeled in coordinates that view it straight on, helping separate appearance from viewpoint. The model also handles different combinations of visible faces and shares learned weights across them.

Detection searches over box positions and rotations and scores the resulting object hypotheses. Although the model's variables are continuous, the inference procedure uses a discretized search. Experiments in indoor and outdoor settings demonstrate effectiveness, with reported improvements over the referenced leading methods for both 2D and 3D detection.
summary.tldr: A deformable 3D cuboid model jointly detects objects and estimates their orientation from a single image.

title: 3D Object Detection and Viewpoint Estimation with a Deformable 3D Cuboid Model

abstract: Local competition among neighboring neurons is common in biological neural networks (NNs). We apply the concept to gradient-based, backprop-trained artificial multilayer NNs. NNs with competing linear units tend to outperform those with non-competing nonlinear units, and avoid catastrophic forgetting when training sets change over time.
originalAbstract: Local competition among neighboring neurons is common in biological neural networks (NNs). We apply the concept to gradient-based, backprop-trained artificial multilayer NNs. NNs with competing linear units tend to outperform those with non-competing nonlinear units, and avoid catastrophic forgetting when training sets change over time.

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether competition between neighboring neurons can improve artificial neural networks. Such local competition is common in biological networks. The authors bring this idea into artificial networks with multiple layers, trained using gradients and backpropagation, so competition becomes part of a familiar learning framework.

The central comparison is between networks containing competing linear units and networks containing non-competing nonlinear units. This changes how units interact as well as the kind of units being used. The reported tendency is that networks with competing linear units perform better. That wording supports competition as a promising design choice, without establishing that it wins for every network or learning problem.

The authors also report that these networks avoid catastrophic forgetting when training sets change over time. Catastrophic forgetting refers to losing previously learned behavior while learning from new data. This finding gives the architectural idea a second motivation: competition may help a network retain earlier learning while its training experience changes, alongside its reported performance benefits.
summary.tldr: Multilayer networks with competing linear units tend to outperform non-competing nonlinear networks and are reported to avoid catastrophic forgetting.

title: Compete to Compute

abstract: Monte Carlo sampling for Bayesian posterior inference is a common approach used in machine learning. The Markov Chain Monte Carlo procedures that are used are often discrete-time analogues of associated stochastic differential equations (SDEs). These SDEs are guaranteed to leave invariant the required posterior distribution. An area of current research addresses the computational benefits of stochastic gradient methods in this setting. Existing techniques rely on estimating the variance or covariance of the subsampling error, and typically assume constant variance. In this article, we propose a covariance-controlled adaptive Langevin thermostat that can effectively dissipate parameter-dependent noise while maintaining a desired target distribution. The proposed method achieves a substantial speedup over popular alternative schemes for large-scale machine learning applications.
originalAbstract: Monte Carlo sampling for Bayesian posterior inference is a common approach used in machine learning. The Markov Chain Monte Carlo procedures that are used are often discrete-time analogues of associated stochastic differential equations (SDEs). These SDEs are guaranteed to leave invariant the required posterior distribution. An area of current research addresses the computational benefits of stochastic gradient methods in this setting. Existing techniques rely on estimating the variance or covariance of the subsampling error, and typically assume constant variance. In this article, we propose a covariance-controlled adaptive Langevin thermostat that can effectively dissipate parameter-dependent noise while maintaining a desired target distribution. The proposed method achieves a substantial speedup over popular alternative schemes for large-scale machine learning applications.

paragraphs: Bayesian inference often uses Monte Carlo samples to represent a posterior distribution. Many sampling algorithms are discrete versions of stochastic differential equations designed to preserve that distribution. For large datasets, stochastic gradients can reduce computation, but using subsets of data introduces additional noise that the sampling dynamics must accommodate.

The paper proposes a covariance-controlled adaptive Langevin thermostat to handle this noise. Existing approaches discussed in the abstract estimate the variance or covariance of subsampling error and typically treat its variance as constant. The proposed thermostat can dissipate noise whose behavior depends on the current parameter values while maintaining the desired target distribution.

This addresses the connection between computational shortcuts and the distribution a sampler is intended to explore. The authors report substantial speed improvements over popular alternative schemes in large-scale machine-learning applications. The stated contribution combines an adaptive treatment of parameter-dependent noise with practical sampling efficiency, rather than assessing computational cost independently of the target-distribution requirement.
summary.tldr: An adaptive Langevin thermostat handles parameter-dependent sampling noise while preserving a target distribution and improving reported sampling speed.

title: Covariance-Controlled Adaptive Langevin Thermostat for Large-Scale Bayesian Sampling

abstract: Expectation Propagation is a very popular algorithm for variational inference, but comes with few theoretical guarantees. In this article, we prove that the approximation errors made by EP can be bounded. Our bounds have an asymptotic interpretation in the number n of datapoints, which allows us to study EP's convergence with respect to the true posterior. In particular, we show that EP converges at a rate of $O(n^{-2})$ for the mean, up to an order of magnitude faster than the traditional Gaussian approximation at the mode. We also give similar asymptotic expansions for moments of order 2 to 4, as well as excess Kullback-Leibler cost (defined as the additional KL cost incurred by using EP rather than the ideal Gaussian approximation). All these expansions highlight the superior convergence properties of EP. Our approach for deriving those results is likely applicable to many similar approximate inference methods. In addition, we introduce bounds on the moments of log-concave distributions that may be of independent interest.
originalAbstract: Expectation Propagation is a very popular algorithm for variational inference, but comes with few theoretical guarantees. In this article, we prove that the approximation errors made by EP can be bounded. Our bounds have an asymptotic interpretation in the number n of datapoints, which allows us to study EP's convergence with respect to the true posterior. In particular, we show that EP converges at a rate of $O(n^{-2})$ for the mean, up to an order of magnitude faster than the traditional Gaussian approximation at the mode. We also give similar asymptotic expansions for moments of order 2 to 4, as well as excess Kullback-Leibler cost (defined as the additional KL cost incurred by using EP rather than the ideal Gaussian approximation). All these expansions highlight the superior convergence properties of EP. Our approach for deriving those results is likely applicable to many similar approximate inference methods. In addition, we introduce bounds on the moments of log-concave distributions that may be of independent interest.

paragraphs: Expectation Propagation, or EP, is a widely used method for approximate probabilistic inference with relatively few theoretical guarantees. This paper establishes bounds on its approximation errors. By expressing their behavior as the number of observations grows, the authors study how closely EP approaches the true posterior distribution.

For the posterior mean, the analysis gives an error convergence rate of O(n^-2), where n is the number of datapoints. The authors describe this as up to an order of magnitude faster than the traditional Gaussian approximation centered at the mode. They also derive asymptotic expansions for moments of orders two through four, extending the comparison beyond the mean alone.

Another result concerns the extra Kullback–Leibler cost of using EP instead of an ideal Gaussian approximation. Together, these expansions support EP’s favorable asymptotic convergence properties. The paper also introduces bounds on moments of log-concave distributions and suggests that its proof approach may apply to related inference methods, without establishing that broader applicability as a certainty.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds Expectation Propagation errors and establishes favorable asymptotic convergence for posterior means and other quantities.

title: Bounding errors of Expectation-Propagation

abstract: We provide finite-sample analysis of a general framework for using k-nearest neighbor statistics to estimate functionals of a nonparametric continuous probability density, including entropies and divergences. Rather than plugging a consistent density estimate (which requires k → ∞ as the sample size n → ∞) into the functional of interest, the estimators we consider fix k and perform a bias correction. This can be more efficient computationally, and, as we show, statistically, leading to faster convergence rates. Our framework unifies several previous estimators, for most of which ours are the first finite sample guarantees.

paragraphs: Many statistical tasks require a quantity derived from a probability density, such as an entropy or divergence, rather than the entire density itself. This paper analyzes a general family of estimators that use nearest-neighbor statistics to estimate such quantities for continuous distributions without specifying a parametric density model.

A conventional route first estimates the density consistently and then inserts that estimate into the desired functional. In the nearest-neighbor setting described here, that route requires the neighbor count k to grow with the sample size. The studied estimators instead keep k fixed and correct for bias, targeting the functional through this different construction.

The authors provide guarantees for finite samples, unifying several earlier estimators within one framework. For most of those estimators, these are the first such guarantees. They also show that keeping k fixed with bias correction can offer computational and statistical benefits, including faster convergence rates. The result clarifies why estimating a density-derived quantity need not follow the same strategy as estimating the full density.
summary.tldr: Finite-sample guarantees show how fixed-k nearest-neighbor statistics with bias correction can efficiently estimate entropies and divergences.

title: Finite-Sample Analysis of Fixed-k Nearest Neighbor Density Functional Estimators

abstract: We learn rich natural sound representations by capitalizing on large amounts of unlabeled sound data collected in the wild. We leverage the natural synchronization between vision and sound to learn an acoustic representation using two-million unlabeled videos. Unlabeled video has the advantage that it can be economically acquired at massive scales, yet contains useful signals about natural sound. We propose a student-teacher training procedure which transfers discriminative visual knowledge from well established visual recognition models into the sound modality using unlabeled video as a bridge. Our sound representation yields significant performance improvements over the state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks for acoustic scene/object classification. Visualizations suggest some high-level semantics automatically emerge in the sound network, even though it is trained without ground truth labels.

The paper uses two million unlabeled videos collected in the wild, treating synchronized visual content as a source of information about accompanying sounds. This makes large amounts of video useful for acoustic learning without requiring ground-truth sound labels for training.

The training procedure follows a student-teacher design. Established visual recognition models act as teachers, transferring their discriminative knowledge into a sound model through the shared videos. The visual and acoustic streams provide the connection between modalities. Consequently, the acoustic representation can benefit from visual recognition knowledge even though its own training examples lack ground-truth annotations.

On standard acoustic scene and object classification benchmarks, the learned representation significantly improves on the state-of-the-art results reported in the paper. Visualizations also suggest that high-level semantic information emerges within the sound network. That visualization claim is suggestive, while the benchmark results provide direct evidence of the representation's usefulness for the evaluated sound-classification tasks.
summary.tldr: SoundNet transfers visual recognition knowledge through unlabeled video to learn sound representations that improve acoustic classification.

title: SoundNet: Learning Sound Representations from Unlabeled Video

abstract: In this paper, we propose a Double Thompson Sampling (D-TS) algorithm for dueling bandit problems. As its name suggests, D-TS selects both the first and the second candidates according to Thompson Sampling. Specifically, D-TS maintains a posterior distribution for the preference matrix, and chooses the pair of arms for comparison according to two sets of samples independently drawn from the posterior distribution. This simple algorithm applies to general Copeland dueling bandits, including Condorcet dueling bandits as its special case. For general Copeland dueling bandits, we show that D-TS achieves $O(K^2 \log T)$ regret. Moreover, using a back substitution argument, we refine the regret to $O(K \log T + K^2 \log \log T)$ in Condorcet dueling bandits and many practical Copeland dueling bandits. In addition, we propose an enhancement of D-TS, referred to as D-TS+, that reduces the regret by carefully breaking ties. Experiments based on both synthetic and real-world data demonstrate that D-TS and D-TS$^+$ significantly improve the overall performance, in terms of regret and robustness.

paragraphs: Dueling bandits learn from comparisons between pairs of options. Double Thompson Sampling, or D-TS, uses posterior sampling to select both members of each comparison. It maintains uncertainty over a preference matrix and draws two independent sets of samples from that posterior to guide the two choices.

The method applies to general Copeland dueling bandits, with Condorcet problems included as a special case. For K options and T rounds, the authors prove regret of order K² log T in the general setting. A refined argument gives order K log T plus K² log log T for Condorcet problems and many practical Copeland problems. The stronger bound therefore applies to a specified subset of settings.

The paper also introduces D-TS+, which uses careful tie-breaking to reduce regret. Experiments with synthetic and real-world data report significant improvements in both regret and robustness for the proposed methods. The appeal is that a simple selection principle—independent posterior sampling for each candidate—supports broad applicability, while the analysis identifies cases where the regret dependence can be substantially sharper.
summary.tldr: Double Thompson Sampling chooses both comparison candidates through independent posterior draws and achieves regret guarantees across general dueling-bandit settings.

title: Double Thompson Sampling for Dueling Bandits

abstract: Stochastic gradient MCMC (SG-MCMC) has played an important role in large-scale Bayesian learning, with well-developed theoretical convergence properties. In such applications of SG-MCMC, it is becoming increasingly popular to employ distributed systems, where stochastic gradients are computed based on some outdated parameters, yielding what are termed stale gradients. While stale gradients could be directly used in SG-MCMC, their impact on convergence properties has not been well studied. In this paper we develop theory to show that while the bias and MSE of an SG-MCMC algorithm depend on the staleness of stochastic gradients, its estimation variance (relative to the expected estimate, based on a prescribed number of samples) is independent of it. In a simple Bayesian distributed system with SG-MCMC, where stale gradients are computed asynchronously by a set of workers, our theory indicates a linear speedup on the decrease of estimation variance w.r.t. the number of workers. Experiments on synthetic data and deep neural networks validate our theory, demonstrating the effectiveness and scalability of SG-MCMC with stale gradients.
