paragraphs: Distributed Bayesian learning often computes gradients on separate workers while model parameters continue changing elsewhere. By the time a gradient is used, it may refer to older parameters. This paper studies how those stale gradients affect stochastic gradient MCMC, focusing on distinctions among bias, mean squared error, and estimation variance.

The authors show that gradient staleness affects bias and mean squared error. However, for a prescribed number of samples, the estimation variance measured around the estimator's own expected value is independent of staleness. That reference point matters: unchanged variance does not mean unchanged total error, because the expected estimate itself can remain biased.

For a simple distributed system with asynchronous workers, the theory indicates a linear speedup in the decrease of estimation variance as the number of workers increases. Experiments on synthetic data and deep neural networks support the analysis and demonstrate scalability. The result offers a precise account of what asynchronous computation can improve while keeping its effect on bias separate from its effect on variability.
summary.tldr: Stale gradients affect SG-MCMC bias and mean squared error, but not its fixed-sample variance around the expected estimate.

title: Stochastic Gradient MCMC with Stale Gradients

abstract: We present an efficient and practical algorithm for the online prediction of discrete-time linear dynamical systems with a symmetric transition matrix. We circumvent the non-convex optimization problem using improper learning: carefully overparameterize the class of LDSs by a polylogarithmic factor, in exchange for convexity of the loss functions. From this arises a polynomial-time algorithm with a near-optimal regret guarantee, with an analogous sample complexity bound for agnostic learning. Our algorithm is based on a novel filtering technique, which may be of independent interest: we convolve the time series with the eigenvectors of a certain Hankel matrix.

From this arises a polynomial-time algorithm with a near-optimal regret guarantee, with an analogous sample complexity bound for agnostic learning. Our algorithm is based on a novel filtering technique, which may be of independent interest: we convolve the time series with the eigenvectors of a certain Hankel matrix.

paragraphs: The paper studies online prediction for discrete-time linear dynamical systems with a symmetric transition matrix. Directly learning a system in its original form leads to a nonconvex optimization problem. The authors instead construct a larger prediction class that makes the learning objective convex, trading a controlled increase in representation size for easier optimization.

This approach uses improper learning: the predictor need not itself belong to the original class of linear dynamical systems. The enlargement is only by a polylogarithmic factor. Its core operation is spectral filtering, which convolves the time series with eigenvectors of a particular Hankel matrix to produce the representation used for prediction.

The resulting algorithm runs in polynomial time and has a near-optimal regret guarantee for online prediction. The paper also derives a corresponding sample complexity bound for agnostic learning. Together, these results show how a carefully chosen expanded representation can bypass nonconvex fitting while retaining strong prediction guarantees for the stated class of systems.
summary.tldr: Spectral filtering enables convex, polynomial-time online prediction with near-optimal regret for linear dynamical systems with symmetric transitions.

title: Learning Linear Dynamical Systems via Spectral Filtering

abstract: Generative Adversarial Nets (GANs) have shown promise in image generation and semi-supervised learning (SSL). However, existing GANs in SSL have two problems: (1) the generator and the discriminator (i.e. the classifier) may not be optimal at the same time; and (2) the generator cannot control the semantics of the generated samples. The problems essentially arise from the two-player formulation, where a single discriminator shares incompatible roles of identifying fake samples and predicting labels and it only estimates the data without considering the labels. To address the problems, we present triple generative adversarial net (Triple-GAN), which consists of three players---a generator, a discriminator and a classifier. The generator and the classifier characterize the conditional distributions between images and labels, and the discriminator solely focuses on identifying fake image-label pairs. We design compatible utilities to ensure that the distributions characterized by the classifier and the generator both converge to the data distribution. Our results on various datasets demonstrate that Triple-GAN as a unified model can simultaneously (1) achieve the state-of-the-art classification results among deep generative models, and (2) disentangle the classes and styles of the input and transfer smoothly in the data space via interpolation in the latent space class-conditionally.

paragraphs: The paper identifies a conflict in GANs used for semi-supervised learning: a single discriminator may be asked both to detect generated examples and to predict class labels. These roles can be incompatible, and a generator that does not model labels cannot directly control the classes of its outputs.

Triple-GAN separates the system into three players: a generator, a classifier, and a discriminator. The generator and classifier model conditional relationships between images and labels, while the discriminator judges image-label pairs. The authors design compatible objectives to ensure that the distributions represented by the generator and classifier both converge to the data distribution.

Experiments across several datasets report state-of-the-art classification performance among deep generative models. The same model also separates class information from style and supports smooth changes through latent-space interpolation while conditioning on a class. The contribution is a unified formulation that supports both classification and controllable generation by giving these functions distinct roles within the adversarial system.
summary.tldr: Triple-GAN separates generation, classification, and discrimination to jointly support semi-supervised classification and class-controlled image generation.

title: Triple Generative Adversarial Nets

abstract: Similarity search is a fundamental problem in computing science with various applications and has attracted significant research attention, especially in large-scale search with high dimensions. Motivated by the evidence in biological science, our work develops a novel approach for similarity search. Fundamentally different from existing methods that typically reduce the dimension of the data to lessen the computational complexity and speed up the search, our approach projects the data into an even higher-dimensional space while ensuring the sparsity of the data in the output space, with the objective of further improving precision and speed. Specifically, our approach has two key steps. Firstly, it computes the optimal sparse lifting for given input samples and increases the dimension of the data while approximately preserving their pairwise similarity. Secondly, it seeks the optimal lifting operator that best maps input samples to the optimal sparse lifting. Computationally, both steps are modeled as optimization problems that can be efficiently and effectively solved by the Frank-Wolfe algorithm. Simple as it is, our approach has reported significantly improved results in empirical evaluations, and exhibited its high potentials in solving practical problems.

paragraphs: Similarity search becomes challenging when datasets are large and each item has many dimensions. Many approaches reduce dimensionality to make searching cheaper. This paper explores a different representation: it raises the dimension while ensuring that the resulting data are sparse. The goal is to improve both search precision and speed through this sparse representation.

The approach has two optimization stages. First, it computes a sparse higher-dimensional representation of the supplied samples while approximately preserving their pairwise similarities. Second, it learns a lifting operator that maps the input samples as closely as possible to that representation. Separating these stages distinguishes the desired representation from the mapping used to produce it.

Both optimization problems can be solved efficiently with the Frank-Wolfe algorithm. The authors report significantly improved results in empirical evaluations and see potential for practical similarity-search applications. The finding supports sparse dimensional expansion as a useful design choice: a representation's number of dimensions is considered together with its sparsity and how well it retains similarities.
summary.tldr: Optimal sparse lifting expands data into a sparse higher-dimensional space that approximately preserves similarities and improves search results empirically.

title: Fast Similarity Search via Optimal Sparse Lifting

abstract: We consider the problem of maximizing a submodular function when given access to its approximate version. Submodular functions are heavily studied in a wide variety of disciplines, since they are used to model many real world phenomena, and are amenable to optimization. However, there are many cases in which the phenomena we observe is only approximately submodular and the approximation guarantees cease to hold. We describe a technique which we call the sampled mean approximation that yields strong guarantees for maximization of submodular functions from approximate surrogates under cardinality and intersection of matroid constraints. In particular, we show tight guarantees for maximization under a cardinality constraint and 1/(1+P) approximation under intersection of P matroids.

paragraphs: This paper considers maximizing a submodular function when only an approximate version of it is available. Submodular structure makes many selection problems amenable to optimization, but guarantees based on exact structure can cease to hold when the observed objective is only approximate. The central question is how to recover meaningful guarantees from an imperfect surrogate.

The authors introduce a technique called sampled mean approximation. It supports maximization from approximate surrogates under two types of feasibility rules: a cardinality constraint, which limits selection size, and an intersection of matroid constraints. This places approximation in the objective alongside restrictions on which subsets may be selected.

The results include tight guarantees for the cardinality-constrained problem and a 1/(1+P) approximation guarantee when feasibility is defined by the intersection of P matroids. The latter explicitly relates the guarantee to the number of matroid constraints. The contribution is a principled way to optimize using approximate access to a submodular objective while retaining guarantees for these stated constraint families.
summary.tldr: Sampled mean approximation provides optimization guarantees when a submodular objective is accessible only through an approximate surrogate.

title: Optimization for Approximate Submodularity

abstract: We present the first accelerated randomized algorithm for solving linear systems in Euclidean spaces. One essential problem of this type is the matrix inversion problem. In particular, our algorithm can be specialized to invert positive definite matrices in such a way that all iterates (approximate solutions) generated by the algorithm are positive definite matrices themselves. This opens the way for many applications in the field of optimization and machine learning. As an application of our general theory, we develop the first accelerated (deterministic and stochastic) quasi-Newton updates. Our updates lead to provably more aggressive approximations of the inverse Hessian, and lead to speed-ups over classical non-accelerated rules in numerical experiments. Experiments with empirical risk minimization show that our rules can accelerate training of machine learning models.

paragraphs: This paper develops an accelerated randomized approach to solving linear systems, with matrix inversion as an important application. Rather than treating inversion only as a calculation performed once, the approach builds successive approximations. For positive definite matrices, the algorithm can preserve positive definiteness at every step, so intermediate approximations retain a structural property useful in optimization.

The authors use this general framework to construct accelerated quasi-Newton updates, including both deterministic and stochastic versions. These updates approximate the inverse Hessian, the matrix describing how an objective's curvature should influence an optimization step. The theoretical contribution is that the new updates produce provably more aggressive inverse-Hessian approximations, connecting accelerated linear algebra with the rules used to train models.

Numerical experiments show speed improvements over classical updates without acceleration. Experiments on empirical risk minimization also show that the proposed rules can accelerate machine-learning training. Together, these findings support the practical value of the theory, while the training improvement remains an experimental finding rather than a guarantee for every model.
summary.tldr: Accelerated randomized linear-system methods yield structure-preserving matrix inversion and quasi-Newton updates that can speed model training.

title: Accelerated Stochastic Matrix Inversion: General Theory and Speeding up BFGS Rules for Faster Second-Order Optimization

abstract: Linear regression in L p-norm is a canonical optimization problem that arises in several applications, including sparse recovery, semi-supervised learning, and signal processing. Generic convex optimization algorithms for solving L p-regression are slow in practice. Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares (IRLS) is an easy to implement family of algorithms for solving these problems that has been studied for over 50 years. However, these algorithms often diverge for p > 3, and since the work of Osborne (1985), it has been an open problem whether there is an IRLS algorithm that converges for p > 3. We propose p-IRLS, the first IRLS algorithm that provably converges geometrically for any p \in [2,\infty). Our algorithm is simple to implement and is guaranteed to find a high accuracy solution in a sub-linear number of iterations. Our experiments demonstrate that it performs even better than our theoretical bounds, beats the standard Matlab/CVX implementation for solving these problems by 10–50x, and is the fastest among available implementations in the high-accuracy regime.

paragraphs: Linear regression with a p-norm objective appears in applications including sparse recovery, semi-supervised learning, and signal processing. Generic convex solvers can be slow for these problems. Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares, or IRLS, offers a simple alternative that repeatedly solves weighted least-squares problems, but existing versions often diverge when p exceeds three.

The paper proposes p-IRLS and proves geometric convergence for every finite p of at least two. Geometric convergence means the error decreases at a multiplicative rate as iterations progress. This resolves the convergence question for p greater than three within the proposed algorithm, while retaining the implementation simplicity that makes IRLS attractive.

The authors also guarantee a high-accuracy solution in a sublinear number of iterations. Their experiments perform better than the theoretical bounds suggest and report speeds 10–50 times those of the standard Matlab/CVX implementation used for comparison. They further report the fastest performance among the available implementations in the high-accuracy regime. These findings combine a broad convergence guarantee over the stated p range with empirical evidence about practical solver speed.
summary.tldr: p-IRLS provides geometric convergence for p-norm regression with finite p ≥ 2 and strong empirical speed in high-accuracy solving.

title: Fast, Provably convergent IRLS Algorithm for p-norm Linear Regression

abstract: We present a novel probabilistic programming framework that couples directly to existing large-scale simulators through a cross-platform probabilistic execution protocol, which allows general-purpose inference engines to record and control random number draws within simulators in a language-agnostic way. The execution of existing simulators as probabilistic programs enables highly interpretable posterior inference in the structured model defined by the simulator code base. We demonstrate the technique in particle physics, on a scientifically accurate simulation of the tau lepton decay, which is a key ingredient in establishing the properties of the Higgs boson. Inference efficiency is achieved via inference compilation where a deep recurrent neural network is trained to parameterize proposal distributions and control the stochastic simulator in a sequential importance sampling scheme, at a fraction of the computational cost of a Markov chain Monte Carlo baseline.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a probabilistic programming framework that connects inference engines directly to existing large-scale simulators. A cross-platform execution protocol lets an engine record and control the simulator's random draws without depending on its implementation language. This makes the simulator's existing code usable as a structured probabilistic model.

Inference then operates within the model expressed by that code, producing interpretable posterior information. To make this computationally efficient, the authors use inference compilation: a deep recurrent neural network learns to parameterize proposal distributions. These proposals guide the simulator's stochastic choices within a sequential importance sampling procedure.

The demonstration uses a scientifically accurate simulation of tau lepton decay, a process relevant to establishing properties of the Higgs boson. In this setting, the approach performs inference at a fraction of the computational cost of a Markov chain Monte Carlo baseline. The contribution combines access to an existing scientific simulator's internal randomness with learned guidance for inference, linking a general-purpose inference system to the detailed structure already encoded in the simulator.
summary.tldr: A language-agnostic protocol and learned proposals enable efficient, interpretable probabilistic inference inside existing scientific simulators.

title: Efficient Probabilistic Inference in the Quest for Physics Beyond the Standard Model

abstract: We propose a novel deep learning method for local self-supervised representation learning that does not require labels nor end-to-end backpropagation but exploits the natural order in data instead. Inspired by the observation that biological neural networks appear to learn without backpropagating a global error signal, we split a deep neural network into a stack of gradient-isolated modules. Each module is trained to maximally preserve the information of its inputs using the InfoNCE bound from Oord et al [2018]. Despite this greedy training, we demonstrate that each module improves upon the output of its predecessor, and that the representations created by the top module yield highly competitive results on downstream classification tasks in the audio and visual domain. The proposal enables optimizing modules asynchronously, allowing large-scale distributed training of very deep neural networks on unlabelled datasets.

Inspired by the observation that biological neural networks appear to learn without backpropagating a global error signal, we split a deep neural network into a stack of gradient-isolated modules. Each module is trained to maximally preserve the information of its inputs using the InfoNCE bound from Oord et al [2018]. Despite this greedy training, we demonstrate that each module improves upon the output of its predecessor, and that the representations created by the top module yield highly competitive results on downstream classification tasks in the audio and visual domain. The proposal enables optimizing modules asynchronously, allowing large-scale distributed training of very deep neural networks on unlabelled datasets.

Motivated by the observation that biological networks appear to learn without a global backpropagated error signal, the authors divide a deep network into modules whose gradients remain isolated.

Each module learns locally to preserve as much information as possible from its inputs, using the InfoNCE bound as its training objective. Training is greedy in the sense that individual modules pursue their own representation objective. This raises a concrete question: whether locally trained stages can still build progressively more useful representations through the depth of the network.

The authors demonstrate that each module improves on its predecessor's output and that the top module produces highly competitive representations for downstream audio and visual classification. Gradient isolation also allows asynchronous optimization of modules, enabling large-scale distributed training of very deep networks on unlabeled datasets. The findings connect local learning objectives with useful final representations and a more flexible training arrangement.
summary.tldr: Locally trained, gradient-isolated modules learn competitive audio and visual representations while enabling asynchronous training without labels or end-to-end backpropagation.

title: Putting An End to End-to-End: Gradient-Isolated Learning of Representations

abstract: Planning methods can solve temporally extended sequential decision making problems by composing simple behaviors. However, planning requires suitable abstractions for the states and transitions, which typically need to be designed by hand. In contrast, reinforcement learning (RL) can acquire behaviors from low-level inputs directly, but struggles with temporally extended tasks. Can we utilize reinforcement learning to automatically form the abstractions needed for planning, thus obtaining the best of both approaches? We show that goal-conditioned policies learned with RL can be incorporated into planning, such that a planner can focus on which states to reach, rather than how those states are reached. However, with complex state observations such as images, not all inputs represent valid states. We therefore also propose using a latent variable model to compactly represent the set of valid states for the planner, such that the policies provide an abstraction of actions, and the latent variable model provides an abstraction of states. We compare our method with planning-based and model-free methods and find that our method significantly outperforms prior work when evaluated on image-based tasks that require non-greedy, multi-staged behavior.

Goal-conditioned policies provide an abstraction of actions: the planner chooses which states to reach, while the policies handle reaching them. For complex observations such as images, arbitrary inputs may not correspond to valid states. The authors therefore add a latent variable model that compactly represents valid states, supplying a complementary abstraction of the planner’s state space.

The method is compared with planning-based and model-free approaches on image-based tasks requiring several stages and choices that are not immediately greedy. It significantly outperforms prior work in those evaluations. The result supports combining learned control behaviors with learned state representations so that planning can organize extended activity using abstractions acquired from low-level inputs.
summary.tldr: Learned goal-conditioned policies and latent state representations give planners useful abstractions for image-based, multistage tasks.

title: Planning with Goal-Conditioned Policies

abstract: Probabilistic forecasting consists in predicting a distribution of possible future outcomes. In this paper, we address this problem for non-stationary time series, which is very challenging yet crucially important. We introduce the STRIPE model for representing structured diversity based on shape and time features, ensuring both probable predictions while being sharp and accurate. STRIPE is agnostic to the forecasting model, and we equip it with a diversification mechanism relying on determinantal point processes (DPP). We introduce two DPP kernels for modelling diverse trajectories in terms of shape and time, which are both differentiable and proved to be positive semi-definite. To have an explicit control on the diversity structure, we also design an iterative sampling mechanism to disentangle shape and time representations in the latent space. Experiments carried out on synthetic datasets show that STRIPE significantly outperforms baseline methods for representing diversity, while maintaining accuracy of the forecasting model. We also highlight the relevance of the iterative sampling scheme and the importance to use different criteria for measuring quality and diversity. Finally, experiments on real datasets illustrate that STRIPE is able to outperform state-of-the-art probabilistic forecasting approaches in the best sample prediction.

paragraphs: Probabilistic forecasting represents multiple possible futures, which is especially challenging for time series whose behavior changes over time. STRIPE organizes this uncertainty around two kinds of variation: the shapes of future trajectories and their timing. It aims to produce diverse forecasts that remain plausible, sharp, and accurate.

The model can work with different forecasting architectures. Its diversification mechanism uses determinantal point processes, with separate kernels describing shape and temporal variation. Both kernels are differentiable and proved positive semi-definite. An iterative sampling procedure separates shape and time representations in the latent space, giving explicit control over how the forecasts differ.

On synthetic datasets, STRIPE improves diversity representation over baseline methods while maintaining forecasting accuracy. The experiments also support the iterative sampling procedure and the use of distinct criteria for quality and diversity. On real datasets, it can outperform state-of-the-art probabilistic methods in best-sample prediction. That result concerns the best forecast among generated samples, preserving the abstract's particular scope of comparison.
summary.tldr: STRIPE structures forecast diversity around trajectory shape and timing while maintaining accuracy and improving reported best-sample predictions.

title: Probabilistic Time Series Forecasting with Shape and Temporal Diversity

abstract: Bayesian neural networks are enjoying a renaissance driven in part by recent advances in variational inference (VI). The most common form of VI employs a fully factorized or mean-field distribution, but this is known to suffer from several pathologies, especially as we expect posterior distributions with highly correlated parameters. Current algorithms that capture these correlations with a Gaussian approximating family are difficult to scale to large models due to computational costs and high variance of gradient updates. By using a new form of the reparametrization trick, we derive a computationally efficient algorithm for performing VI with a Gaussian family with a low-rank plus diagonal covariance structure. We scale to deep feed-forward and convolutional architectures. We find that adding low-rank terms to parametrized diagonal covariance does not improve predictive performance except on small networks, but low-rank terms added to a constant diagonal covariance improves performance on small and large-scale network architectures.

paragraphs: Bayesian neural networks represent uncertainty over their parameters, but approximating that uncertainty can be expensive. A common simplification treats parameters independently, even though their posterior values may be strongly related. This paper develops a more efficient way to include correlations through a Gaussian approximation with a low-rank-plus-diagonal covariance.

The diagonal component represents individual parameter variation, while the low-rank component represents shared variation across parameters. A new form of the reparameterization trick makes variational inference with this structure computationally practical. The authors scale the resulting algorithm to both deep feed-forward networks and convolutional architectures, addressing the cost and gradient-update difficulties associated with correlated Gaussian approximations.

The predictive findings depend on how the diagonal component is specified. Adding low-rank terms to a parameterized diagonal covariance improves predictions only on small networks in the reported results. Adding them to a constant diagonal covariance improves performance on both small and large architectures. This distinction shows that the benefit of modeling correlations depends on the surrounding covariance design, rather than following automatically from a richer approximation.
summary.tldr: An efficient correlated Gaussian approximation scales Bayesian neural-network inference, with predictive gains depending on how its diagonal covariance is defined.

title: Efficient Low Rank Gaussian Variational Inference for Neural Networks

abstract: Despite its promise, reinforcement learning’s real-world adoption has been hampered by the need for costly exploration to learn a good policy. Imitation learning (IL) mitigates this shortcoming by using an oracle policy during training as a bootstrap to accelerate the learning process. However, in many practical situations, the learner has access to multiple suboptimal oracles, which may provide conﬂicting advice in a state. The existing IL literature provides a limited treatment of such scenarios. Whereas in the single-oracle case, the return of the oracle’s policy provides an obvious benchmark for the learner to compete against, neither such a benchmark nor principled ways of outperforming it are known for the multi-oracle setting. In this paper, we propose the state-wise maximum of the oracle policies’ values as a natural baseline to resolve conﬂicting advice from multiple oracles. Using a reduction of policy optimization to online learning, we introduce a novel IL algorithm MAMBA, which can provably learn a policy competitive with this benchmark. In particular, MAMBA optimizes policies by using a gradient estimator in the style of generalized advantage estimation (GAE). Our theoretical analysis shows that this design makes MAMBA robust and enables it to outperform the oracle policies by a larger margin than the IL state of the art, even in the single-oracle case. In an evaluation against standard policy gradient with GAE and AggreVaTe(D), we showcase MAMBA’s ability to leverage demonstrations both from a single and from multiple weak oracles, and signiﬁcantly speed up policy optimization.

This paper proposes comparing the learner against the highest oracle value at each state, giving a benchmark that can draw on different oracles’ strengths.

They demonstrate faster policy optimization using demonstrations from either one oracle or multiple weak oracles, supporting the value of learning beyond simple imitation.
summary.tldr: MAMBA learns from imperfect oracles using their state-wise maximum value as a benchmark, with theoretical guarantees and faster policy optimization in experiments.

title: Policy Improvement via Imitation of Multiple Oracles

abstract: We study the problem of {\em list-decodable mean estimation} for bounded covariance distributions. Specifically, we are given a set $T$ of points in $\R^d$ with the promise that an unknown $\alpha$-fraction of points in $T$, where $0< \alpha < 1/2$, are drawn from an unknown mean and bounded covariance distribution $D$, and no assumptions are made on the remaining points. The goal is to output a small list of hypothesis vectors such that at least one of them is close to the mean of $D$. We give the first practically viable estimator for this problem. In more detail, our algorithm is sample and computationally efficient, and achieves information-theoretically near-optimal error. While the only prior algorithm for this setting inherently relied on the ellipsoid method, our algorithm is iterative and only uses spectral techniques. Our main technical innovation is the design of a soft outlier removal procedure for high-dimensional heavy-tailed datasets with a majority of outliers.

paragraphs: This paper studies estimating a distribution's mean when fewer than half the observed points come from that distribution. The remaining points are unrestricted, so outliers can form a majority. The reliable fraction is unknown within the dataset, and its underlying distribution is assumed to have bounded covariance.

The objective is to produce a small list of candidate means with at least one candidate close to the desired mean. The authors develop an iterative algorithm based only on spectral techniques. Its central innovation is a soft outlier removal procedure designed for high-dimensional, heavy-tailed data even when most observations are outliers.

The estimator is efficient in both sample use and computation, and its error is close to the information-theoretic optimum. The authors describe it as the first practically viable estimator for this setting, replacing an earlier approach that inherently relied on the ellipsoid method. The contribution makes a particularly demanding form of robust estimation more computationally accessible while retaining strong accuracy guarantees.
summary.tldr: An iterative spectral estimator produces a short list containing an accurate mean estimate even when most data points are unrestricted outliers.

title: List-Decodable Mean Estimation via Iterative Multi-Filtering

abstract: We consider the question of learning $Q$-function in a sample efficient manner for reinforcement learning with continuous state and action spaces under a generative model. If $Q$-function is Lipschitz continuous, then the minimal sample complexity for estimating $\epsilon$-optimal $Q$-function is known to scale as $\Omega(\frac{1}{\epsilon^{d_1+d_2+2}})$ per classical non-parametric learning theory, where $d_1$ and $d_2$ denote the dimensions of the state and action spaces respectively. The $Q$-function, when viewed as a kernel, induces a Hilbert-Schmidt operator and hence possesses square-summable spectrum. This motivates us to consider a parametric class of $Q$-functions parameterized by its "rank" $r$, which contains all Lipschitz $Q$-functions as $r\to\infty$. As our key contribution, we develop a simple, iterative learning algorithm that finds $\epsilon$-optimal $Q$-function with sample complexity of $\widetilde{O}(\frac{1}{\epsilon^{\max(d_1, d_2)+2}})$ when the optimal $Q$-function has low rank $r$ and the discounting factor $\gamma$ is below a certain threshold. Thus, this provides an exponential improvement in sample complexity. To enable our result, we develop a novel Matrix Estimation algorithm that faithfully estimates an unknown low-rank matrix in the $\ell_\infty$ sense even in the presence of arbitrary bounded noise, which might be of interest in its own right. Empirical results on several stochastic control tasks confirm the efficacy of our "low-rank" algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper studies how many samples are needed to learn a Q-function over continuous states and actions when a generative model is available. With only Lipschitz continuity, the known sample-complexity scaling depends on the sum of state and action dimensions. The authors investigate whether low-rank structure can reduce that dimensional burden.

Viewing the Q-function as a kernel motivates a rank-parameterized function class that includes all Lipschitz Q-functions as rank grows without bound. For low-rank optimal Q-functions, and when the discount factor is below a specified threshold, their iterative algorithm changes the accuracy exponent from the sum of the two dimensions plus two to their maximum plus two, up to logarithmic factors.

The guarantee depends on those low-rank and discounting conditions. A key ingredient is a new matrix-estimation method that controls the largest entrywise error despite arbitrary bounded noise, enabling the reinforcement-learning result. Experiments on several stochastic control tasks support the algorithms’ effectiveness. The paper thus connects structural assumptions about value functions to substantial reductions in the samples required for learning.
summary.tldr: Low-rank Q-functions enable substantially better sample-complexity scaling under a generative model and a condition on the discount factor.

title: Sample Efficient Reinforcement Learning via Low-Rank Matrix Estimation

abstract: Program synthesis techniques construct or infer programs from user-provided specifications, such as input-output examples. Yet most specifications, especially those given by end-users, leave the synthesis problem radically ill-posed, because many programs may simultaneously satisfy the specification. Prior work resolves this ambiguity by using various inductive biases, such as a preference for simpler programs. This work introduces a new inductive bias derived by modeling the program synthesis task as rational communication, drawing insights from recursive reasoning models of pragmatics. Given a specification, we score a candidate program both on its consistency with the specification, and also whether a rational speaker would chose this particular specification to communicate that program. We develop efficient algorithms for such an approach when learning from input-output examples, and build a pragmatic program synthesizer over a simple grid-like layout domain. A user study finds that end-user participants communicate more effectively with the pragmatic program synthesizer over a non-pragmatic one.

paragraphs: A few input-output examples often fit many possible programs, leaving a program synthesizer uncertain about what the user intended. A preference for simpler programs can resolve some ambiguity, but it does not use the fact that a person deliberately selected those examples. This paper treats that selection as part of a communication process.

The proposed approach evaluates a candidate program in two ways: whether it satisfies the supplied examples, and whether a rational person trying to communicate that program would have chosen those examples. Recursive reasoning about the speaker's intent therefore becomes an inductive bias. The examples provide evidence through both their contents and their suitability as a message.

The authors develop efficient algorithms for learning from input-output examples and implement a synthesizer in a simple grid-like layout domain. A user study finds that participants communicate more effectively with this pragmatic system than with a non-pragmatic counterpart. The result supports using a model of communication to interpret underspecified program requests in the studied domain.
summary.tldr: A program synthesizer resolves ambiguity by considering why a rational user would choose particular examples to communicate a program.

title: Program Synthesis with Pragmatic Communication

abstract: Multiple object tracking and segmentation requires detecting, tracking, and segmenting objects belonging to a set of given classes. Most approaches only exploit the temporal dimension to address the association problem, while relying on single frame predictions for the segmentation mask itself. We propose Prototypical Cross-Attention Network (PCAN), capable of leveraging rich spatio-temporal information for online multiple object tracking and segmentation. PCAN first distills a space-time memory into a set of prototypes and then employs cross-attention to retrieve rich information from the past frames. To segment each object, PCAN adopts a prototypical appearance module to learn a set of contrastive foreground and background prototypes, which are then propagated over time. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PCAN outperforms current video instance tracking and segmentation competition winners on both Youtube-VIS and BDD100K datasets, and shows efficacy to both one-stage and two-stage segmentation frameworks. Code and video resources are available at http://vis.xyz/pub/pcan.

paragraphs: Multiple-object tracking and segmentation combines detecting objects, maintaining their identities over time, and marking their pixels. Many approaches use temporal information to associate objects across frames while predicting each segmentation mask from a single frame. PCAN brings information from earlier frames into the segmentation process as well as the broader online tracking task.

The network compresses a space-time memory into a set of prototypes and uses cross-attention to retrieve information from past frames. For individual objects, an appearance module learns contrasting foreground and background prototypes. These representations are propagated over time, allowing the model to carry forward information about both the object and its surroundings.

The authors report that PCAN outperforms the compared video tracking and segmentation competition winners on Youtube-VIS and BDD100K. They also demonstrate effectiveness with both one-stage and two-stage segmentation frameworks. These findings support prototype-based temporal memory as a useful way to improve object masks and tracking together, with evidence across the two evaluated framework types.
summary.tldr: PCAN uses prototype-based temporal memory and cross-attention to improve online multiple-object tracking and segmentation.

title: Prototypical Cross-Attention Networks for Multiple Object Tracking and Segmentation

abstract: While attention is all you need may be proving true, we do not know why: attention-based transformer models such as BERT are superior but how information flows from input tokens to output predictions are unclear. We introduce influence patterns, abstractions of sets of paths through a transformer model. Patterns quantify and localize the flow of information to paths passing through a sequence of model nodes. Experimentally, we find that significant portion of information flow in BERT goes through skip connections instead of attention heads. We further show that consistency of patterns across instances is an indicator of BERT’s performance. Finally, we demonstrate that patterns account for far more model performance than previous attention-based and layer-based methods.

paragraphs: BERT's predictions emerge from information moving through many internal components, making it difficult to explain how particular input tokens affect an output. This paper introduces influence patterns to describe that movement. Each pattern summarizes a collection of paths through the transformer, locating and quantifying information flow through a specified sequence of model nodes.

This path-based view lets the analysis capture routes that are not represented by attention heads alone. In experiments, the authors find that a significant share of information flow passes through skip connections rather than attention heads. The finding matters for explanations because concentrating only on attention can leave out routes that the measured information flow actually uses.

The authors also find that patterns recurring consistently across examples indicate BERT's performance. Their patterns account for substantially more model performance than the attention-based and layer-based explanation methods they compare against. These results support examining connected routes through the network as an explanatory unit, while the evidence presented remains experimental rather than a universal characterization of all transformer behavior.
summary.tldr: Influence patterns trace information routes through BERT, revealing substantial flow through skip connections and stronger explanatory coverage in experiments.

title: Influence Patterns for Explaining Information Flow in BERT

abstract: UMAP has supplanted $t$-SNE as state-of-the-art for visualizing high-dimensional datasets in many disciplines, but the reason for its success is not well understood. In this work, we investigate UMAP's sampling based optimization scheme in detail. We derive UMAP's true loss function in closed form and find that it differs from the published one in a dataset size dependent way. As a consequence, we show that UMAP does not aim to reproduce its theoretically motivated high-dimensional UMAP similarities. Instead, it tries to reproduce similarities that only encode the $k$ nearest neighbor graph, thereby challenging the previous understanding of UMAP's effectiveness. Alternatively, we consider the implicit balancing of attraction and repulsion due to the negative sampling to be key to UMAP's success. We corroborate our theoretical findings on toy and single cell RNA sequencing data.

paragraphs: UMAP is widely used to visualize high-dimensional data, but its effective optimization behavior is not fully explained by its published objective. This paper analyzes the sampling procedure used during optimization and derives the loss function that the procedure actually implements. The resulting expression differs from the published loss in a way that depends on dataset size.

That difference changes the interpretation of what UMAP seeks to preserve. The authors show that it does not aim to reproduce the theoretically motivated high-dimensional similarities usually associated with the method. Instead, its effective targets encode the nearest-neighbor graph. The analysis therefore shifts attention from those original similarity values to the neighborhood relationships represented by that graph.

The authors suggest that negative sampling's implicit balance between attraction and repulsion is key to UMAP's success. They support their theoretical findings with experiments on toy data and single-cell RNA sequencing data. The work offers a revised explanation of the algorithm's behavior, while presenting the importance of that balance as their interpretation of its effectiveness.
summary.tldr: The paper derives UMAP's effective loss and shows that its sampling procedure changes which high-dimensional relationships it aims to preserve.

title: On UMAP's True Loss Function

abstract: Conducting efficient performance estimations of neural architectures is a major challenge in neural architecture search (NAS). To reduce the architecture training costs in NAS, one-shot estimators (OSEs) amortize the architecture training costs by sharing the parameters of one supernet between all architectures. Recently, zero-shot estimators (ZSEs) that involve no training are proposed to further reduce the architecture evaluation cost. Despite the high efficiency of these estimators, the quality of such estimations has not been thoroughly studied. In this paper, we conduct an extensive and organized assessment of OSEs and ZSEs on five NAS benchmarks: NAS-Bench-101/201/301, and NDS ResNet/ResNeXt-A. Specifically, we employ a set of NAS-oriented criteria to study the behavior of OSEs and ZSEs, and reveal their biases and variances. After analyzing how and why the OSE estimations are unsatisfying, we explore how to mitigate the correlation gap of OSEs from three perspectives. Through our analysis, we give out suggestions for future application and development of efficient architecture performance estimators. Furthermore, the analysis framework proposed in our work could be utilized in future research to give a more comprehensive understanding of newly designed architecture performance estimators. The code is available at https://github.com/walkerning/aw_nas.
originalAbstract: Conducting efficient performance estimations of neural architectures is a major challenge in neural architecture search (NAS). To reduce the architecture training costs in NAS, one-shot estimators (OSEs) amortize the architecture training costs by sharing the parameters of one supernet between all architectures. Recently, zero-shot estimators (ZSEs) that involve no training are proposed to further reduce the architecture evaluation cost. Despite the high efficiency of these estimators, the quality of such estimations has not been thoroughly studied. In this paper, we conduct an extensive and organized assessment of OSEs and ZSEs on five NAS benchmarks: NAS-Bench-101/201/301, and NDS ResNet/ResNeXt-A. Specifically, we employ a set of NAS-oriented criteria to study the behavior of OSEs and ZSEs, and reveal their biases and variances. After analyzing how and why the OSE estimations are unsatisfying, we explore how to mitigate the correlation gap of OSEs from three perspectives. Through our analysis, we give out suggestions for future application and development of efficient architecture performance estimators. Furthermore, the analysis framework proposed in our work could be utilized in future research to give a more comprehensive understanding of newly designed architecture performance estimators. The code is available at https://github.com/walkerning/aw_nas.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search needs inexpensive ways to estimate how candidate networks will perform. One-shot estimators reduce training costs by sharing a supernet's parameters across candidates, while zero-shot estimators avoid training altogether. This paper asks how reliable these efficient estimates are, beyond their clear computational advantages.

The authors systematically assess both estimator families on five architecture-search benchmarks: NAS-Bench-101, NAS-Bench-201, NAS-Bench-301, and the NDS ResNet and ResNeXt-A benchmarks. They use criteria tailored to architecture search to examine estimator behavior, including biases and variances. This makes the evaluation about the quality of information supplied to search, rather than efficiency alone.

For one-shot estimators, the analysis investigates why estimates are unsatisfactory and explores three perspectives for reducing the correlation gap. The paper then offers suggestions for applying and developing performance estimators. Its broader contribution is an assessment framework that future work can use to examine new estimators more comprehensively, helping distinguish computational savings from the reliability of the resulting architecture evaluations.
summary.tldr: A systematic benchmark study examines the biases, variances, and reliability of one-shot and zero-shot neural architecture performance estimators.

title: Evaluating Efficient Performance Estimators of Neural Architectures

abstract: Due to the high communication cost in distributed and federated learning, methods relying on compressed communication are becoming increasingly popular. Besides, the best theoretically and practically performing gradient-type methods invariably rely on some form of acceleration/momentum to reduce the number of communications (faster convergence), e.g., Nesterov's accelerated gradient descent [31, 32] and Adam [14]. In order to combine the benefits of communication compression and convergence acceleration, we propose a \emph{compressed and accelerated} gradient method based on ANITA [20] for distributed optimization, which we call CANITA. Our CANITA achieves the \emph{first accelerated rate} $O\bigg(\sqrt{\Big(1+\sqrt{\frac{\omega^3}{n}}\Big)\frac{L}{\epsilon}} + \omega\big(\frac{1}{\epsilon}\big)^{\frac{1}{3}}\bigg)$, which improves upon the state-of-the-art non-accelerated rate $O\left((1+\frac{\omega}{n})\frac{L}{\epsilon} + \frac{\omega^2+\omega}{\omega+n}\frac{1}{\epsilon}\right)$ of DIANA [12] for distributed general convex problems, where $\epsilon$ is the target error, $L$ is the smooth parameter of the objective, $n$ is the number of machines/devices, and $\omega$ is the compression parameter (larger $\omega$ means more compression can be applied, and no compression implies $\omega=0$). Our results show that as long as the number of devices $n$ is large (often true in distributed/federated learning), or the compression $\omega$ is not very high, CANITA achieves the faster convergence rate $O\Big(\sqrt{\frac{L}{\epsilon}}\Big)$, i.e., the number of communication rounds is $O\Big(\sqrt{\frac{L}{\epsilon}}\Big)$ (vs. $O\big(\frac{L}{\epsilon}\big)$ achieved by previous works). As a result, CANITA enjoys the advantages of both compression (compressed communication in each round) and acceleration (much fewer communication rounds).

paragraphs: Distributed learning can spend substantial effort communicating between devices. Compression reduces the information sent during each exchange, while accelerated optimization reduces how many exchanges are needed. This paper develops CANITA to combine these two benefits for distributed optimization of general convex objectives.

CANITA builds on the ANITA gradient method and incorporates compressed communication. Its convergence guarantee accounts for the objective's smoothness, the desired error, the number of devices, and the compression parameter. This matters because reducing communication per round is only part of the problem: the overall benefit also depends on how compression affects the number of rounds required.

The authors establish an accelerated rate that improves on the stated nonaccelerated DIANA rate. When there are sufficiently many devices or compression is not too high, CANITA achieves a communication-round dependence proportional to the square root of smoothness divided by target error. Earlier bounds scale directly with that ratio. The result shows that compressed messages and fewer rounds can coexist under the stated conditions.
summary.tldr: CANITA combines communication compression with provable acceleration for distributed convex optimization under conditions on device count and compression.

title: CANITA: Faster Rates for Distributed Convex Optimization with Communication Compression

abstract: Recently, there has been much interest in studying the convergence rates of without-replacement SGD, and proving that it is faster than with-replacement SGD in the worst case. However, known lower bounds ignore the problem's geometry, including its condition number, whereas the upper bounds explicitly depend on it. Perhaps surprisingly, we prove that when the condition number is taken into account, without-replacement SGD \emph{does not} significantly improve on with-replacement SGD in terms of worst-case bounds, unless the number of epochs (passes over the data) is larger than the condition number. Since many problems in machine learning and other areas are both ill-conditioned and involve large datasets, this indicates that without-replacement does not necessarily improve over with-replacement sampling for realistic iteration budgets. We show this by providing new lower and upper bounds which are tight (up to log factors), for quadratic problems with commuting quadratic terms, precisely quantifying the dependence on the problem parameters.

paragraphs: The paper compares stochastic gradient descent that samples with replacement against sampling without replacement, as in random shuffling. Previous convergence analyses suggested advantages for the latter, but their lower bounds did not account for the problem's condition number even though upper bounds did. The authors examine how including this measure of problem geometry changes the comparison.

They prove that without-replacement sampling does not significantly improve worst-case bounds unless the number of epochs exceeds the condition number. This is a necessary threshold for the stated worst-case improvement, rather than a claim that shuffling becomes better immediately afterward. It also concerns worst-case guarantees, rather than the outcome of every individual training run.

The analysis provides lower and upper bounds that match up to logarithmic factors for quadratic problems whose quadratic terms commute. Because ill-conditioned problems can have large condition numbers, exceeding the threshold may require many data passes. The result explains why a theoretical sampling advantage need not translate into an improvement within realistic iteration budgets.
summary.tldr: For the studied quadratic problems, random shuffling needs more epochs than the condition number before significant worst-case improvements over replacement sampling are possible.

title: Random Shuffling Beats SGD Only After Many Epochs on Ill-Conditioned Problems

abstract: Bayesian inference in the space of functions has been an important topic for Bayesian modeling in the past. In this paper, we propose a new solution to this problem called Functional Variational Inference (FVI). In FVI, we minimize a divergence in function space between the variational distribution and the posterior process. This is done by using as functional variational family a new class of flexible distributions called Stochastic Process Generators (SPGs), which are cleverly designed so that the functional ELBO can be estimated efficiently using analytic solutions and mini-batch sampling. FVI can be applied to stochastic process priors when random function samples from those priors are available. Our experiments show that FVI consistently outperforms weight-space and function space VI methods on several tasks, which validates the effectiveness of our approach.

paragraphs: This paper approaches Bayesian inference by approximating a distribution over functions. Its Functional Variational Inference method minimizes a divergence between a variational distribution and the posterior process directly in function space. The object being approximated is therefore the posterior distribution of possible functions, which is the central focus of the proposed inference procedure.

The authors introduce Stochastic Process Generators as a flexible family of distributions for this approximation. Their design makes the functional evidence lower bound efficiently estimable using analytic solutions together with mini-batch sampling. This connection between a flexible variational family and a tractable training objective is what makes the proposed function-space approach computationally usable.

FVI can be applied to stochastic-process priors when random function samples from those priors are available. That sampling requirement specifies the stated scope of applicability. Across several experimental tasks, the authors report consistently better performance than the compared weight-space and function-space variational inference methods. The results support the effectiveness of the generator-based approximation in the settings studied.
summary.tldr: Stochastic Process Generators enable efficient variational inference directly over functions when prior function samples are available.

title: Functional Variational Inference based on Stochastic Process Generators

abstract: In causal discovery, linear non-Gaussian acyclic models (LiNGAMs) have been studied extensively. While the causally sufficient case is well understood, in many real problems the observed variables are not causally related. Rather, they are generated by latent variables, such as confounders and mediators, which may themselves be causally related. Existing results on the identification of the causal structure among the latent variables often require very strong graphical assumptions. In this paper, we consider partially observed linear models with either non-Gaussian or heterogeneous errors. In that case we give two graphical conditions which are necessary for identification of the causal structure. These conditions are closely related to sparsity of the causal edges. Together with one additional condition on the coefficients, which holds generically for any graph, the two graphical conditions are also sufficient for identifiability. These new conditions can be satisfied even when there is a large number of latent variables. We demonstrate the validity of our results on synthetic data.

paragraphs: Observed variables can arise from hidden causes that also influence one another. Recovering the causal structure among those latent variables is harder than working in a setting without hidden causes. This paper studies partially observed linear causal models whose errors are either non-Gaussian or heterogeneous, seeking conditions under which their causal structure is identifiable.

The authors establish two graphical conditions that are necessary for identification. Both are closely connected to sparsity in the causal edges. When combined with an additional condition on the numerical coefficients, the same graphical conditions become sufficient. The coefficient condition holds generically for any graph, so the result carefully separates requirements on graph structure from requirements on parameter values.

These conditions can hold even with many latent variables, extending the range of hidden-variable structures covered by identification results. Synthetic-data experiments support the theory. The main finding is a characterization of when recovery is possible in the studied model class, with sufficiency depending on the graphical and coefficient conditions together.
summary.tldr: The paper gives necessary graphical conditions that, with a generic coefficient condition, suffice to identify partially observed linear causal structures.

title: Identification of Partially Observed Linear Causal Models: Graphical Conditions for the Non-Gaussian and Heterogeneous Cases

abstract: The curse of dimensionality is a widely known issue in reinforcement learning (RL). In the tabular setting where the state space $\mathcal{S}$ and the action space $\mathcal{A}$ are both finite, to obtain a near optimal policy with sampling access to a generative model, the minimax optimal sample complexity scales linearly with $|\mathcal{S}|\times|\mathcal{A}|$, which can be prohibitively large when $\mathcal{S}$ or $\mathcal{A}$ is large. This paper considers a Markov decision process (MDP) that admits a set of state-action features, which can linearly express (or approximate) its probability transition kernel. We show that a model-based approach (resp.$~$Q-learning) provably learns an $\varepsilon$-optimal policy (resp.$~$Q-function) with high probability as soon as the sample size exceeds the order of $\frac{K}{(1-\gamma)^{3}\varepsilon^{2}}$ (resp.$~$$\frac{K}{(1-\gamma)^{4}\varepsilon^{2}}$), up to some logarithmic factor. Here $K$ is the feature dimension and $\gamma\in(0,1)$ is the discount factor of the MDP. Both sample complexity bounds are provably tight, and our result for the model-based approach matches the minimax lower bound. Our results show that for arbitrarily large-scale MDP, both the model-based approach and Q-learning are sample-efficient when $K$ is relatively small, and hence the title of this paper.

paragraphs: Learning a separate description for every state-action pair can require too many samples when a decision process is large. This paper studies processes whose transition probabilities can be represented or approximated linearly using state-action features. Sampling access to a generative model provides the interaction data, and the feature dimension K becomes central to the sample requirements.

The model-based approach learns an epsilon-optimal policy with high probability using samples on the order of K divided by (1 minus gamma) cubed and epsilon squared, ignoring logarithmic factors. Q-learning obtains an epsilon-optimal Q-function with a corresponding fourth-power dependence on 1 minus gamma. Here gamma is the discount factor.

The paper establishes tight bounds for both approaches, with the model-based result matching the minimax lower bound. The different discount-factor dependencies distinguish their guarantees even though both scale with feature dimension. These findings explain how very large decision processes can remain sample-efficient when their transitions have the stated linear structure and K is relatively small.
summary.tldr: With generative-model access, linear transition features yield tight sample-complexity guarantees governed by feature dimension rather than state-action count.

title: Sample-Efficient Reinforcement Learning for Linearly-Parameterized MDPs with a Generative Model

abstract: A recent line of research focuses on the study of stochastic multi-armed bandits (MAB), in the case where temporal correlations of specific structure are imposed between the player's actions and the reward distributions of the arms. These correlations lead to (sub-)optimal solutions that exhibit interesting dynamical patterns -- a phenomenon that yields new challenges both from an algorithmic as well as a learning perspective. In this work, we extend the above direction to a combinatorial semi-bandit setting and study a variant of stochastic MAB, where arms are subject to matroid constraints and each arm becomes unavailable (blocked) for a fixed number of rounds after each play. A natural common generalization of the state-of-the-art for blocking bandits, and that for matroid bandits, only guarantees a $\frac{1}{2}$-approximation for general matroids. In this paper we develop the novel technique of correlated (interleaved) scheduling, which allows us to obtain a polynomial-time $(1 - \frac{1}{e})$-approximation algorithm (asymptotically and in expectation) for any matroid. Along the way, we discover an interesting connection to a variant of Submodular Welfare Maximization, for which we provide (asymptotically) matching upper and lower approximability bounds. In the case where the mean arm rewards are unknown, our technique naturally decouples the scheduling from the learning problem, and thus allows to control the $(1-\frac{1}{e})$-approximate regret of a UCB-based adaptation of our online algorithm.

The contribution is a scheduling technique with both approximation and learning guarantees, while the stated asymptotic and expectation qualifications remain essential to interpreting its performance.
summary.tldr: Correlated scheduling improves approximation guarantees for matroid-constrained blocking bandits and separates scheduling from reward learning.

title: Recurrent Submodular Welfare and Matroid Blocking Semi-Bandits

abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) is a powerful approach for optimizing black-box, expensive-to-evaluate functions. To enable a flexible trade-off between the cost and accuracy, many applications allow the function to be evaluated at different fidelities. In order to reduce the optimization cost while maximizing the benefit-cost ratio, in this paper we propose Batch Multi-fidelity Bayesian Optimization with Deep Auto-Regressive Networks (BMBO-DARN). We use a set of Bayesian neural networks to construct a fully auto-regressive model, which is expressive enough to capture strong yet complex relationships across all the fidelities, so as to improve the surrogate learning and optimization performance. Furthermore, to enhance the quality and diversity of queries, we develop a simple yet efficient batch querying method, without any combinatorial search over the fidelities. We propose a batch acquisition function based on Max-value Entropy Search (MES) principle, which penalizes highly correlated queries and encourages diversity. We use posterior samples and moment matching to fulfill efficient computation of the acquisition function, and conduct alternating optimization over every fidelity-input pair, which guarantees an improvement at each step. We demonstrate the advantage of our approach on four real-world hyperparameter optimization applications.

paragraphs: Optimizing an expensive black-box function often means deciding both where to evaluate it and how accurately to do so. Cheaper, lower-fidelity evaluations can provide useful information, but their relationship to accurate evaluations may be complicated. BMBO-DARN addresses this setting while choosing batches of evaluations, aiming to obtain more optimization benefit for the evaluation cost.

The method builds a surrogate from Bayesian neural networks arranged in a fully autoregressive structure. This lets the model represent complex dependencies across fidelity levels. Its batch acquisition function follows the Max-value Entropy Search principle and penalizes highly correlated queries, encouraging a batch to contain complementary information instead of repeatedly asking similar questions.

To make query selection practical, the authors use posterior samples and moment matching to compute the acquisition function efficiently. They alternate optimization over fidelity–input pairs without a combinatorial search over fidelity assignments, guaranteeing improvement at each optimization step. Experiments on four real-world hyperparameter optimization applications demonstrate advantages for the approach, supporting the combination of expressive fidelity modeling and diversity-aware batch selection.
summary.tldr: BMBO-DARN combines neural models of relationships across evaluation fidelities with diverse batch selection for cost-conscious Bayesian optimization.

title: Batch Multi-Fidelity Bayesian Optimization with Deep Auto-Regressive Networks

abstract: Previous works have proved that recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are Turing-complete. However, in the proofs, the RNNs allow for neurons with unbounded precision, which is neither practical in implementation nor biologically plausible. To remove this assumption, we propose a dynamically growing memory module made of neurons of fixed precision. The memory module dynamically recruits new neurons when more memories are needed, and releases them when memories become irrelevant. We prove that a 54-neuron bounded-precision RNN with growing memory modules can simulate a Universal Turing Machine, with time complexity linear in the simulated machine's time and independent of the memory size. The result is extendable to various other stack-augmented RNNs. Furthermore, we analyze the Turing completeness of both unbounded-precision and bounded-precision RNNs, revisiting and extending the theoretical foundations of RNNs.

paragraphs: Earlier proofs of recurrent neural networks' Turing completeness allowed neurons to store values with unbounded precision. This paper removes that precision assumption by giving a bounded-precision network a dynamically growing memory module. Its focus is the computational capacity of the resulting system rather than a training procedure for discovering programs.

The memory consists of fixed-precision neurons. It recruits neurons when more storage is needed and releases them when stored information becomes irrelevant. The construction therefore accommodates increasing memory requirements through growth in the memory module. The distinction matters: bounded precision does not mean the entire computing system has a fixed amount of memory.

The authors prove that a 54-neuron bounded-precision RNN equipped with growing memory modules can simulate a Universal Turing Machine. Simulation time is linear in the simulated machine's running time and independent of memory size. They extend the result to other stack-augmented RNNs and revisit both bounded- and unbounded-precision cases. The result strengthens the theoretical foundation for recurrent computation with finite-precision components and expandable storage.
summary.tldr: A 54-neuron bounded-precision RNN with dynamically growing memory can simulate a Universal Turing Machine with linear-time overhead.

title: Turing Completeness of Bounded-Precision Recurrent Neural Networks

abstract: Computational methods that operate on three-dimensional (3D) molecular structure have the potential to solve important problems in biology and chemistry. Deep neural networks have gained significant attention, but their widespread adoption in the biomolecular domain has been limited by a lack of either systematic performance benchmarks or a unified toolkit for interacting with 3D molecular data. To address this, we present ATOM3D, a collection of both novel and existing benchmark datasets spanning several key classes of biomolecules. We implement several types of 3D molecular learning methods for each of these tasks and show that they consistently improve performance relative to methods based on one- and two-dimensional representations. The choice of architecture proves to be important for performance, with 3D convolutional networks excelling at tasks involving complex geometries, graph networks performing well on systems requiring detailed positional information, and the more recently developed equivariant networks showing significant promise. Our results indicate that many molecular problems stand to gain from 3D molecular learning, and that there is potential for substantial further improvement on many tasks. To lower the barrier to entry and facilitate further developments in the field, we also provide a comprehensive suite of tools for dataset processing, model training, and evaluation in our open-source atom3d Python package. All datasets are available for download from www.atom3d.ai.

The paper assembles new and existing datasets covering several major classes of biomolecules, creating a shared basis for evaluating methods across different molecular problems.

summary.tldr: ATOM3D benchmarks molecular learning and finds consistent benefits from three-dimensional representations, with architecture choice affecting performance across tasks.

title: ATOM3D: Tasks on Molecules in Three Dimensions

abstract: Semi-supervised learning seeks to learn a machine learning model when only a small amount of the available data is labeled. The most widespread approach uses a graph prior, which encourages similar instances to have similar predictions. This has been very successful with models ranging from kernel machines to neural networks, but has remained inapplicable to decision trees, for which the optimization problem is much harder. We solve this based on a reformulation of the problem which requires iteratively solving two simpler problems: a supervised tree learning problem, which can be solved by the Tree Alternating Optimization algorithm; and a label smoothing problem, which can be solved through a sparse linear system. The algorithm is scalable and highly effective even with very few labeled instances, and makes it possible to learn accurate, interpretable models based on decision trees in such situations.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning uses a small labeled subset together with additional unlabeled data. A common strategy connects similar examples in a graph and encourages them to receive similar predictions. Although this strategy has worked with neural networks and kernel methods, applying it to decision trees creates a much harder optimization problem.

The paper reformulates that problem as an iteration between two simpler tasks. One is supervised tree learning, handled by Tree Alternating Optimization. The other smooths labels according to the graph and is solved using a sparse linear system. Alternating these steps provides a way to bring the similarity information into tree learning through manageable subproblems.

The authors report that the resulting algorithm is scalable and highly effective even when very few examples have labels. Its practical importance is that it makes graph-based semi-supervised learning available for decision-tree models. This allows the information in unlabeled examples to support accurate predictions while retaining the interpretability associated with the resulting tree models.
summary.tldr: Alternating tree fitting with graph-based label smoothing enables effective semi-supervised learning with interpretable decision trees.

title: Semi-Supervised Learning with Decision Trees: Graph Laplacian Tree Alternating Optimization

abstract: Theorem proving in natural mathematical language – the mixture of symbolic and natural language used by humans – plays a central role in mathematical advances and education, and tests aspects of reasoning that are core to intelligence. Yet it has remained underexplored with modern generative models. We study large-scale language models on two new generation tasks: suggesting the next step in a mathematical proof, and full proof generation. We develop NaturalProver, a language model that generates proofs by conditioning on background references (e.g. theorems and definitions that are either retrieved or human-provided), and optionally enforces their presence with constrained decoding. On theorems from the NaturalProofs benchmark, NaturalProver improves the quality of next-step suggestions and generated proofs over fine-tuned GPT-3, according to human evaluations from university-level mathematics students. NaturalProver is capable of proving some theorems that require short (2-6 step) proofs, and providing next-step suggestions that are rated as correct and useful over 40% of the time, which is to our knowledge the first demonstration of these capabilities using neural language models.
