paragraphs: NaturalProver studies mathematical proofs written in the mixture of symbols and ordinary language used by people. The paper considers two tasks: suggesting the next step of a proof and generating a complete proof. Both require connecting the statement being proved to relevant mathematical background.

The model conditions its generation on references such as definitions and theorems, supplied either through retrieval or by a person. An optional constrained decoding procedure enforces the presence of those references in the output. This makes background material an explicit part of proof generation and gives the generation process a way to incorporate selected references.

On NaturalProofs theorems, university-level mathematics students judge NaturalProver's next-step suggestions and complete proofs more favorably than those of fine-tuned GPT-3. The model proves some theorems requiring short proofs of two to six steps, and more than 40% of its next-step suggestions are rated correct and useful. These findings establish partial proof-generation and assistance capabilities in the evaluated setting, with the strongest demonstrated complete proofs remaining short.
summary.tldr: NaturalProver uses mathematical references to improve human-rated proof suggestions and generate some correct short proofs.

title: NaturalProver: Grounded Mathematical Proof Generation with Language Models

abstract: Extracting informative representations of molecules using Graph neural networks (GNNs) is crucial in AI-driven drug discovery. Recently, the graph research community has been trying to replicate the success of self-supervised pretraining in natural language processing, with several successes claimed. However, we find the benefit brought by self-supervised pretraining on small molecular data can be negligible in many cases. We conduct thorough ablation studies on the key components of GNN pretraining, including pretraining objectives, data splitting methods, input features, pretraining dataset scales, and GNN architectures, to see how they affect the accuracy of the downstream tasks. Our first important finding is, self-supervised graph pretraining do not always have statistically significant advantages over non-pretraining methods in many settings. Secondly, although noticeable improvement can be observed with additional supervised pretraining, the improvement may diminish with richer features or more balanced data splits. Thirdly, hyper-parameters could have larger impacts on accuracy of downstream tasks than the choice of pretraining tasks, especially when the scales of downstream tasks are small. Finally, we provide our conjectures where the complexity of some pretraining methods on small molecules might be insufficient, followed by empirical evidences on different pretraining datasets.

paragraphs: Self-supervised pretraining has motivated efforts to improve molecular representations learned by graph neural networks. This paper investigates how much those efforts help on small molecules. Its central finding is qualified: across many examined settings, self-supervised graph pretraining does not provide a statistically significant advantage over training without it.

The authors systematically vary pretraining objectives, data splits, input features, pretraining dataset sizes, and network architectures. This helps separate the contribution of pretraining from other choices that affect downstream accuracy. Additional supervised pretraining can produce noticeable improvements, but those gains may shrink when input features are richer or data splits are more balanced.

Hyperparameter choices can also affect downstream accuracy more than the choice of pretraining task, especially when downstream datasets are small. The paper further offers conjectures, supported by empirical evidence across pretraining datasets, that some pretraining methods may be insufficiently complex for small molecules. Together, the results make the value of pretraining a setting-dependent question and emphasize careful comparisons of the surrounding experimental choices.
summary.tldr: Ablation studies find that molecular GNN pretraining often brings limited gains, with features, data splits, and hyperparameters strongly affecting its apparent value.

title: Does GNN Pretraining Help Molecular Representation?

abstract: Recent studies have shown that deep learning models such as RNNs and Transformers have brought significant performance gains for long-term forecasting of time series because they effectively utilize historical information. We found, however, that there is still great room for improvement in how to preserve historical information in neural networks while avoiding overfitting to noise present in the history. Addressing this allows better utilization of the capabilities of deep learning models. To this end, we design a Frequency improved Legendre Memory model, or FiLM: it applies Legendre polynomial projections to approximate historical information, uses Fourier projection to remove noise, and adds a low-rank approximation to speed up computation. Our empirical studies show that the proposed FiLM significantly improves the accuracy of state-of-the-art models in multivariate and univariate long-term forecasting by (19.2%, 22.6%), respectively. We also demonstrate that the representation module developed in this work can be used as a general plugin to improve the long-term prediction performance of other deep learning modules. Code is available at https://github.com/tianzhou2011/FiLM/.

paragraphs: Long-term forecasting requires a model to preserve useful information from the past without fitting the noise mixed into that history. This paper argues that historical representation still leaves considerable room for improvement, even with strong recurrent and Transformer models. FiLM addresses that issue by combining a structured memory of past observations with frequency-based processing.

The model uses projections onto Legendre polynomials to approximate historical information. It then applies Fourier projection to remove noise and incorporates a low-rank approximation to accelerate computation. These components address related requirements: representing the history, reducing distracting variation, and keeping the resulting computation manageable. The method therefore focuses on how the past is stored and processed for future prediction.

The empirical study reports accuracy improvements over state-of-the-art models of 19.2% for multivariate forecasting and 22.6% for univariate forecasting. The authors also demonstrate that the representation module can improve other deep learning modules when used as a plugin. This extends the contribution beyond the complete FiLM model.
summary.tldr: FiLM combines Legendre memory, Fourier-based noise removal, and low-rank computation to improve long-term time-series forecasting.

title: FiLM: Frequency improved Legendre Memory Model for Long-term Time Series Forecasting

abstract: Amid mounting concern about the reliability and credibility of machine learning research, we present a principled framework for making robust and generalizable claims: the multiverse analysis. Our framework builds upon the multiverse analysis introduced in response to psychology's own reproducibility crisis. To efficiently explore high-dimensional and often continuous ML search spaces, we model the multiverse with a Gaussian Process surrogate and apply Bayesian experimental design. Our framework is designed to facilitate drawing robust scientific conclusions about model performance, and thus our approach focuses on exploration rather than conventional optimization. In the first of two case studies, we investigate disputed claims about the relative merit of adaptive optimizers. Second, we synthesize conflicting research on the effect of learning rate on the large batch training generalization gap. For the machine learning community, the multiverse analysis is a simple and effective technique for identifying robust claims, for increasing transparency, and a step toward improved reproducibility.

paragraphs: A research claim about model performance may depend on the experimental choices under which it was obtained. This paper proposes multiverse analysis as a framework for investigating whether conclusions remain robust across a broader space of choices. It adapts an approach developed in response to reproducibility concerns in psychology to machine-learning research.

Machine-learning search spaces can have many dimensions and continuous settings, making broad exploration expensive. The framework uses a Gaussian Process surrogate to model that space and Bayesian experimental design to guide further exploration. Its purpose is to learn where scientific conclusions hold, so it prioritizes understanding variation in outcomes over finding a single configuration with the best performance.

Two case studies illustrate this approach. One examines disputed claims about the relative merits of adaptive optimizers; the other brings together conflicting findings about learning rate and the generalization gap in large-batch training. The contribution is a method for making performance claims more transparent and robust by examining their dependence on experimental choices, supporting improved reproducibility.
summary.tldr: Multiverse analysis uses surrogate modeling and experimental design to test how robust machine-learning conclusions are across experimental choices.

title: Modeling the Machine Learning Multiverse

abstract: This paper presents a multi-granularity method for the task of source code summarization, which generates a concise functional description for the given code snippet. We notice that skilled programmers write and read source codes hierarchically and pay close attention to conceptual entities like statements, tokens, sub-tokens, and the mapping relations between them. The entities have specific emphasis according to their granularities, e.g., statements in coarse-granularity re- veal the global logical semantics of code, and the sub-tokens in fine-granularity are more related to the textual semantics. Driven by this observation, we argue that a multi-granularity formulation incorporating these conceptual entities may benefit the code summarization task. Concretely, the source code is trans- formed into a pyramidal representation, and then a pyramid attention mechanism is applied for efficient feature aggregation among different hierarchies in it. We instantiate our multi-granularity method using the proposed pyramid attention and name it PA-former (Pyramid Attention transformer), which is evaluated on two source code summarization benchmarks where it surpasses the prior works and achieves new state-of-the-art results. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/leichainju/pa-former.

paragraphs: Source-code summarization generates a short description of what a code snippet does. The paper starts from the observation that programmers understand code at several levels, including statements, tokens, and subtokens. These levels emphasize different information: statements help express overall logic, while smaller textual pieces contribute meaning through names and other fine-grained details.

The proposed method transforms code into a pyramidal representation that includes these different granularities and their relationships. A pyramid attention mechanism then aggregates features efficiently across the hierarchy. The resulting transformer, PA-former, is designed to bring coarse logical information and fine textual information into the same summarization process.

On two source-code summarization benchmarks, PA-former surpasses previous methods and achieves the reported state-of-the-art results. The findings support the usefulness of organizing code representations around multiple conceptual levels. Rather than relying on just one level of description, the architecture explicitly makes relationships among levels available when learning to generate a concise functional summary.
summary.tldr: PA-former summarizes code using pyramid attention to combine statement-, token-, and subtoken-level information.

title: Pyramid Attention For Source Code Summarization

abstract: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) is a ubiquitous on-policy reinforcement learning algorithm but is significantly less utilized than off-policy learning algorithms in multi-agent settings. This is often due to the belief that PPO is significantly less sample efficient than off-policy methods in multi-agent systems. In this work, we carefully study the performance of PPO in cooperative multi-agent settings. We show that PPO-based multi-agent algorithms achieve surprisingly strong performance in four popular multi-agent testbeds: the particle-world environments, the StarCraft multi-agent challenge, the Hanabi challenge, and Google Research Football, with minimal hyperparameter tuning and without any domain-specific algorithmic modifications or architectures. Importantly, compared to competitive off-policy methods, PPO often achieves competitive or superior results in both final returns and sample efficiency. Finally, through ablation studies, we analyze implementation and hyperparameter factors that are critical to PPO's empirical performance, and give concrete practical suggestions regarding these factors. Our results show that when using these practices, simple PPO-based methods are a strong baseline in cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning. Source code is released at https://github.com/marlbenchmark/on-policy.

paragraphs: Proximal Policy Optimization, or PPO, is widely used in reinforcement learning but has been less common in multi-agent systems. One reason is the belief that its on-policy learning is substantially less sample efficient than off-policy alternatives. This paper tests that belief in settings where multiple agents cooperate.

The study evaluates PPO-based methods in particle-world environments, the StarCraft multi-agent challenge, Hanabi, and Google Research Football. The methods use minimal hyperparameter tuning and no domain-specific algorithmic changes or architectures. Across these testbeds, PPO often matches or exceeds competitive off-policy methods in both final returns and sample efficiency.

The authors also use ablation studies to examine which implementation choices and hyperparameters are critical to empirical performance. They turn these findings into practical recommendations. The result supports simple PPO-based methods as strong baselines when those practices are followed. Its significance is that a broadly applicable algorithm can be highly competitive across several cooperative settings, and that careful implementation materially affects the comparison with more commonly used alternatives.
summary.tldr: With suitable implementation practices, PPO is often competitive or superior to off-policy methods across four cooperative multi-agent testbeds.

title: The Surprising Effectiveness of PPO in Cooperative Multi-Agent Games

abstract: The standard supervised learning paradigm works effectively when training data shares the same distribution as the upcoming testing samples. However, this stationary assumption is often violated in real-world applications, especially when testing data appear in an online fashion. In this paper, we formulate and investigate the problem of \emph{online label shift} (OLaS): the learner trains an initial model from the labeled offline data and then deploys it to an unlabeled online environment where the underlying label distribution changes over time but the label-conditional density does not. The non-stationarity nature and the lack of supervision make the problem challenging to be tackled. To address the difficulty, we construct a new unbiased risk estimator that utilizes the unlabeled data, which exhibits many benign properties albeit with potential non-convexity. Building upon that, we propose novel online ensemble algorithms to deal with the non-stationarity of the environments. Our approach enjoys optimal \emph{dynamic regret}, indicating that the performance is competitive with a clairvoyant who knows the online environments in hindsight and then chooses the best decision for each round. The obtained dynamic regret bound scales with the intensity and pattern of label distribution shift, hence exhibiting the adaptivity in the OLaS problem. Extensive experiments are conducted to validate the effectiveness and support our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: A classifier deployed over time may encounter changing proportions of classes without receiving new labels. This paper studies that situation under a specific assumption: class frequencies may change, but the distribution of inputs within each class stays fixed. A model is initially trained on labeled offline data and must then adapt using an unlabeled stream.

The authors construct an unbiased estimator of prediction risk from the unlabeled observations. This provides a way to assess decisions despite the absence of direct supervision, although the resulting estimation problem can be nonconvex. They then build online ensemble algorithms that use this foundation to respond to changes in the environment.

The theoretical guarantee concerns dynamic regret, which compares accumulated performance with an ideal decision-maker that knows the environments afterward and selects the best decision at each round. The authors obtain an optimal bound that depends on both the intensity and pattern of the label shifts. This captures adaptation to changing conditions within the stated label-shift setting. Experiments support the theoretical findings and demonstrate the approach's effectiveness.
summary.tldr: Online ensemble algorithms adapt to changing class frequencies using unlabeled data, with optimal dynamic-regret guarantees under label-shift assumptions.

title: Adapting to Online Label Shift with Provable Guarantees

abstract: Although PIFu-based 3D human reconstruction methods are popular, the quality of recovered details is still unsatisfactory. In a sparse (e.g., 3 RGBD sensors) capture setting, the depth noise is typically amplified in the PIFu representation, resulting in flat facial surfaces and geometry-fallible bodies. In this paper, we propose a novel geometry-aware two-scale PIFu for 3D human reconstruction from sparse, noisy inputs. Our key idea is to exploit the complementary properties of depth denoising and 3D reconstruction, for learning a two-scale PIFu representation to reconstruct high-frequency facial details and consistent bodies separately. To this end, we first formulate depth denoising and 3D reconstruction as a multi-task learning problem. The depth denoising process enriches the local geometry information of the reconstruction features, while the reconstruction process enhances depth denoising with global topology information. We then propose to learn the two-scale PIFu representation using two MLPs based on the denoised depth and geometry-aware features. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in reconstructing facial details and bodies of different poses and its superiority over state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a person in 3D from a few noisy RGBD views can lose both fine detail and overall geometric consistency. The paper identifies a particular problem in PIFu-based methods: their representations can amplify depth noise, producing flattened faces and faulty body geometry. It targets reconstruction from sparse, noisy captures.

The proposed method trains depth denoising and 3D reconstruction together so that each task informs the other. Denoising supplies richer local geometry to reconstruction features, while reconstruction contributes information about global topology to denoising. This reciprocal relationship aims to improve the inputs and representations used to recover the person.

A two-scale PIFu representation then uses two multilayer perceptrons with denoised depth and geometry-aware features. The scales separately address detailed facial structure and consistent body reconstruction. Experiments show improved reconstruction of faces and bodies in different poses, outperforming the compared state-of-the-art methods. The approach connects noise handling with the differing geometric demands of facial detail and whole-body shape.
summary.tldr: Joint depth denoising and two-scale reconstruction improve facial detail and body geometry from sparse, noisy RGBD inputs.

title: Geometry-aware Two-scale PIFu Representation for Human Reconstruction

abstract: Designing learning systems which are invariant to certain data transformations is critical in machine learning. Practitioners can typically enforce a desired invariance on the trained model through the choice of a network architecture, e.g. using convolutions for translations, or using data augmentation. Yet, enforcing true invariance in the network can be difficult, and data invariances are not always known a piori. State-of-the-art methods for learning data augmentation policies require held-out data and are based on bilevel optimization problems, which are complex to solve and often computationally demanding. In this work we investigate new ways of learning invariances only from the training data. Using learnable augmentation layers built directly in the network, we demonstrate that our method is very versatile. It can incorporate any type of differentiable augmentation and be applied to a broad class of learning problems beyond computer vision. We provide empirical evidence showing that our approach is easier and faster to train than modern automatic data augmentation techniques based on bilevel optimization, while achieving comparable results. Experiments show that while the invariances transferred to a model through automatic data augmentation are limited by the model expressivity, the invariance yielded by our approach is insensitive to it by design.

paragraphs: A useful prediction should sometimes remain unchanged when its input undergoes a particular transformation. Choosing an architecture or augmenting training data can encourage this invariance, but the relevant transformations may not be known beforehand. This paper explores learning invariances directly from training data, without the held-out data required by the augmentation-policy methods it discusses.

The approach places learnable augmentation layers inside the network. These layers can incorporate any differentiable augmentation, making the framework applicable beyond computer vision. This formulation also avoids the complex bilevel optimization used by the compared automatic augmentation techniques, which involve an additional level of optimization.

Experiments provide evidence that the method trains more easily and quickly while reaching comparable results. They also reveal a distinction in how invariance is obtained: invariance transferred through automatic augmentation is constrained by the model’s expressive capacity, whereas the proposed approach is designed to be insensitive to that capacity. The contribution is therefore both a simpler training approach and a different mechanism for building invariance into a learned system.
summary.tldr: Learnable augmentation layers build invariance into networks using training data alone, with easier and faster training in the reported comparisons.

title: Deep invariant networks with differentiable augmentation layers

abstract: Developing interactive software, such as websites or games, is a particularly engaging way to learn computer science. However, teaching and giving feedback on such software is time-consuming — standard approaches require instructors to manually grade student-implemented interactive programs. As a result, online platforms that serve millions, like Code.org, are unable to provide any feedback on assignments for implementing interactive programs, which critically hinders students’ ability to learn. One approach toward automatic grading is to learn an agent that interacts with a student’s program and explores states indicative of errors via reinforcement learning. However, existing work on this approach only provides binary feedback of whether a program is correct or not, while students require finer-grained feedback on the specific errors in their programs to understand their mistakes. In this work, we show that exploring to discover errors can be cast as a meta-exploration problem. This enables us to construct a principled objective for discovering errors and an algorithm for optimizing this objective, which provides fine-grained feedback. We evaluate our approach on a set of over 700K real anonymized student programs from a Code.org interactive assignment. Our approach provides feedback with 94.3% accuracy, improving over existing approaches by 17.7% and coming within 1.5% of human-level accuracy. Project web page: https://ezliu.github.io/dreamgrader.

This enables us to construct a principled objective for discovering errors and an algorithm for optimizing this objective, which provides fine-grained feedback. We evaluate our approach on a set of over 700K real anonymized student programs from a Code.org interactive assignment. Our approach provides feedback with 94.3% accuracy, improving over existing approaches by 17.7% and coming within 1.5% of human-level accuracy. Project web page: https://ezliu.github.io/dreamgrader.

paragraphs: Interactive assignments such as games and websites can engage students, but evaluating them requires examining how they behave during interaction. Manual grading is costly, and a simple correct-or-incorrect verdict gives students little guidance about their mistakes. This paper develops an automated approach that seeks specific errors by interacting with a student's program.

The authors formulate error discovery as a meta-exploration problem. This provides an objective for deciding how to explore programs and an algorithm for optimizing that objective. The aim is to reach states that reveal particular mistakes, allowing the system to give finer-grained feedback than a binary assessment.

Evaluation uses more than 700,000 real anonymized submissions from one Code.org interactive assignment. The method achieves 94.3% feedback accuracy, with a reported improvement of 17.7% over existing approaches and performance within 1.5% of human-level accuracy. These results show that learning how to explore program behavior can support detailed automated feedback in the studied assignment, addressing an important obstacle to grading interactive work at scale.
summary.tldr: A meta-exploration agent interacts with student programs to discover specific errors, achieving 94.3% feedback accuracy on a large Code.org assignment dataset.

title: Giving Feedback on Interactive Student Programs with Meta-Exploration

abstract: Fully cooperative, partially observable multi-agent problems are ubiquitous in the real world. In this paper, we focus on a specific subclass of coordination problems in which humans are able to discover self-explaining deviations (SEDs). SEDs are actions that deviate from the common understanding of what reasonable behavior would be in normal circumstances. They are taken with the intention of causing another agent or other agents to realize, using theory of mind, that the circumstance must be abnormal. We motivate this idea with a real world example and formalize its definition. Next, we introduce an algorithm for improvement maximizing SEDs (IMPROVISED). Lastly, we evaluate IMPROVISED both in an illustrative toy setting and the popular benchmark setting Hanabi, where we show that it can produce so called finesse plays.

paragraphs: Cooperating agents may see different parts of a situation while needing to act toward a shared goal. This paper studies a subclass of these partially observable coordination problems in which an unusual action can communicate that something unusual is happening. The authors call such actions self-explaining deviations.

A self-explaining deviation departs from the agents’ shared understanding of reasonable behavior under normal circumstances. Its purpose is to lead another agent to infer, using reasoning about the actor’s intentions, that the circumstances must be abnormal. The explanation comes from the action’s departure from expectations and the observer’s interpretation of why a cooperative partner would choose it.

The authors motivate the idea with a real-world example, formalize it, and introduce IMPROVISED, an algorithm for finding improvement-maximizing deviations. They evaluate it in a toy setting and in Hanabi, where it produces finesse plays. The contribution is a formal and algorithmic treatment of how deliberate departures from expected behavior can help agents coordinate under partial information.
summary.tldr: IMPROVISED finds unusual cooperative actions that help other agents infer abnormal circumstances, including finesse plays in Hanabi.

title: Self-Explaining Deviations for Coordination

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) are vulnerable to adversarial perturbations, including those that affect both node features and graph topology. This paper investigates GNNs derived from diverse neural flows, concentrating on their connection to various stability notions such as BIBO stability, Lyapunov stability, structural stability, and conservative stability. We argue that Lyapunov stability, despite its common use, does not necessarily ensure adversarial robustness. Inspired by physics principles, we advocate for the use of conservative Hamiltonian neural flows to construct GNNs that are robust to adversarial attacks. The adversarial robustness of different neural flow GNNs is empirically compared on several benchmark datasets under a variety of adversarial attacks. Extensive numerical experiments demonstrate that GNNs leveraging conservative Hamiltonian flows with Lyapunov stability substantially improve robustness against adversarial perturbations. The implementation code of experiments is available at \url{https://github.com/zknus/NeurIPS-2023-HANG-Robustness}.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can be disrupted by adversarial changes to node information or to the connections between nodes. This paper investigates whether the dynamics underlying a graph network help explain its resistance to these changes. It examines networks derived from different neural flows and relates them to several mathematical notions of stability.

A central argument is that Lyapunov stability, despite its common use, does not necessarily imply adversarial robustness. The authors therefore examine other stability properties as well, including bounded-input bounded-output, structural, and conservative stability. Drawing on physics, they propose constructing graph networks using conservative Hamiltonian neural flows.

Experiments compare different neural-flow graph networks across several benchmark datasets and multiple adversarial attacks. The authors report substantially improved robustness for networks combining conservative Hamiltonian flows with Lyapunov stability. This supports the proposed combination empirically, while the conceptual contribution is to separate different meanings of stability: a model satisfying one stability notion need not automatically resist adversarial changes to graph inputs.
summary.tldr: Conservative Hamiltonian graph networks improve robustness in experiments, while the paper argues that Lyapunov stability alone does not ensure adversarial robustness.

title: Adversarial Robustness in Graph Neural Networks: A Hamiltonian Approach

abstract: Domain adaptive object detection (DAOD) aims to generalize detectors trained on an annotated source domain to an unlabelled target domain. However, existing methods focus on reducing the domain bias of the detection backbone by inferring a discriminative visual encoder, while ignoring the domain bias in the detection head. Inspired by the high generalization of vision-language models (VLMs), applying a VLM as the robust detection backbone following a domain-aware detection head is a reasonable way to learn the discriminative detector for each domain, rather than reducing the domain bias in traditional methods. To achieve the above issue, we thus propose a novel DAOD framework named Domain-Aware detection head with Prompt tuning (DA-Pro), which applies the learnable domain-adaptive prompt to generate the dynamic detection head for each domain. Formally, the domain-adaptive prompt consists of the domain-invariant tokens, domain-specific tokens, and the domain-related textual description along with the class label. Furthermore, two constraints between the source and target domains are applied to ensure that the domain-adaptive prompt can capture the domains-shared and domain-specific knowledge. A prompt ensemble strategy is also proposed to reduce the effect of prompt disturbance. Comprehensive experiments over multiple cross-domain adaptation tasks demonstrate that using the domain-adaptive prompt can produce an effectively domain-related detection head for boosting domain-adaptive object detection. Our code is available at https://github.com/Therock90421/DA-Pro.

paragraphs: Domain-adaptive object detection transfers a detector from labeled source images to an unlabeled target domain. Existing approaches often concentrate on adapting the visual backbone that extracts image features. This paper highlights a second source of mismatch: the detection head that turns those features into detections can also carry domain-specific bias.

DA-Pro combines a vision-language-model backbone with a detection head generated through learnable, domain-adaptive prompts. Each prompt includes shared tokens, domain-specific tokens, and a textual description of the domain alongside the class label. Two constraints across source and target domains encourage the prompts to capture both common knowledge and information particular to each domain.

The framework also ensembles prompts to reduce sensitivity to prompt disturbance. Across multiple adaptation tasks, the experiments show that the learned prompts produce useful domain-related detection heads and improve detection performance. The approach therefore expands where adaptation happens: a robust feature extractor is paired with a head that can reflect the domain in which detection is performed.
summary.tldr: DA-Pro uses domain-adaptive prompts to generate detection heads that capture shared and domain-specific knowledge for cross-domain object detection.

title: Learning Domain-Aware Detection Head with Prompt Tuning

abstract: Collaborative machine learning involves training models on data from multiple parties but must incentivize their participation. Existing data valuation methods fairly value and reward each party based on shared data or model parameters but neglect the privacy risks involved. To address this, we introduce _differential privacy_ (DP) as an incentive. Each party can select its required DP guarantee and perturb its _sufficient statistic_ (SS) accordingly. The mediator values the perturbed SS by the Bayesian surprise it elicits about the model parameters. As our valuation function enforces a _privacy-valuation trade-off_, parties are deterred from selecting excessive DP guarantees that reduce the utility of the grand coalition's model. Finally, the mediator rewards each party with different posterior samples of the model parameters. Such rewards still satisfy existing incentives like fairness but additionally preserve DP and a high similarity to the grand coalition's posterior. We empirically demonstrate the effectiveness and practicality of our approach on synthetic and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Collaborative learning needs participants to contribute useful information, but valuing contributions without considering privacy can overlook a major cost of participation. This paper builds differential privacy into the incentive mechanism. Each participant chooses a required privacy guarantee and perturbs a sufficient statistic, a summary of data relevant to the model, accordingly.

A mediator values each perturbed summary through Bayesian surprise: how much it changes beliefs about model parameters. This creates a privacy-valuation trade-off. Stronger privacy protection that makes a contribution less informative also reduces its assessed value, discouraging choices that excessively diminish the usefulness of the combined model. Participants can therefore express privacy requirements within the same process that evaluates their contributions.

Rewards take the form of different posterior samples of model parameters for different participants. The authors state that these rewards satisfy existing incentive properties such as fairness while preserving differential privacy and remaining highly similar to the full coalition’s posterior. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets support the approach’s effectiveness and practicality. The contribution links privacy choices, information value, and access to learned model knowledge in one collaborative mechanism.
summary.tldr: A collaborative-learning mechanism connects participants’ privacy choices to contribution value and rewards them with privacy-preserving posterior samples.

title: Incentives in Private Collaborative Machine Learning

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in proving formal theorems using proof assistants such as Lean. However, existing methods are difficult to reproduce or build on, due to private code, data, and large compute requirements. This has created substantial barriers to research on machine learning methods for theorem proving. This paper removes these barriers by introducing LeanDojo: an open-source Lean playground consisting of toolkits, data, models, and benchmarks. LeanDojo extracts data from Lean and enables interaction with the proof environment programmatically. It contains fine-grained annotations of premises in proofs, providing valuable data for premise selection—a key bottleneck in theorem proving. Using this data, we develop ReProver (Retrieval-Augmented Prover): an LLM-based prover augmented with retrieval for selecting premises from a vast math library. It is inexpensive and needs only one GPU week of training. Our retriever leverages LeanDojo's program analysis capability to identify accessible premises and hard negative examples, which makes retrieval much more effective. Furthermore, we construct a new benchmark consisting of 98,734 theorems and proofs extracted from Lean's math library. It features challenging data split requiring the prover to generalize to theorems relying on novel premises that are never used in training. We use this benchmark for training and evaluation, and experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of ReProver over non-retrieval baselines and GPT-4. We thus provide the first set of open-source LLM-based theorem provers without any proprietary datasets and release it under a permissive MIT license to facilitate further research.

paragraphs: Formal theorem proving requires selecting useful mathematical premises as well as constructing proof steps. Research has also faced practical barriers from private datasets, unavailable code, and demanding training requirements. LeanDojo supplies an open environment with tools, data, models, and benchmarks for studying language-model theorem proving in Lean.

The system extracts proof data and supports programmatic interaction with Lean. Detailed annotations identify premises used in proofs, enabling the authors to train ReProver, a language-model prover with retrieval from a large mathematical library. Program analysis helps the retriever identify available premises and difficult negative examples. The reported training requirement is one GPU week.

This tests whether the prover can use newly relevant library material. Experiments show ReProver outperforming non-retrieval baselines and GPT-4. Together, the retrieval method and openly released infrastructure make premise selection more effective and the research workflow easier to reproduce.
summary.tldr: LeanDojo provides open theorem-proving infrastructure, while ReProver improves proof generation by retrieving relevant mathematical premises.

title: LeanDojo: Theorem Proving with Retrieval-Augmented Language Models

abstract: Two-sided matching markets have long existed to pair agents in the absence of regulated exchanges. A common example is school choice, where a matching mechanism uses student and school preferences to assign students to schools. In such settings, forming preferences is both difficult and critical. Prior work has suggested various prediction mechanisms that help agents make decisions about their preferences. Although often deployed together, these matching and prediction mechanisms are almost always analyzed separately. The present work shows that at the intersection of the two lies a previously unexplored type of strategic behavior: agents returning to the market (e.g., schools) can attack future predictions by interacting short-term non-optimally with their matches. Here, we first introduce this type of strategic behavior, which we call an adversarial interaction attack. Next, we construct a formal economic model that captures the feedback loop between prediction mechanisms designed to assist agents and the matching mechanism used to pair them. Finally, in a simplified setting, we prove that returning agents can benefit from using adversarial interaction attacks and gain progressively more as the trust in and accuracy of predictions increases. We also show that this attack increases inequality in the student population.

paragraphs: In matching markets such as school choice, predictions can help participants decide which matches they prefer. Those preferences then feed into the mechanism that assigns matches. This paper examines the feedback between prediction and matching, arguing that analyzing the two mechanisms separately can miss an incentive to manipulate future outcomes.

The authors introduce an adversarial interaction attack. A participant that returns to the market, such as a school, can interact with its current matches in a way that sacrifices short-term performance but distorts future predictions. They build a formal economic model that captures how these interactions affect predictions, preference formation, and later matching decisions.

In a simplified setting, the authors prove that returning participants can benefit from this strategy. The gains increase as predictions become more accurate and more trusted. They also show that the attack increases inequality among students. The result identifies a specific vulnerability in the combined system: better predictive assistance can strengthen strategic incentives when the behavior generating future prediction data is itself controllable.
summary.tldr: A formal matching-market model shows how returning participants can sacrifice short-term performance to manipulate predictions and improve future matches.

title: Strategic Behavior in Two-sided Matching Markets with Prediction-enhanced Preference-formation

abstract: Generating plans of action, and reasoning about change have long been considered a core competence of intelligent agents. It is thus no surprise that evaluating the planning and reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) has become a hot topic of research. Most claims about LLM planning capabilities are however based on common sense tasks–where it becomes hard to tell whether LLMs are planning or merely retrieving from their vast world knowledge. There is a strong need for systematic and extensible planning benchmarks with sufficient diversity to evaluate whether LLMs have innate planning capabilities. Motivated by this, we propose PlanBench, an extensible benchmark suite based on the kinds of domains used in the automated planning community, especially in the International Planning Competition, to test the capabilities of LLMs in planning or reasoning about actions and change. PlanBench provides sufficient diversity in both the task domains and the specific planning capabilities. Our studies also show that on many critical capabilities–including plan generation–LLM performance falls quite short, even with the SOTA models. PlanBench can thus function as a useful marker of progress of LLMs in planning and reasoning.

paragraphs: PlanBench addresses a problem in evaluating language-model planning: success on a familiar commonsense task may reflect recalled knowledge rather than reasoning about an action sequence. The authors argue that testing planning requires a systematic range of domains and capabilities. This makes it easier to examine whether a model can reason about actions and the changes they cause.

The benchmark draws on domains used by the automated planning community, especially those associated with the International Planning Competition. It covers both different task settings and different planning abilities, and its extensible design allows the evaluation suite to grow. The focus therefore includes generating plans and reasoning about how actions affect the state of a problem.

The reported studies find substantial weaknesses in several important capabilities, including plan generation, even among the state-of-the-art models evaluated. These findings identify a gap between broad language competence and the planning performance measured by the suite. PlanBench supplies a structured reference point for tracking improvements in action planning and reasoning about change.
summary.tldr: PlanBench systematically evaluates language-model planning and reasoning about change, revealing substantial weaknesses in the tested models.

title: PlanBench: An Extensible Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Models on Planning and Reasoning about Change

abstract: Academic tabular benchmarks often contain small sets of curated features. In contrast, data scientists typically collect as many features as possible into their datasets, and even engineer new features from existing ones. To prevent over-fitting in subsequent downstream modeling, practitioners commonly use automated feature selection methods that identify a reduced subset of informative features. Existing benchmarks for tabular feature selection consider classical downstream models, toy synthetic datasets, or do not evaluate feature selectors on the basis of downstream performance. We construct a challenging feature selection benchmark evaluated on downstream neural networks including transformers, using real datasets and multiple methods for generating extraneous features. We also propose an input-gradient-based analogue of LASSO for neural networks that outperforms classical feature selection methods on challenging problems such as selecting from corrupted or second-order features.

paragraphs: Real tabular datasets often contain many collected or engineered features, only some of which help prediction. Choosing a smaller informative subset can reduce overfitting. The paper argues that existing feature-selection benchmarks do not adequately reflect this situation: some use small curated feature sets, some rely on synthetic problems, and others do not judge selection by the performance of the eventual predictive model.

The authors build a benchmark around real datasets with additional extraneous features generated in multiple ways. Feature selectors are evaluated through the neural networks subsequently trained on their chosen inputs, including transformers. This makes the evaluation directly about whether selecting features helps the model that will actually use them.

They also propose a neural-network counterpart to LASSO based on input gradients. It outperforms classical feature-selection methods on challenging cases involving corrupted or second-order features. The contribution therefore combines a more practically motivated evaluation setting with a selection method that shows advantages within that setting.
summary.tldr: This benchmark evaluates feature selection by downstream neural-network performance and introduces an input-gradient method that improves selection on challenging feature sets.

title: A Performance-Driven Benchmark for Feature Selection in Tabular Deep Learning

abstract: Reward specification is a notoriously difficult problem in reinforcement learning, requiring extensive expert supervision to design robust reward functions. Imitation learning (IL) methods attempt to circumvent these problems by utilizing expert demonstrations instead of using an extrinsic reward function but typically require a large number of in-domain expert demonstrations. Inspired by advances in the field of Video-and-Language Models (VLMs), we present RoboCLIP, an online imitation learning method that uses a single demonstration (overcoming the large data requirement) in the form of a video demonstration or a textual description of the task to generate rewards without manual reward function design. Additionally, RoboCLIP can also utilize out-of-domain demonstrations, like videos of humans solving the task for reward generation, circumventing the need to have the same demonstration and deployment domains. RoboCLIP utilizes pretrained VLMs without any finetuning for reward generation. Reinforcement learning agents trained with RoboCLIP rewards demonstrate 2-3 times higher zero-shot performance than competing imitation learning methods on downstream robot manipulation tasks, doing so using only one video/text demonstration. Visit our website at https://sites.google.com/view/roboclip/home for experiment videos.

paragraphs: Teaching a robot through reinforcement learning usually requires a reward function, and designing one can demand substantial expertise. Imitation learning avoids some of that work by using demonstrations, but often needs many examples from the deployment domain. RoboCLIP addresses both burdens by generating rewards from a single video demonstration or a textual task description.

The method uses pretrained video-and-language models without fine-tuning them for reward generation. A reinforcement-learning agent then learns using those generated rewards. RoboCLIP can also accept demonstrations from another domain, including videos of humans completing a task, so the demonstration need not come from a robot operating in the same setting.

On downstream robot-manipulation tasks, agents trained with RoboCLIP rewards achieve reported zero-shot performance two to three times that of competing imitation-learning methods. Those results use only one video or text demonstration. The finding supports pretrained video-and-language representations as a useful source of task feedback, reducing demonstration and manual reward-design requirements while retaining an online policy-learning process.
summary.tldr: RoboCLIP uses a frozen video-and-language model to generate robot-learning rewards from one video demonstration or text description.

title: RoboCLIP: One Demonstration is Enough to Learn Robot Policies

abstract: As machine learning-enabled Text-to-Image (TTI) systems are becoming increasingly prevalent and seeing growing adoption as commercial services, characterizing the social biases they exhibit is a necessary first step to lowering their risk of discriminatory outcomes. This evaluation, however, is made more difficult by the synthetic nature of these systems’ outputs: common definitions of diversity are grounded in social categories of people living in the world, whereas the artificial depictions of fictive humans created by these systems have no inherent gender or ethnicity. To address this need, we propose a new method for exploring the social biases in TTI systems. Our approach relies on characterizing the variation in generated images triggered by enumerating gender and ethnicity markers in the prompts, and comparing it to the variation engendered by spanning different professions. This allows us to (1) identify specific bias trends, (2) provide targeted scores to directly compare models in terms of diversity and representation, and (3) jointly model interdependent social variables to support a multidimensional analysis. We leverage this method to analyze images generated by 3 popular TTI systems (Dall·E 2 , Stable Diffusion v 1.4 and 2) and find that while all of their outputs show correlations with US labor demographics, they also consistently under-represent marginalized identities to different extents. We also release the datasets and low-code interactive bias exploration platforms developed forthis work, as well as the necessary tools to similarly evaluate additional TTI systems.

paragraphs: Evaluating representation in generated images requires care because fictitious people do not have inherent gender or ethnicity. This paper develops a method for studying social bias through how image outputs change when prompts include different gender and ethnicity markers. It compares that variation with changes produced by prompting for different professions.

The method identifies bias trends, produces targeted scores for comparing diversity and representation across models, and analyzes interacting social variables together. This multidimensional approach lets the evaluation examine relationships among prompt attributes rather than treating each attribute as an isolated category assigned to a synthetic person.

The authors apply the method to Dall·E 2 and Stable Diffusion versions 1.4 and 2. Outputs from all three correlate with United States labor demographics while consistently underrepresenting marginalized identities to varying degrees. The paper also releases datasets, interactive exploration platforms, and tools for evaluating additional systems. These contributions make the observed patterns inspectable and provide a reusable approach to comparing representational behavior across image generators.
summary.tldr: A prompt-based analysis compares social representation across image generators and finds underrepresentation of marginalized identities in all three systems studied.

title: Stable Bias: Evaluating Societal Representations in Diffusion Models

abstract: Distributional reinforcement learning algorithms have attempted to utilize estimated uncertainty for exploration, such as optimism in the face of uncertainty. However, using the estimated variance for optimistic exploration may cause biased data collection and hinder convergence or performance. In this paper, we present a novel distributional reinforcement learning that selects actions by randomizing risk criterion without losing the risk-neutral objective. We provide a perturbed distributional Bellman optimality operator by distorting the risk measure. Also,we prove the convergence and optimality of the proposed method with the weaker contraction property. Our theoretical results support that the proposed method does not fall into biased exploration and is guaranteed to converge to an optimal return. Finally, we empirically show that our method outperforms other existing distribution-based algorithms in various environments including Atari 55 games.

paragraphs: Distributional reinforcement learning estimates distributions of returns, providing information beyond an average reward. Some algorithms use estimated uncertainty to explore optimistically. This paper identifies a potential problem: using estimated variance in that way can bias the data an agent collects and interfere with convergence or performance.

The proposed method randomizes the risk criterion used to choose actions while retaining a risk-neutral objective. Thus, variation in how the agent evaluates return distributions guides exploration without changing the overall objective to a permanently risk-seeking or risk-averse one. The authors formalize the approach through a perturbed distributional Bellman optimality operator that distorts the risk measure.

They prove convergence and optimality using a weaker contraction property. Their theoretical results support avoiding the biased exploration problem and converging to an optimal return within the analyzed framework. Empirical evaluation across multiple environments, including 55 Atari games, shows improvements over the compared distribution-based algorithms. The contribution connects an exploration design with both mathematical guarantees and experimental evidence, while identifying why variance-driven optimism can sometimes mislead learning.
summary.tldr: Randomizing action-selection risk criteria supports exploration while preserving a risk-neutral objective, with convergence guarantees and empirical gains.

title: Pitfall of Optimism: Distributional Reinforcement Learning by Randomizing Risk Criterion

abstract: Understanding the learned representation and underlying mechanisms of Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) often poses a challenge. In this paper, we ‘reverse engineer’ SSL, conducting an in-depth empirical analysis of its learned internal representations, encompassing diverse models, architectures, and hyperparameters. Our study reveals an intriguing process within the SSL training: an inherent facilitation of semantic label-based clustering, which is surprisingly driven by the regularization component of the SSL objective. This clustering not only enhances downstream classification, but also compresses the information. We further illustrate that the alignment of the SSL-trained representation is more pronounced with semantic classes rather than random functions. Remarkably, the learned representations align with semantic classes across various hierarchical levels, with this alignment intensifying when going deeper into the network. This ‘reverse engineering’ approach provides valuable insights into the inner mechanism of SSL and their influences on the performance across different class sets.

paragraphs: This paper investigates what self-supervised learning builds inside a network by inspecting its learned representations. The empirical study spans different models, architectures, and hyperparameters. Its focus is the internal organization that develops during training and how that organization relates to later classification performance.

The analysis finds that representations develop clusters associated with semantic labels, with the regularization component of the training objective driving this process. These clusters both improve downstream classification and compress information. The finding assigns regularization a substantive role in shaping useful semantic structure within the learned representation.

The authors also compare alignment with meaningful classes against alignment with random functions and find stronger alignment with the former. Semantic organization appears at multiple levels of a class hierarchy and becomes more pronounced deeper in the network. Together, these empirical observations explain how representations can become useful for different class sets. They connect the training objective, network depth, and semantic clustering to the behavior observed after self-supervised training.
summary.tldr: An empirical analysis finds that self-supervised regularization promotes semantic clustering, with stronger class alignment in deeper network representations.

title: Reverse Engineering Self-Supervised Learning

abstract: Data imbalance and open-ended distribution are two intrinsic characteristics of the real visual world. Though encouraging progress has been made in tackling each challenge separately, few works dedicated to combining them towards real-world scenarios. While several previous works have focused on classifying close-set samples and detecting open-set samples during testing, it's still essential to be able to classify unknown subjects as human beings. In this paper, we formally define a more realistic task as distribution-agnostic generalized category discovery (DA-GCD): generating fine-grained predictions for both close- and open-set classes in a long-tailed open-world setting. To tackle the challenging problem, we propose a Self-**Ba**lanced **Co**-Advice co**n**trastive framework (BaCon), which consists of a contrastive-learning branch and a pseudo-labeling branch, working collaboratively to provide interactive supervision to resolve the DA-GCD task. In particular, the contrastive-learning branch provides reliable distribution estimation to regularize the predictions of the pseudo-labeling branch, which in turn guides contrastive learning through self-balanced knowledge transfer and a proposed novel contrastive loss. We compare BaCon with state-of-the-art methods from two closely related fields: imbalanced semi-supervised learning and generalized category discovery. The effectiveness of BaCon is demonstrated with superior performance over all baselines and comprehensive analysis across various datasets. Our code is publicly available.

paragraphs: Real visual data contain both unevenly represented categories and categories unknown during training. This paper combines those challenges in distribution-agnostic generalized category discovery. The task requires detailed predictions for both known and unknown classes in a long-tailed, open-world setting, extending beyond simply flagging unfamiliar examples as unknown.

The proposed BaCon framework has two collaborating branches: contrastive learning and pseudo-labeling. The contrastive branch estimates the data distribution and uses that information to regularize the pseudo-labeling branch’s predictions. In return, pseudo-labeling guides contrastive learning through self-balanced knowledge transfer and a new contrastive loss. Each branch therefore supplies supervision that helps the other address the combined discovery and imbalance problem.

The authors compare BaCon with methods from imbalanced semi-supervised learning and generalized category discovery. Across the evaluated datasets, it outperforms all compared baselines, with additional analysis supporting its effectiveness. The contribution is both a task formulation that brings imbalance and unknown categories together and a mutually supervising architecture designed for that setting. The reported advantage is empirical across the studied datasets.
summary.tldr: BaCon combines contrastive learning and pseudo-labeling to discover known and unknown categories under class imbalance.

title: Towards Distribution-Agnostic Generalized Category Discovery

abstract: Though LLMs are capable of generating plausible programs, it’s challenging to interact with the LLMs further to revise the program, especially if the user’s specific requirements are different from the initial proposal. In this paper, we introduce ANPL, an interactive programming system that ensures users can always refine the generated code towards their specific programmatic intents via structureddecompositions. Borrowing the paradigm of sketching from program synthesis, an ANPL program consists of a set of input-outputs that it must satisfy, a “sketch” — control/data flow expressed in precise code (e.g. Python), and “holes” — sub-modules to be implemented by the LLM specified with natural language. The user revises an ANPL program by either modifying the sketch, changing the language used to describe the holes, or providing additional input-outputs to a particular hole, turning it into a sub-ANPL program that can be solved recursively. This workflow allows the users to offload programming burdens to the LLM as much as possible while retaining the ability to pinpoint and resolve bugs locally, without exposing the rest of the program to the LLM. We deploy ANPL on the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC), a set of unique tasks that are challenging for state-of-the-art AI systems, showing it outperforms baseline programming systems that (a) without the ability to decompose tasks interactively and (b) without the guarantee that the modules can be correctly composed together. Additional evaluations on APPS, HumanEval, and real-world programming tasks have validated that the ANPL framework is applicable to multiple programming domains. We release the ANPL solutions to the ARC tasks as a dataset, providing insights into how humans decompose novel tasks programmatically.

paragraphs: Generating a plausible program is only part of programming: users also need to revise it when its behavior misses their intent. ANPL addresses this interaction problem by giving users a structured way to divide a program into precise code and pieces described in natural language. The system also accepts input-output examples that the resulting program must satisfy.

Its organizing idea is a program sketch. The sketch specifies control and data flow, while designated holes contain submodules for a language model to implement. Users can change the sketch, rewrite a hole's description, or add examples for a particular hole. A hole can itself become another ANPL program, allowing the same process to repeat at a smaller scale. This makes local debugging possible without handing the rest of the program back to the model.

On ARC, ANPL outperforms programming baselines lacking interactive decomposition or guarantees about composing modules correctly. Evaluations on APPS, HumanEval, and practical programming tasks support its applicability across multiple domains. The released ARC solutions additionally document how people break unfamiliar tasks into programmable pieces.
summary.tldr: ANPL combines precise program sketches, natural-language submodules, and examples so users can recursively refine and debug generated code.

title: ANPL: Towards Natural Programming with Interactive Decomposition

abstract: Large multimodal models trained on natural documents, which interleave images and text, outperform models trained on image-text pairs on various multimodal benchmarks. However, the datasets used to train these models have not been released, and the collection process has not been fully specified. We introduce the OBELICS dataset, an open web-scale filtered dataset of interleaved image-text documents comprising 141 million web pages extracted from Common Crawl, 353 million associated images, and 115 billion text tokens. We describe the dataset creation process, present comprehensive filtering rules, and provide an analysis of the dataset's content. To show the viability of OBELICS, we train on the dataset vision and language models of 9 and 80 billion parameters, IDEFICS-9B and IDEFICS, and obtain competitive performance on different multimodal benchmarks. We release our dataset, models and code.

paragraphs: Multimodal training can use natural documents containing images interspersed with text, rather than only isolated image-text pairs. The abstract describes benchmark advantages for models trained on such documents, but notes that the underlying datasets and collection procedures have often been unavailable. OBELICS addresses this access and documentation gap.

The dataset contains 141 million web pages drawn from Common Crawl, with 353 million associated images and 115 billion text tokens. The authors explain how they created it, provide detailed filtering rules, and analyze its contents. These contributions make both the training material and its construction process available for examination and reuse.

To demonstrate that the dataset supports multimodal learning, the authors train models with 9 billion and 80 billion parameters, called IDEFICS-9B and IDEFICS. They report competitive results across different multimodal benchmarks. Releasing the dataset, models, and code provides a shared basis for work on learning from interleaved documents, with trained models serving as evidence of the dataset's practical viability.
summary.tldr: OBELICS releases a large, documented collection of interleaved image-text web documents and demonstrates its usefulness through competitive multimodal models.

title: OBELICS: An Open Web-Scale Filtered Dataset of Interleaved Image-Text Documents

abstract: Masked pre-training removes random input dimensions and learns a model that can predict the missing values. Empirical results indicate that this intuitive form of self-supervised learning yields models that generalize very well to new domains. A theoretical understanding is, however, lacking. This paper shows that masked pre-training with a suitable cumulative scoring function corresponds to maximizing the model's marginal likelihood, which is de facto the Bayesian model selection measure of generalization. Beyond shedding light on the success of masked pre-training, this insight also suggests that Bayesian models can be trained with appropriately designed self-supervision. Empirically, we confirm the developed theory and explore the main learning principles of masked pre-training in large language models.

paragraphs: Masked pre-training hides randomly selected parts of an input and trains a model to predict what is missing. Although this form of self-supervision has shown strong transfer to new domains, the paper seeks a theoretical account of that success. Its contribution connects the prediction task to a criterion used in Bayesian model selection.

The authors show that masked pre-training corresponds to maximizing a model's marginal likelihood when it uses a suitable cumulative scoring function. The scoring condition is essential to the stated equivalence. The result gives the masking objective a Bayesian interpretation, connecting how missing-value predictions are combined with a model-level measure associated with generalization.

This connection also suggests that appropriately designed self-supervision can be used to train Bayesian models. The authors empirically confirm their theory and investigate the learning principles of masked pre-training in large language models. The paper thus supplies both an explanation for a successful training approach and a route for designing self-supervised objectives around a Bayesian criterion.
summary.tldr: With a suitable cumulative scoring function, masked pre-training is equivalent to maximizing marginal likelihood, giving it a Bayesian interpretation.

title: On Masked Pre-training and the Marginal Likelihood

abstract: Quantifying dependence between high-dimensional random variables is central to statistical learning and inference. Two classical methods are canonical correlation analysis (CCA), which identifies maximally correlated projected versions of the original variables, and Shannon's mutual information, which is a universal dependence measure that also captures high-order dependencies. However, CCA only accounts for linear dependence, which may be insufficient for certain applications, while mutual information is often infeasible to compute/estimate in high dimensions. This work proposes a middle ground in the form of a scalable information-theoretic generalization of CCA, termed max-sliced mutual information (mSMI). mSMI equals the maximal mutual information between low-dimensional projections of the high-dimensional variables, which reduces back to CCA in the Gaussian case. It enjoys the best of both worlds: capturing intricate dependencies in the data while being amenable to fast computation and scalable estimation from samples. We show that mSMI retains favorable structural properties of Shannon's mutual information, like variational forms and identification of independence. We then study statistical estimation of mSMI, propose an efficiently computable neural estimator, and couple it with formal non-asymptotic error bounds. We present experiments that demonstrate the utility of mSMI for several tasks, encompassing independence testing, multi-view representation learning, algorithmic fairness, and generative modeling. We observe that mSMI consistently outperforms competing methods with little-to-no computational overhead.

paragraphs: Measuring relationships between high-dimensional variables presents a tradeoff. Canonical correlation analysis finds strongly correlated projections but captures only linear dependence. Mutual information can describe more intricate dependencies, yet estimating it directly in high dimensions is often impractical. This paper introduces max-sliced mutual information as a computationally manageable connection between these approaches.

The measure searches for low-dimensional projections with the greatest mutual information. It reduces to canonical correlation analysis in the Gaussian case while retaining useful properties of mutual information, including identification of independence and variational representations. The projection step moves estimation into smaller spaces, while the information-based objective can capture dependencies beyond linear correlation.

The authors study statistical estimation, develop an efficient neural estimator, and provide finite-sample error bounds. Experiments examine independence testing, learning from multiple views, algorithmic fairness, and generative modeling. Across those evaluations, the method consistently outperforms competing approaches with little or no computational overhead. These results support the proposed measure as a practical dependence objective for several different learning problems.
summary.tldr: Max-sliced mutual information measures rich dependence through optimized low-dimensional projections, combining scalable estimation with formal statistical guarantees.

title: Max-Sliced Mutual Information

abstract: The promising zero-shot generalization of vision-language models such as CLIP has led to their adoption using prompt learning for numerous downstream tasks. Previous works have shown test-time prompt tuning using entropy minimization to adapt text prompts for unseen domains. While effective, this overlooks the key cause for performance degradation to unseen domains -- distribution shift. In this work, we explicitly handle this problem by aligning the out-of-distribution (OOD) test sample statistics to those of the source data using prompt tuning. We use a single test sample to adapt multi-modal prompts at test time by minimizing the feature distribution shift to bridge the gap in the test domain. Evaluating against the domain generalization benchmark, our method improves zero-shot top-1 accuracy beyond existing prompt-learning techniques, with a 3.08% improvement over the baseline MaPLe. In cross-dataset generalization with unseen categories across 10 datasets, our method improves consistently across all datasets compared to the existing state-of-the-art. Our source code and models are available at [https://jameelhassan.github.io/promptalign](https://jameelhassan.github.io/promptalign)

paragraphs: Vision-language models can recognize categories through prompts, but their performance can decline when test images differ from the data used to prepare them. Earlier test-time prompt methods adapt prompts by reducing prediction uncertainty. This paper instead explicitly targets distribution shift: the mismatch between feature statistics at test time and those of the source data.

The method uses a single test example to adapt multimodal prompts. Its adjustment objective brings the example's feature statistics closer to the source statistics. This gives prompt adaptation a reference beyond the model's confidence: the representation of the new input should better align with the distribution on which the model was prepared.

On a domain-generalization benchmark, the authors report a 3.08% improvement in zero-shot top-1 accuracy over MaPLe. They also evaluate transfer across ten datasets containing unseen categories and report improvements over the existing state of the art on every dataset. These findings support distribution alignment as a useful test-time adaptation objective in the evaluated settings, including settings where the category set changes.
summary.tldr: Aligning test-example feature statistics with source statistics through prompt adaptation improves zero-shot generalization in the reported evaluations.

title: Align Your Prompts: Test-Time Prompting with Distribution Alignment for Zero-Shot Generalization

abstract: Recently, knowledge editing on large language models (LLMs) has received considerable attention. Compared to this, editing Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) faces extra challenges from diverse data modalities and complicated model components, and data for LVLMs editing are limited. The existing LVLM editing benchmark, which comprises three metrics (Reliability, Locality, and Generality), falls short in the quality of synthesized evaluation images and cannot assess whether models apply edited knowledge in relevant content. Therefore, we employ more reliable data collection methods to construct a new Large $\textbf{V}$ision-$\textbf{L}$anguage Model $\textbf{K}$nowledge $\textbf{E}$diting $\textbf{B}$enchmark, $\textbf{VLKEB}$, and extend the Portability metric for more comprehensive evaluation. Leveraging a multi-modal knowledge graph, our image data are bound with knowledge entities. This can be further used to extract entity-related knowledge, which constitutes the base of editing data. We conduct experiments of different editing methods on five LVLMs, and thoroughly analyze how do they impact the models. The results reveal strengths and deficiencies of these methods and hopefully provide insights for future research. The codes and dataset are available at: https://github.com/VLKEB/VLKEB.
