paragraphs: Knowledge editing changes information held by a model, but evaluating edits becomes more complicated when both images and language are involved. The paper identifies shortcomings in an existing vision-language editing benchmark: unreliable synthesized evaluation images and insufficient assessment of whether edited knowledge is used in related content. VLKEB is designed to improve that evaluation.

The benchmark uses a multimodal knowledge graph to connect images with knowledge entities. These connections allow the authors to extract entity-related information as the basis for editing examples. Alongside the existing reliability, locality, and generality measures, the work extends portability to assess whether an edit carries into relevant content, broadening what successful editing means in the evaluation.

The authors test different editing methods on five large vision-language models and analyze their effects. The results reveal strengths and deficiencies among the evaluated approaches. VLKEB's contribution is a more comprehensive benchmark and a more grounded construction of image-linked editing data, providing a way to study both the immediate edit and its use beyond the directly edited example.
summary.tldr: VLKEB links images to knowledge entities and adds portability evaluation to assess knowledge editing across five vision-language models.

title: VLKEB: A Large Vision-Language Model Knowledge Editing Benchmark

abstract: A major obstacle to the advancements of machine learning models in marine science, particularly in sonar imagery analysis, is the scarcity of AI-ready datasets. While there have been efforts to make AI-ready sonar image dataset publicly available, they suffer from limitations in terms of environment setting and scale. To bridge this gap, we introduce $\texttt{SeafloorAI}$, the first extensive AI-ready datasets for seafloor mapping across 5 geological layers that is curated in collaboration with marine scientists. We further extend the dataset to $\texttt{SeafloorGenAI}$ by incorporating the language component in order to facilitate the development of both $\textit{vision}$- and $\textit{language}$-capable machine learning models for sonar imagery. The dataset consists of 62 geo-distributed data surveys spanning 17,300 square kilometers, with 696K sonar images, 827K annotated segmentation masks, 696K detailed language descriptions and approximately 7M question-answer pairs. By making our data processing source code publicly available, we aim to engage the marine science community to enrich the data pool and inspire the machine learning community to develop more robust models. This collaborative approach will enhance the capabilities and applications of our datasets within both fields.

paragraphs: Machine learning for sonar imagery is constrained by the availability of datasets prepared for AI research. Existing public resources have limitations in scale and environmental coverage. SeafloorAI addresses this by assembling an extensive seafloor-mapping dataset across five geological layers in collaboration with marine scientists.

The collection spans 62 geographically distributed surveys covering 17,300 square kilometers. It includes 696,000 sonar images and 827,000 annotated segmentation masks. The authors extend this resource into SeafloorGenAI by adding a language component: 696,000 detailed descriptions and approximately seven million question-answer pairs. These additions support work on models that process sonar imagery together with language, alongside models focused on visual analysis.

The contribution centers on providing data and annotations at a scale intended to broaden research opportunities in marine science. Publicly available processing code is meant to help the marine science community expand the collection and encourage machine-learning researchers to develop more robust models. The proposed benefits are opportunities enabled by the resource and continued collaboration, rather than reported evidence of a particular model's performance improvement.
summary.tldr: SeafloorAI and its language-augmented extension provide large-scale sonar imagery, geological annotations, descriptions, and question-answer data for marine AI research.

title: SeafloorAI: A Large-scale Vision-Language Dataset for Seafloor Geological Survey

abstract: This study proves the two-phase dynamics of a deep neural network (DNN) learning interactions. Despite the long disappointing view of the faithfulness of post-hoc explanation of a DNN, a series of theorems have been proven [27] in recent years to show that for a given input sample, a small set of interactions between input variables can be considered as primitive inference patterns that faithfully represent a DNN's detailed inference logic on that sample. Particularly, Zhang et al. [41] have observed that various DNNs all learn interactions of different complexities in two distinct phases, and this two-phase dynamics well explains how a DNN changes from under-fitting to over-fitting. Therefore, in this study, we mathematically prove the two-phase dynamics of interactions, providing a theoretical mechanism for how the generalization power of a DNN changes during the training process. The explanation operates at the level of interaction learning, bringing a mathematical account to a training phenomenon that had previously been observed experimentally.

abstract: Reconstruction of static visual stimuli from non-invasion brain activity fMRI achieves great success, owning to advanced deep learning models such as CLIP and Stable Diffusion. However, the research on fMRI-to-video reconstruction remains limited since decoding the spatiotemporal perception of continuous visual experiences is formidably challenging. We contend that the key to addressing these challenges lies in accurately decoding both high-level semantics and low-level perception flows, as perceived by the brain in response to video stimuli. To the end, we propose NeuroClips, an innovative framework to decode high-fidelity and smooth video from fMRI. NeuroClips utilizes a semantics reconstructor to reconstruct video keyframes, guiding semantic accuracy and consistency, and employs a perception reconstructor to capture low-level perceptual details, ensuring video smoothness. During inference, it adopts a pre-trained T2V diffusion model injected with both keyframes and low-level perception flows for video reconstruction. Evaluated on a publicly available fMRI-video dataset, NeuroClips achieves smooth high-fidelity video reconstruction of up to 6s at 8FPS, gaining significant improvements over state-of-the-art models in various metrics, e.g., a 128% improvement in SSIM and an 81% improvement in spatiotemporal metrics. Our project is available at https://github.com/gongzix/NeuroClips.

paragraphs: Reconstructing video from fMRI requires recovering a continuous visual experience, including both its meaning and how its appearance changes over time. NeuroClips builds on the view that high-level semantics and low-level perceptual flows must both be decoded accurately. This separates two demands that a reconstruction must satisfy: recognizable content and smooth temporal behavior.

A semantics reconstructor produces video keyframes to guide content accuracy and consistency. A separate perception reconstructor captures lower-level visual details associated with smoothness. During inference, the framework supplies both keyframes and perceptual flows to a pretrained text-to-video diffusion model, which uses them to generate the reconstructed sequence.

The authors report improvements over state-of-the-art models, including 128% in SSIM and 81% in spatiotemporal metrics. These measured gains support the framework's division of semantic and perceptual decoding as a way to improve both fidelity and temporal quality in the evaluated reconstruction task.
summary.tldr: NeuroClips combines decoded keyframes and perceptual flows to reconstruct more faithful, smoother videos from fMRI.

title: NeuroClips: Towards High-fidelity and Smooth fMRI-to-Video Reconstruction

abstract: We consider the challenge of mitigating the generation of negative or toxic content by the Large Language Models (LLMs) in response to certain prompts. We propose integrating risk-averse principles into LLM fine-tuning to minimize the occurrence of harmful outputs, particularly rare but significant events. By optimizing the risk measure of Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR), our methodology trains LLMs to exhibit superior performance in avoiding toxic outputs while maintaining effectiveness in generative tasks. Empirical evaluations on sentiment modification and toxicity mitigation tasks demonstrate the efficacy of risk-averse reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF) in promoting a safer and more constructive online discourse environment.

paragraphs: This paper addresses language models producing negative or toxic content in response to some prompts. Its focus includes harmful outcomes that occur rarely but remain significant. The proposed approach brings risk aversion into fine-tuning so that these undesirable outcomes receive explicit attention in the training objective.

The method optimizes Conditional Value at Risk, or CVaR, within reinforcement learning with human feedback. CVaR directs attention toward the unfavorable part of an outcome distribution, making it relevant when occasional severe failures matter. Applied here, the objective is to reduce harmful generations while preserving the model's effectiveness on generative tasks.

The authors evaluate the approach on sentiment modification and toxicity mitigation, reporting that risk-averse training improves avoidance of toxic outputs while maintaining task effectiveness. These findings support treating the distribution of undesirable outcomes as part of the fine-tuning problem. The contribution is an objective-level approach to reducing harmful responses, with the reported empirical support coming from the two evaluated task types.
summary.tldr: Risk-averse fine-tuning uses CVaR to reduce toxic language-model outputs while preserving effectiveness in the evaluated generative tasks.

title: Risk-Averse Fine-tuning of Large Language Models

abstract: Diffusion-based models have achieved notable empirical successes in reinforcement learning (RL) due to their expressiveness in modeling complex distributions. Despite existing methods being promising, the key challenge of extending existing methods for broader real-world applications lies in the computational cost at inference time, i.e., sampling from a diffusion model is considerably slow as it often requires tens to hundreds of iterations to generate even one sample. To circumvent this issue, we propose to leverage the flexibility of diffusion models for RL from a representation learning perspective. In particular, by exploiting the connection between diffusion models and energy-based models, we develop Diffusion Spectral Representation (Diff-SR), a coherent algorithm framework that enables extracting sufficient representations for value functions in Markov decision processes (MDP) and partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDP). We further demonstrate how Diff-SR facilitates efficient policy optimization and practical algorithms while explicitly bypassing the difficulty and inference cost of sampling from the diffusion model. Finally, we provide comprehensive empirical studies to verify the benefits of Diff-SR in delivering robust and advantageous performance across various benchmarks with both fully and partially observable settings.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can represent complex distributions that are useful in reinforcement learning, but generating samples often takes many iterative steps. That inference cost creates an obstacle when using them to support decisions. Diffusion Spectral Representation, or Diff-SR, investigates how to obtain their representational benefits without relying on expensive diffusion sampling.

The framework uses a connection between diffusion models and energy-based models to extract representations for value functions. These representations are described as sufficient for value functions in both fully observable Markov decision processes and partially observable ones. The focus is therefore on retaining information needed to evaluate decisions, rather than directly generating samples through the diffusion process.

The paper shows how these representations support efficient policy optimization and practical algorithms that bypass diffusion sampling and its inference cost. Empirical studies cover benchmarks with both full and partial observability and report robust, advantageous performance. Together, the theoretical framework and experiments support representation learning as another route for applying expressive diffusion models to reinforcement learning.
summary.tldr: Diff-SR extracts value-function representations from diffusion models to support reinforcement learning without costly diffusion sampling.

title: Diffusion Spectral Representation for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Techniques that learn improved representations via offline data or self-supervised objectives have shown impressive results in traditional reinforcement learning.Nevertheless, it is unclear how improved representation learning can benefit reinforcement learning from human feedback on language models.In this work, we propose training reward models (RMs) in a contrastive, $\textit{goal-conditioned}$ fashion by increasing the representation similarity of future states along sampled preferred trajectories and decreasing the similarity along randomly sampled dispreferred trajectories.This objective significantly improves reward model performance by up to 0.09 AUROC across challenging benchmarks, such as MATH and GSM8k. These findings extend to general alignment as well -- on the Helpful-Harmless dataset, we observe 2.3\% increase in accuracy.Beyond improving reward model performance, we show this way of training RM representations enables improved steerability because it allows us to evaluate the likelihood of an action achieving a particular goal-state (e.g. whether a solution is correct or helpful).Leveraging this insight, we find that we can filter up to 55\% of generated tokens during majority voting by discarding trajectories likely to end up in an "incorrect" state, which leads to significant cost savings.We additionally find that these representations can perform fine-grained control by conditioning on desired future goal-states.For example, we show that steering a Llama 3 model towards helpful generations with our approach improves helpfulness by $9.6$\% over a supervised-fine-tuning trained baseline.Similarly, steering the model towards complex generations improves complexity by $21.6$\% over the baseline.Overall, we find that training RMs in this contrastive, goal-conditioned fashion significantly improves performance and enables model steerability.

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether learning better internal representations can improve reward models used in reinforcement learning from human feedback. Its approach connects those representations to possible future outcomes, such as a correct solution or a helpful response, making them useful for evaluating where a generation is heading.

The authors train with a contrastive objective: they increase representation similarity for future states along sampled preferred trajectories and decrease similarity along randomly sampled dispreferred trajectories. This ties representation learning to preferences and future goals. They report reward-model improvements of up to 0.09 AUROC across challenging benchmarks including MATH and GSM8k, plus a 2.3% accuracy increase on Helpful-Harmless.

The learned representations also let the system evaluate how likely an action is to reach a particular goal. During majority voting, the authors use this capability to discard trajectories predicted to end incorrectly. They report filtering up to 55% of generated tokens, yielding cost savings by avoiding further generation along those trajectories.

Conditioning on desired future states also supports control over response characteristics. When steering Llama 3, the approach improves helpfulness by 9.6% and complexity by 21.6% over a baseline trained with supervised fine-tuning. These findings suggest that the same representation-training approach can improve reward evaluation and guide generation toward specified outcomes.
summary.tldr: Training reward models to connect preferred generation paths with future goals improves reported evaluation performance and enables more efficient, controllable generation.

title: Learning Goal-Conditioned Representations for Language Reward Models

abstract: The softmax function is ubiquitous in machine learning and optimization applications. Computing the full softmax evaluation of a matrix-vector product can be computationally expensive in high-dimensional settings. In many applications, however, it is sufficient to calculate only the top few outputs of the softmax function. In this work, we present an algorithm, dubbed AdaptiveSoftmax, that adaptively computes the top k softmax values more efficiently than the full softmax computation, with probabilistic guarantees. We demonstrate the sample efficiency improvements afforded by AdaptiveSoftmax on real and synthetic data to corroborate our theoretical results. AdaptiveSoftmax yields >10x gain over full softmax computation on most datasets, yielding up to 30x improvement for Mistral7B evaluated on the Wikitext dataset. The adaptive method we propose for estimating the partition function (the softmax denominator) is of independent interest and can be used in other applications such as kernel density estimation.

paragraphs: Softmax turns a collection of scores into normalized values, but evaluating it after a large matrix-vector product can be expensive. Many applications only need the largest few outputs. This paper asks how to exploit that narrower requirement without paying the full computational cost of evaluating every output precisely.

The proposed algorithm, AdaptiveSoftmax, uses adaptive sampling to approximate the top k softmax values with probabilistic guarantees. A central part of the approach is estimating the partition function: the denominator that normalizes the scores. Even when only a few outputs matter, their normalized values still depend on this shared denominator, making its efficient estimation an important part of the problem.

Experiments on real and synthetic data support the theoretical sample-efficiency results. The authors report gains exceeding tenfold over full softmax computation on most evaluated datasets, reaching thirtyfold for Mistral7B on Wikitext. These are reported results for the evaluated settings. The denominator-estimation method also has potential uses beyond softmax, including kernel density estimation.
summary.tldr: AdaptiveSoftmax uses adaptive sampling to approximate the largest softmax values efficiently, with probabilistic guarantees and substantial reported computational gains.

title: Adaptive Sampling for Efficient Softmax Approximation

abstract: Intelligent agents must be generalists, capable of quickly adapting to various tasks. In reinforcement learning (RL), model-based RL learns a dynamics model of the world, in principle enabling transfer to arbitrary reward functions through planning. However, autoregressive model rollouts suffer from compounding error, making model-based RL ineffective for long-horizon problems. Successor features offer an alternative by modeling a policy's long-term state occupancy, reducing policy evaluation under new rewards to linear regression. Yet, policy optimization with successor features can be challenging. This work proposes a novel class of models, i.e., Distributional Successor Features for Zero-Shot Policy Optimization (DiSPOs), that learn a distribution of successor features of a stationary dataset's behavior policy, along with a policy that acts to realize different successor features within the dataset. By directly modeling long-term outcomes in the dataset, DiSPOs avoid compounding error while enabling a simple scheme for zero-shot policy optimization across reward functions. We present a practical instantiation of DiSPOs using diffusion models and show their efficacy as a new class of transferable models, both theoretically and empirically across various simulated robotics problems. Videos and code are available at https://weirdlabuw.github.io/dispo/.

paragraphs: Adapting an agent to a new reward function requires understanding which behavior will produce valuable outcomes. Predicting the world one step at a time can accumulate errors over long horizons. Successor features offer another route by summarizing a policy's long-term state occupancy, making evaluation under new rewards simpler, although optimizing policies through those summaries remains challenging.

DiSPO learns a distribution of successor features associated with the behavior policy in a stationary dataset. It also learns a policy that can act to realize different successor features available within that dataset. This links a collection of long-term outcome summaries to behaviors that can pursue them, enabling a simple procedure for policy optimization across reward functions.

Because the model represents long-term outcomes directly, it avoids the compounding error associated with autoregressive rollouts. The authors implement the approach using diffusion models and provide theoretical and empirical support across simulated robotics problems. Its transfer capability is grounded in the outcomes represented in the dataset, which is central to how its zero-shot policy optimization operates.
summary.tldr: DiSPO models distributions of long-term outcomes and corresponding behaviors to enable zero-shot policy optimization across reward functions.

title: Distributional Successor Features Enable Zero-Shot Policy Optimization

abstract: The optimal policy in various real-world strategic decision-making problems depends both on the environmental configuration and exogenous events. For these settings, we introduce Contextual Bilevel Reinforcement Learning (CB-RL), a stochastic bilevel decision-making model, where the lower level consists of solving a contextual Markov Decision Process (CMDP). CB-RL can be viewed as a Stackelberg Game where the leader and a random context beyond the leader’s control together decide the setup of many MDPs that potentially multiple followers best respond to. This framework extends beyond traditional bilevel optimization and finds relevance in diverse fields such as RLHF, tax design, reward shaping, contract theory and mechanism design. We propose a stochastic Hyper Policy Gradient Descent (HPGD) algorithm to solve CB-RL, and demonstrate its convergence. Notably, HPGD uses stochastic hypergradient estimates, based on observations of the followers’ trajectories. Therefore, it allows followers to use any training procedure and the leader to be agnostic of the specific algorithm, which aligns with various real-world scenarios. We further consider the setting when the leader can influence the training of followers and propose an accelerated algorithm. We empirically demonstrate the performance of our algorithm for reward shaping and tax design.

paragraphs: An incentive designer chooses rules, but the outcome also depends on how others respond and on circumstances outside the designer’s control. Contextual Bilevel Reinforcement Learning models this interaction as a two-level decision problem. A leader and a random context jointly determine the environments in which one or more followers choose their best responses.

The lower-level problem is a contextual Markov decision process. This allows the framework to describe settings such as reward shaping and tax design, where changing incentives alters learned behavior. The authors propose Hyper Policy Gradient Descent, a stochastic algorithm for updating the leader’s policy, and demonstrate its convergence.

The algorithm estimates the leader’s learning signal from observed follower trajectories. Consequently, followers can use any training procedure without requiring the leader to know its specific implementation. The paper also considers a setting where the leader can influence follower training and introduces an accelerated algorithm for that case. Empirical demonstrations in reward shaping and tax design show how the framework can be applied to incentive problems with contextual variation.
summary.tldr: CB-RL learns incentives from followers’ observed behavior while accounting for random context and allowing unknown follower training procedures.

title: Contextual Bilevel Reinforcement Learning for Incentive Alignment

abstract: Large Language Models for code (code LLMs) have witnessed tremendous progress in recent years. With the rapid development of code LLMs, many popular evaluation benchmarks, such as HumanEval, DS-1000, and MBPP, have emerged to measure the performance of code LLMs with a particular focus on code generation tasks. However, they are insufficient to cover the full range of expected capabilities of code LLMs, which span beyond code generation to answering diverse coding-related questions. To fill this gap, we propose InfiBench, the first large-scale freeform question-answering (QA) benchmark for code to our knowledge, comprising 234 carefully selected high-quality Stack Overflow questions that span across 15 programming languages. InfiBench uses four types of model-free automatic metrics to evaluate response correctness where domain experts carefully concretize the criterion for each question. We conduct a systematic evaluation for over 100 latest code LLMs on InfiBench, leading to a series of novel and insightful findings. Our detailed analyses showcase potential directions for further advancement of code LLMs. InfiBench is fully open source at https://infi-coder.github.io/infibench and continuously expanding to foster more scientific and systematic practices for code LLM evaluation.

paragraphs: A coding assistant needs to answer questions as well as generate code. Benchmarks centered on code generation therefore cover only part of its expected capabilities. InfiBench addresses this gap with a freeform question-answering benchmark intended to evaluate how models respond to diverse coding-related questions.

The benchmark contains 234 carefully selected Stack Overflow questions covering 15 programming languages. It uses four types of automatic correctness metrics that do not depend on another model acting as the evaluator. Domain experts specify concrete criteria for each question. This combination connects automated assessment to question-specific expectations, allowing freeform answers to be evaluated against deliberately defined requirements.

The authors systematically evaluate more than 100 code language models and use the results to analyze opportunities for improvement. The abstract does not enumerate those individual findings, so the main supported takeaway is the expanded evaluation scope and its expert-defined assessment process. InfiBench is released openly and described as continuing to expand, providing a shared resource for studying coding assistance beyond code generation alone.
summary.tldr: InfiBench evaluates coding-question answers using 234 Stack Overflow questions across 15 languages and expert-defined automatic correctness criteria.

title: InfiBench: Evaluating the Question-Answering Capabilities of Code Large Language Models

abstract: Privacy protection of users' entire contribution of samples is important in distributed systems. The most effective approach is the two-stage scheme, which finds a small interval first and then gets a refined estimate by clipping samples into the interval. However, the clipping operation induces bias, which is serious if the sample distribution is heavy-tailed. Besides, users with large local sample sizes can make the sensitivity much larger, thus the method is not suitable for imbalanced users. Motivated by these challenges, we propose a Huber loss minimization approach to mean estimation under user-level differential privacy. The connecting points of Huber loss can be adaptively adjusted to deal with imbalanced users. Moreover, it avoids the clipping operation, thus significantly reducing the bias compared with the two-stage approach. We provide a theoretical analysis of our approach, which gives the noise strength needed for privacy protection, as well as the bound of mean squared error. The result shows that the new method is much less sensitive to the imbalance of user-wise sample sizes and the tail of sample distributions. Finally, we perform numerical experiments to validate our theoretical analysis.

paragraphs: The paper studies estimating a mean while protecting each user's entire contribution of samples. A prominent existing approach first identifies a small interval and then clips samples into it before refining the estimate. The authors identify two problems: clipping can create substantial bias for heavy-tailed data, and users contributing many samples can greatly increase sensitivity.

Their alternative estimates the mean by minimizing Huber loss. Its connecting points can be adjusted adaptively to accommodate users with unequal sample counts. Because the method avoids the clipping operation used by the two-stage approach, it substantially reduces the associated bias. This connects the estimation procedure directly to the two difficulties motivating the work.

The theoretical analysis specifies the noise strength needed for privacy protection and bounds mean squared error. It indicates that the method is much less sensitive to unequal user contributions and distribution tails. Numerical experiments validate that analysis. The contribution is therefore both a private estimation method and an account of its privacy and accuracy behavior.
summary.tldr: Adaptive Huber-loss minimization estimates means with user-level privacy while reducing sensitivity to heavy tails and unequal user sample counts.

title: A Huber Loss Minimization Approach to Mean Estimation under User-level Differential Privacy

abstract: Ensemble learning is a popular technique to improve the accuracy of machine learning models. It traditionally hinges on the rationale that aggregating multiple weak models can lead to better models with lower variance and hence higher stability, especially for discontinuous base learners. In this paper, we provide a new perspective on ensembling. By selecting the most frequently generated model from the base learner when repeatedly applied to subsamples, we can attain exponentially decaying tails for the excess risk, even if the base learner suffers from slow (i.e., polynomial) decay rates. This tail enhancement power of ensembling applies to base learners that have reasonable predictive power to begin with and is stronger than variance reduction in the sense of exhibiting rate improvement. We demonstrate how our ensemble methods can substantially improve out-of-sample performances in a range of numerical examples involving heavy-tailed data or intrinsically slow rates.

paragraphs: Ensemble learning is commonly explained as a way to reduce variance by combining several models. This paper studies a different benefit: reducing the probability of unusually poor generalization. Its focus is the tail of excess risk, which describes how likely a learned model is to perform substantially worse than the relevant risk reference.

The proposed procedure repeatedly applies a base learner to subsamples and selects the model that appears most frequently. For base learners with reasonable predictive ability, the authors show that this can produce exponentially decaying excess-risk tails even when the original learner has only polynomial decay. The qualification about the starting learner matters: the result does not assert that ensembling supplies predictive ability from an arbitrary ineffective learner.

An improvement in the decay rate goes beyond merely lowering a variance value; it changes how sharply the probability of poor outcomes diminishes. Numerical examples involving heavy-tailed data or intrinsically slow rates show substantial improvements in out-of-sample performance. The paper thus offers a reliability-oriented explanation for why subsampled ensembles can help.
summary.tldr: Selecting the most frequent model across subsamples can improve excess-risk tails from polynomial to exponential decay for suitably predictive base learners.

title: Subsampled Ensemble Can Improve Generalization Tail Exponentially

abstract: In large-scale recommendation systems, multimodal (MM) content is increasingly introduced to enhance the generalization of ID features. The rise of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) enables the construction of unified user and item representations. However, the semantic distribution gap between MM and ID representations leads to \textit{convergence inconsistency} during joint training: the ID branch converges quickly, while the MM branch requires more epochs, thus limiting overall performance. To address this, we propose a two-stage framework including MM representation learning and joint training optimization. First, we fine-tune the MLLM to generate unified user and item representations, and introduce collaborative signals by post-aligning user ID representations to alleviate semantic differences. Then, we propose an Adaptive Gradient Masking (AGM) training strategy to dynamically regulate parameter updates between ID and MLLM branches. AGM estimates the contribution of each representation with mutual information, and applies non-uniform gradient masking at the sub-network level to balance optimization. We provide theoretical analysis of AGM's effectiveness and further introduce an unbiased variant, AGM*, to enhance training stability. Experiments on offline and online A/B tests validate the effectiveness of our approach in mitigating convergence inconsistency and improving performance.

paragraphs: Recommendation systems can combine representations learned from user and item identifiers with representations of multimodal content. These sources contribute different information, but they do not necessarily learn at the same pace. The paper identifies a training mismatch: the identifier branch converges quickly, while the multimodal branch needs more epochs, limiting the benefit of training them together.

The proposed framework first fine-tunes a multimodal language model to produce unified user and item representations. It then incorporates collaborative information through an alignment step involving user identifier representations. This prepares the representations for joint training by reducing their semantic differences.

During joint training, Adaptive Gradient Masking estimates each representation's contribution using mutual information and selectively masks parameter updates across subnetworks. This gives the branches different update patterns to balance their optimization. The authors provide theoretical analysis and introduce an unbiased variant, AGM*, intended to improve stability. Offline experiments and online A/B tests support improvements in recommendation performance and reduced convergence inconsistency, connecting the training intervention to both experimental and deployed evaluation.
summary.tldr: Adaptive Gradient Masking balances updates between identifier and multimodal recommendation branches that learn at different speeds.

title: Adaptive Gradient Masking for Balancing ID and MLLM-based Representations in Recommendation

abstract: We introduce MIRAGE, a new benchmark for multimodal expert-level reasoning and decision-making in consultative interaction settings. Designed for the domain of agriculture, MIRAGE captures the full complexity of expert consultations by combining natural user queries, expert-authored responses, and image-based context, offering a high-fidelity benchmark for evaluating models on grounded reasoning, clarification strategies, and long-form generation in a real-world, knowledge-intensive domain. Grounded in over 35,000 real user-expert interactions, and curated through a carefully designed multi-step pipeline, MIRAGE spans diverse crop health, pest diagnosis, and crop management scenarios. The benchmark includes more than 7,000 unique biological entities, covering plant species, pests, and diseases, making it one of the most taxonomically diverse benchmarks available for vision-language models in real-world expert-guided domains. Unlike existing benchmarks that rely on well-specified user inputs, MIRAGE features underspecified, context-rich scenarios, requiring models to infer latent knowledge gaps and either proactively guide the interaction or respond. Our benchmark comprises two core components. The Single-turn Challenge to reason over a single user turn and image set, identify relevant entities, infer causal explanations, and generate actionable recommendations; and a Multi-Turn challenge for dialogue state tracking, goal-driven generation, and expert-level conversational decision-making. We evaluate more than 20 closed and open-source frontier vision-language models (VLMs), using three reasoning language models as evaluators, highlighting the significant challenges posed by MIRAGE in both single-turn and multi-turn interaction settings. Even the advanced GPT4.1 and GPT4o models achieve 44.6% and 40.9% accuracy, respectively, indicating significant room for improvement.

paragraphs: Agricultural consultations often begin with incomplete descriptions and images, leaving an expert to determine what information is missing. MIRAGE evaluates this kind of interaction by combining real user queries, expert-written responses, and visual context. It draws on more than 35,000 user-expert interactions and covers over 7,000 biological entities across crop health, pest diagnosis, and crop management.

The benchmark has two components. The single-turn challenge tests entity identification, causal explanations, and actionable recommendations from one query and its images. The multi-turn challenge tests tracking the conversation, pursuing its goals, and deciding how to proceed. Because inputs are underspecified, models must assess whether to answer or actively guide the exchange toward needed information.

The authors evaluate more than 20 open and closed frontier vision-language models with three reasoning language models serving as evaluators. GPT4.1 and GPT4o reach reported accuracies of 44.6% and 40.9%, respectively. These results show substantial difficulty in the benchmark’s expert consultation tasks, including both individual responses and sustained interactions.
summary.tldr: MIRAGE tests whether vision-language models can reason, seek missing information, and guide agricultural consultations grounded in real expert interactions.

title: MIRAGE: A Benchmark for Multimodal Information-Seeking and Reasoning in Agricultural Expert-Guided Conversations

abstract: Planning under opponent uncertainty is a fundamental challenge in multi-agent environments, where an agent must act while inferring the hidden policies of its opponents. Existing type-based methods rely on manually defined behavior classes and struggle to scale, while model-free approaches are sample-inefficient and lack a principled way to incorporate uncertainty into planning. We propose Quantized Opponent Models (QOM), which learn a compact catalog of opponent types via a quantized autoencoder and maintain a Bayesian belief over these types online. This posterior supports both a belief-weighted meta-policy and a Monte-Carlo planning algorithm that directly integrates uncertainty, enabling real-time belief updates and focused exploration. Experiments show that QOM achieves superior performance with lower search cost, offering a tractable and effective solution for belief-aware planning.

paragraphs: An agent facing other decision-makers must choose actions while remaining uncertain about how its opponents behave. Quantized Opponent Models address this by learning a compact collection of opponent types. This replaces manually specified behavior categories with types discovered through a quantized autoencoder, giving the planner a manageable set of possibilities to consider.

During interaction, the agent maintains a Bayesian belief over those types and updates it as evidence arrives. The belief supports two ways to act: a meta-policy weighted by the probabilities of different types, and a Monte Carlo planner that explicitly incorporates uncertainty. Both use the current distribution over possible opponents rather than requiring certainty about a single opponent model.

The authors report better performance with lower search cost in their experiments. The proposed organization makes uncertainty operational: it influences both action selection and focused exploration, with beliefs updated in real time. The central contribution is therefore a learned, compact interface between opponent modeling and planning, allowing the system to reason about multiple plausible behaviors without relying on a manually designed catalog.
summary.tldr: Quantized Opponent Models learn compact opponent types and maintain Bayesian beliefs over them to support efficient planning under uncertainty.

title: Planning with Quantized Opponent Models

abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has proven effective in integrating knowledge into large language models (LLMs). However, conventional RAGs struggle to capture complex relationships between pieces of knowledge, limiting their performance in intricate reasoning that requires integrating knowledge from multiple sources. Recently, graph-enhanced retrieval augmented generation (GraphRAG) builds a graph structure to explicitly model these relationships, enabling more effective and efficient retrievers. Nevertheless, its performance is still hindered by the noise and incompleteness within the graph structure. To address this, we introduce GFM-RAG, a novel graph foundation model (GFM) for retrieval augmented generation. GFM-RAG is powered by an innovative graph neural network that reasons over graph structure to capture complex query-knowledge relationships. The GFM with 8M parameters undergoes a two-stage training process on large-scale datasets, comprising 60 knowledge graphs with over 14M triples and 700k documents. This results in impressive performance and generalizability for GFM-RAG, making it the first graph foundation model applicable to unseen datasets for retrieval without any fine-tuning required. Extensive experiments on three multi-hop QA datasets and seven domain-specific RAG datasets demonstrate that GFM-RAG achieves state-of-the-art performance while maintaining efficiency and alignment with neural scaling laws, highlighting its potential for further improvement.

paragraphs: Retrieval-augmented generation supplies a language model with relevant external knowledge. Questions requiring several connected facts can be difficult when retrieval does not capture their relationships. Graph-based retrieval makes those links explicit, but noisy or missing connections can still weaken its results.

GFM-RAG uses a graph neural network to reason about the relationship between a query and knowledge represented in a graph. Its eight-million-parameter graph foundation model is trained in two stages using 60 knowledge graphs containing more than 14 million triples and 700,000 documents. The resulting retriever can be applied to unseen datasets without fine-tuning, making transfer across knowledge collections a central part of the contribution.

Experiments cover three multi-hop question-answering datasets and seven domain-specific retrieval-augmented generation datasets. The authors report state-of-the-art performance while maintaining efficiency. They also observe behavior consistent with neural scaling laws, which they present as suggesting further improvement through scaling. The findings support learning a reusable graph retrieval model for reasoning that depends on relationships among multiple pieces of evidence.
summary.tldr: GFM-RAG learns a reusable graph retriever that transfers to unseen datasets without fine-tuning and improves multi-source question answering.

title: GFM-RAG: Graph Foundation Model for Retrieval Augmented Generation

abstract: Discovering symbolic Partial Differential Equation (PDE) from data is one of the most promising directions of modern scientific discovery. Effectively constructing an expressive yet concise hypothesis space and accurately evaluating expression values, however, remain challenging due to the exponential explosion with the spatial dimension and the noise in the measurements. To address these challenges, we propose the ABL-PDE approach that employs the Abductive Learning (ABL) framework to discover symbolic PDEs. By introducing a First-Order Logic (FOL) knowledge base, ABL-PDE can represent various PDEs, significantly constraining the hypothesis space without sacrificing expressive power, while also facilitating the incorporation of problem-specific knowledge. The proposed consistency optimization process establishes a synergistic interaction between the knowledge base and the neural network learning module, achieving robust structure identification, accurate coefficient estimation, and enhanced stability against hyperparameter variation. Experimental results on three benchmarks across different noise levels demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in PDE discovery.

paragraphs: Discovering a symbolic partial differential equation from measurements requires finding both an equation's structure and its numerical coefficients. The search becomes difficult as spatial dimension increases, while measurement noise makes candidate expressions harder to evaluate accurately. ABL-PDE addresses these two challenges by combining logical knowledge with a neural learning module.

Its first-order logic knowledge base represents a variety of PDEs while constraining the candidate search space. The authors state that this restriction preserves expressive power and allows problem-specific knowledge to be incorporated. A consistency optimization process then links the knowledge base and the neural network, so symbolic reasoning and learning interact during equation discovery.

The paper reports robust identification of equation structure, accurate coefficient estimation, and improved stability as hyperparameters vary. Experiments on three benchmarks at different noise levels support the approach's effectiveness. The significance is that symbolic knowledge contributes directly to organizing the search, while the neural component participates in the same optimization process, addressing both the size of the hypothesis space and noisy evaluation.
summary.tldr: ABL-PDE combines logical constraints and neural learning to discover symbolic PDE structures and coefficients from noisy data.

title: Discovering Symbolic Partial Differential Equation by Abductive Learning

abstract: This paper presents a unified framework that allows high-quality dynamic Gaussian Splatting from both defocused and motion-blurred monocular videos. Due to the significant difference between the formation processes of defocus blur and motion blur, existing methods are tailored for either one of them, lacking the ability to simultaneously deal with both of them. Although the two can be jointly modeled as blur kernel-based convolution, the inherent difficulty in estimating accurate blur kernels greatly limits the progress in this direction. In this work, we go a step further towards this direction. Particularly, we propose to estimate per-pixel reliable blur kernels using a blur prediction network that exploits blur-related scene and camera information and is subject to a blur-aware sparsity constraint. Besides, we introduce a dynamic Gaussian densification strategy to mitigate the lack of Gaussians for incomplete regions, and boost the performance of novel view synthesis by incorporating unseen view information to constrain scene optimization. Extensive experiments show that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art methods in generating photorealistic novel view synthesis from defocused and motion-blurred monocular videos. Our code is available at https://github.com/hhhddddddd/dydeblur.

paragraphs: This paper reconstructs dynamic scenes from single-camera videos containing both defocus blur and motion blur. These forms of blur arise differently, and existing approaches tend to address one at a time. Although both can be represented using blur kernels, accurately estimating those kernels is a central obstacle to handling them together.

The proposed framework predicts a blur kernel for each pixel using a network informed by scene and camera information. A blur-aware sparsity constraint helps guide those predictions. The method also dynamically adds Gaussians to address incomplete regions with too few scene elements. Information from unseen views provides an additional constraint during scene optimization.

Experiments show better photorealistic synthesis of new views than the state-of-the-art methods used for comparison. The contribution combines blur estimation with improvements to the underlying scene representation. This matters because resolving blur alone does not address incomplete reconstruction: the framework tackles both sources of difficulty when learning a dynamic scene from degraded video.
summary.tldr: A unified Gaussian-splatting framework reconstructs dynamic scenes from videos containing both defocus and motion blur.

title: Dynamic Gaussian Splatting from Defocused and Motion-blurred Monocular Videos

abstract: This paper studies the problem of class-incremental learning (CIL), a core setting within continual learning where a model learns a sequence of tasks, each containing a distinct set of classes. Traditional CIL methods, which do not leverage pre-trained models (PTMs), suffer from catastrophic forgetting (CF) due to the need to incrementally learn both feature representations and the classifier. The integration of PTMs into CIL has recently led to efficient approaches that treat the PTM as a fixed feature extractor combined with analytic classifiers, achieving state-of-the-art performance. However, they still face a major limitation: the inability to continually adapt feature representations to best suit the CIL tasks, leading to suboptimal performance. To address this, we propose AnaCP (Analytic Contrastive Projection), a novel method that preserves the efficiency of analytic classifiers while enabling incremental feature adaptation without gradient-based training, thereby eliminating the CF caused by gradient updates. Our experiments show that AnaCP not only outperforms existing baselines but also achieves the accuracy level of joint training, which is regarded as the upper bound of CIL.

paragraphs: Class-incremental learning asks a model to learn successive groups of classes while retaining what it learned earlier. Updating both its feature representations and classifier can cause catastrophic forgetting. One efficient approach uses a pretrained model as a fixed feature extractor and combines it with an analytic classifier, but fixed features cannot continually adjust to the incoming tasks.

AnaCP addresses this restriction by enabling incremental feature adaptation while preserving the efficiency of analytic classification. Its adaptation does not require gradient-based training. This targets a specific source of forgetting: changes introduced by gradient updates. The central idea is to make the representation more suitable for successive classification tasks without giving up the computational advantages of analytic methods.

In the reported experiments, AnaCP outperforms existing baselines and reaches the accuracy of joint training, which the paper treats as the upper reference level for this setting. This is an empirical result, rather than a guarantee for every task sequence. It shows that adapting features analytically can substantially narrow the observed gap between sequential and joint learning.
summary.tldr: AnaCP adapts features without gradient training and matches joint-training accuracy in the reported class-incremental learning experiments.

title: AnaCP: Toward Upper-Bound Continual Learning via Analytic Contrastive Projection

abstract: The advancements in generative models and the real-world attack of machine-generated text(MGT) create a demand for more robust detection methods. The existing MGT detection methods for adversarial environments primarily consist of manually designed statistical-based methods and fine-tuned classifier-based approaches. Statistical-based methods extract intrinsic features but suffer from rigid decision boundaries vulnerable to adaptive attacks, while fine-tuned classifiers achieve outstanding performance at the cost of overfitting to superficial textual feature. We argue that the key to detection in current adversarial environments lies in how to extract intrinsic invariant features and ensure that the classifier possesses dynamic adaptability. In that case, we propose OSTAR, a novel MGT detection framework designed for adversarial environments which composed of a statistical enhanced classifier and a Multi-Faceted Contrastive Learning(MFCL). In the classifier aspect, our Multi-Dimensional Statistical Profiling (MDSP) module extracts intrinsic difference between human and machine texts, complementing classifiers with useful stable features. In the model optimization aspect, the MFCL strategy enhances robustness by contrasting feature variations before and after text attacks, jointly optimizing statistical feature mapping and baseline pre-trained models. Experimental results on three public datasets under various adversarial scenarios demonstrate that our framework outperforms existing MGT detection methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance and robust against attacks.The code is available at https://github.com/BUPT-SN/OSTAR.

paragraphs: Detecting machine-generated text becomes harder when text is deliberately modified to evade a detector. The authors describe a tension between statistical methods, whose decision rules can be rigid, and trained classifiers, which can overfit superficial textual cues. OSTAR combines statistical information with classifier training to seek more stable features and better adaptability under attacks.

Its Multi-Dimensional Statistical Profiling module extracts statistical differences between human and machine text and supplies them to the classifier. A second component, Multi-Faceted Contrastive Learning, compares feature variations before and after text attacks. Training jointly adjusts the statistical feature mapping and the underlying pretrained model, so robustness is addressed in both the supplied features and their learned use.

Experiments cover three public datasets and several adversarial scenarios. The authors report state-of-the-art performance relative to existing detection methods and improved resistance to the tested attacks. The results support combining statistical profiling with attack-aware representation learning, rather than relying on either component alone to provide the detector’s decision-making capability.
summary.tldr: OSTAR combines statistical text features with contrastive learning on attacked text to improve machine-generated-text detection under adversarial conditions.

title: OSTAR: Optimized Statistical Text-classifier with Adversarial Resistance

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly central to agentic systems due to their strong reasoning and planning capabilities. By interacting with external environments through predefined tools, these agents can carry out complex user tasks. Nonetheless, this interaction also introduces the risk of prompt injection attacks, where malicious inputs from external sources can mislead the agent’s behavior, potentially resulting in economic loss, privacy leakage, or system compromise. System-level defenses have recently shown promise by enforcing static or predefined policies, but they still face two key challenges: the ability to dynamically update security rules and the need for memory stream isolation. To address these challenges, we propose DRIFT, a Dynamic Rule-based Isolation Framework for Trustworthy agentic systems, which enforces both control- and data-level constraints. A Secure Planner first constructs a minimal function trajectory and a JSON-schema-style parameter checklist for each function node based on the user query. A Dynamic Validator then monitors deviations from the original plan, assessing whether changes comply with privilege limitations and the user's intent. Finally, an \textit{Injection Isolator} detects and masks any instructions that may conflict with the user query from the memory stream to mitigate long-term risks. We empirically validate the effectiveness of DRIFT on the AgentDojo and ASB benchmark, demonstrating its strong security performance while maintaining high utility across diverse models—showcasing both its robustness and adaptability. The code is released at https://github.com/SaFoLab-WISC/DRIFT.

paragraphs: Language-model agents interact with external information and tools while carrying out user requests. Malicious instructions encountered through those interactions can redirect their behavior. DRIFT addresses two challenges for system-level defenses: adapting security checks as execution changes and preventing hostile instructions from persisting in the agent’s memory.

A Secure Planner first derives a minimal sequence of function calls from the user’s request, together with structured checklists for their parameters. A Dynamic Validator monitors departures from this plan and checks whether changes remain consistent with the user’s intent and permitted privileges. This gives the defense an explicit reference for assessing the agent’s evolving actions.

An Injection Isolator separately detects and masks instructions in the memory stream that may conflict with the request. The framework thus constrains both execution and the information retained for later use. Evaluations on AgentDojo and ASB report strong security performance while preserving high task utility across diverse models. These results provide empirical support for combining dynamic execution checks with memory isolation.
summary.tldr: DRIFT defends language-model agents by validating changes to execution plans and masking conflicting instructions in memory.

title: DRIFT: Dynamic Rule-Based Defense with Injection Isolation for Securing LLM Agents

abstract: Accelerating large language model (LLM) inference is critical for real-world deployments requiring high throughput and low latency. Contextual sparsity, where each token dynamically activates only a small subset of the model parameters, shows promise but does not scale to large batch sizes due to union of active neurons quickly approaching dense computation. We introduce Polar Sparsity, highlighting a key shift in sparsity importance from MLP to Attention layers as we scale batch size and sequence length. While MLP layers become more compute-efficient under batching, their sparsity vanishes. In contrast, attention becomes increasingly more expensive at scale, while their head sparsity remains stable and batch-invariant. We develop Selective Head Attention with hardware-efficient, sparsity-aware GPU kernels, delivering up to \(2.2\times\) end-to-end speedups for models like OPT, LLaMA-2 \& 3, Qwen, Mistral across various batch sizes and sequence lengths without compromising accuracy. To our knowledge, this is the first work to demonstrate that contextual sparsity can scale effectively to large batch sizes, delivering substantial inference acceleration with minimal changes, making Polar Sparsity practical for large-scale, high-throughput LLM deployment systems.

Contextual sparsity, where each token dynamically activates only a small subset of the model parameters, shows promise but does not scale to large batch sizes due to union of active neurons quickly approaching dense computation. We introduce Polar Sparsity, highlighting a key shift in sparsity importance from MLP to Attention layers as we scale batch size and sequence length. While MLP layers become more compute-efficient under batching, their sparsity vanishes. In contrast, attention becomes increasingly more expensive at scale, while their head sparsity remains stable and batch-invariant. We develop Selective Head Attention with hardware-efficient, sparsity-aware GPU kernels, delivering up to \(2.2\times\) end-to-end speedups for models like OPT, LLaMA-2 \& 3, Qwen, Mistral across various batch sizes and sequence lengths without compromising accuracy. To our knowledge, this is the first work to demonstrate that contextual sparsity can scale effectively to large batch sizes, delivering substantial inference acceleration with minimal changes, making Polar Sparsity practical for large-scale, high-throughput LLM deployment systems.

paragraphs: Contextual sparsity accelerates language models by activating only some parameters for each token. Its benefit can disappear when many tokens are processed together: their different active neurons collectively cover nearly the full model. Polar Sparsity examines how this problem changes across model components as batch size and sequence length increase.

The authors identify a shift from feed-forward MLP layers toward attention. Batching makes MLP computation more efficient while eroding its sparsity. Attention, meanwhile, becomes increasingly expensive, but sparsity among attention heads remains stable across batch sizes. The proposed Selective Head Attention mechanism targets this opportunity, supported by GPU kernels designed to execute sparse attention efficiently.

Across models including OPT, LLaMA-2 and 3, Qwen, and Mistral, the authors report end-to-end speedups of up to 2.2 times without compromising accuracy. The experiments cover varied batch sizes and sequence lengths. The contribution is evidence that contextual sparsity can remain useful for high-throughput inference when the sparsity mechanism and hardware implementation focus on attention heads rather than relying on MLP sparsity alone.
summary.tldr: Polar Sparsity targets attention heads to preserve contextual-sparsity benefits in batched inference, reporting up to 2.2-times end-to-end speedups.

title: Polar Sparsity: High Throughput Batched LLM Inferencing with Scalable Contextual Sparsity

abstract: Graph embeddings play a critical role in graph representation learning, allowing machine learning models to explore and interpret graph-structured data. However, existing methods often rely on opaque, high-dimensional embeddings, limiting interpretability and practical visualization. In this work, we introduce Topological Evolution Rate (TopER), a novel, low-dimensional embedding approach grounded in topological data analysis. TopER simplifies a key topological approach, Persistent Homology, by calculating the evolution rate of graph substructures, resulting in intuitive and interpretable visualizations of graph data. This approach not only enhances the exploration of graph datasets but also delivers competitive performance in graph clustering and classification tasks. Our TopER-based models achieve or surpass state-of-the-art results across molecular, biological, and social network datasets in tasks such as classification, clustering, and visualization.

TopER aims to provide a compact alternative whose features have a clearer connection to graph structure, making the representations useful for both analysis and prediction.

Topological Evolution Rate draws on topological data analysis and simplifies an approach based on persistent homology. They report results that match or exceed state-of-the-art methods across these evaluations. TopER therefore connects a representation suited to human inspection with one that remains useful for automated graph learning.
summary.tldr: TopER creates compact, interpretable graph embeddings from topological evolution rates while achieving competitive classification and clustering performance.

title: TopER: Topological Embeddings in Graph Representation Learning

abstract: In recent years, artificial intelligence has significantly advanced medical image segmentation. Nonetheless, challenges remain, including efficient 3D medical image processing across diverse modalities and handling data variability. In this work, we introduce Hierarchical Soft Mixture-of-Experts (HoME), a two-level token-routing layer for efficient long-context modeling, specifically designed for 3D medical image segmentation. Built on the Mamba Selective State Space Model (SSM) backbone, HoME enhances sequential modeling through adaptive expert routing. In the first level, a Soft Mixture-of-Experts (SMoE) layer partitions input sequences into local groups, routing tokens to specialized per-group experts for localized feature extraction. The second level aggregates these outputs through a global SMoE layer, enabling cross-group information fusion and global context refinement. This hierarchical design, combining local expert routing with global expert refinement, enhances generalizability and segmentation performance, surpassing state-of-the-art results across datasets from the three most widely used 3D medical imaging modalities and varying data qualities. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/gmum/MambaHoME.

HoME introduces a hierarchical mixture-of-experts routing layer built on the Mamba selective state space model to address this combination of requirements.

The routing process has two levels. First, a soft mixture-of-experts layer divides input sequences into local groups and sends tokens to specialized experts within each group. These experts extract localized features. A second, global layer then combines the group outputs, allowing information to move across groups and refining the wider context. The hierarchy explicitly connects local processing with global information fusion.

The central contribution is the two-stage organization of expertise, which gives local specialization and global refinement distinct roles.
summary.tldr: HoME adds local and global expert routing to Mamba, improving reported 3D medical-image segmentation across modalities and data qualities.

title: Mamba Goes HoME: Hierarchical Soft Mixture-of-Experts for 3D Medical Image Segmentation

abstract: Text-to-motion generation has experienced remarkable progress in recent years. However, current approaches remain limited to synthesizing motion from short or general text prompts, primarily due to dataset constraints. This limitation undermines fine-grained controllability and generalization to unseen prompts. In this paper, we introduce SnapMoGen, a new text-motion dataset featuring high-quality motion capture data paired with accurate, \textit{expressive} textual annotations. The dataset comprises 20K motion clips totaling 44 hours, accompanied by 122 detailed textual descriptions averaging 48 words per description (vs. 12 words of HumanML3D). Importantly, these motion clips preserve original temporal continuity as they were in long sequences, facilitating research in long-term motion generation and blending. We also improve upon previous generative masked modeling approaches. Our model, MoMask++, transforms motion into \textbf{multi-scale} token sequences that better exploit the token capacity, and learns to generate all tokens using a single generative masked transformer. MoMask++ achieves state-of-the-art performance on both HumanML3D and OmniMotion benchmarks. Additionally, we demonstrate the ability to process casual user prompts by employing an LLM to reformat inputs to align with the expressivity and narration style of SnapMoGen.

The paper therefore contributes both richer supervision for detailed motion requests and a generation method evaluated on established motion benchmarks.
summary.tldr: SnapMoGen pairs motion capture with expressive descriptions, while MoMask++ uses multiscale motion tokens to improve text-driven motion generation.

title: SnapMoGen: Human Motion Generation from Expressive Texts

abstract: Understanding and reasoning over long videos pose significant challenges for large video language models (LVLMs) due to the difficulty in processing intensive video tokens beyond context window and retaining long-term sequential information. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has demonstrated effectiveness in processing long context for Large Language Models (LLMs); however, applying RAG to long video faces challenges such as disrupted temporal dependencies and inclusion of irrelevant information that can hinder accurate reasoning. To address these limitations, we propose Vgent, a novel \textbf{graph-based retrieval-reasoning-augmented generation framework} to enhance LVLMs for long video understanding. Our approach introduces two key innovations: (i) It represents videos by structured graphs with semantic relationships across video clips preserved to improve retrieval effectiveness. (ii) It introduces an intermediate reasoning step to mitigate the reasoning limitation of LVLMs, which leverages structured verification to reduce retrieval noise and facilitate the explicit aggregation of relevant information across clips, resulting in more accurate and context-aware responses. We comprehensively evaluate our framework with various open-source LVLMs on three long-video understanding benchmarks. Our approach yielded an overall performance improvement of $3.0\%\sim 5.4\%$ over base models on MLVU, and outperformed state-of-the-art video RAG methods by $8.6\%$. Our code is publicly available at https://xiaoqian-shen.github.io/Vgent.

The graph preserves semantic relationships across clips, giving retrieval access to structured connections within the video. This helps the model assemble evidence across the video before producing its response, addressing weaknesses in both selection and reasoning.

On MLVU, they report overall improvements of 3.0% to 5.4% over the base models, and an 8.6% advantage over leading video-retrieval methods. These results support the value of combining relationship-preserving retrieval with explicit verification and aggregation for answering questions about extended video content.
summary.tldr: Vgent combines graph-based clip retrieval with structured verification and reasoning to improve long-video understanding.

title: Vgent: Graph-based Retrieval-Reasoning-Augmented Generation For Long Video Understanding

abstract: Hierarchical clustering is a powerful tool for exploratory data analysis, organizing data into a tree of clusterings from which a partition can be chosen. This paper generalizes these ideas by proving that, for any reasonable hierarchy, one can optimally solve any center-based clustering objective over it (such as $k$-means). Moreover, these solutions can be found exceedingly quickly and are *themselves* necessarily hierarchical. Thus, given a cluster tree, we show that one can quickly access a plethora of new, equally meaningful hierarchies. Just as in standard hierarchical clustering, one can then choose any desired partition from these new hierarchies. We conclude by verifying the utility of our proposed techniques across datasets, hierarchies, and partitioning schemes.

paragraphs: Hierarchical clustering organizes data into a tree that offers partitions at different levels of detail. This paper asks how much more can be obtained from an existing cluster tree. It shows that a suitable hierarchy can support efficient optimization of center-based clustering objectives, including k-means, over that hierarchy.

The theoretical result applies to any hierarchy satisfying the paper’s reasonableness condition. Beyond finding an optimal solution for an objective over the supplied hierarchy, the authors show that these solutions themselves form hierarchies. Consequently, a starting tree can give access to additional meaningful trees, each offering its own collection of partitions for exploratory analysis.

This changes the role of the original hierarchy from a single menu of clusterings into a basis for generating many alternatives. The authors report that these alternatives can be accessed very quickly and verify their utility across datasets, input hierarchies, and partitioning schemes. The optimality claim concerns objectives solved over the given hierarchy, making that structure the foundation for both the computational result and the resulting cluster organization.
summary.tldr: A suitable cluster tree supports fast, optimal center-based clustering over its hierarchy, with solutions that form additional hierarchies.

title: Ultrametric Cluster Hierarchies: I Want ‘em All!

abstract: The Object Goal Navigation (ObjectNav) task challenges agents to locate a specified object in an unseen environment by imagining unobserved regions of the scene. Prior approaches rely on deterministic and discriminative models to complete semantic maps, overlooking the inherent uncertainty in indoor layouts and limiting their ability to generalize to unseen environments. In this work, we propose GOAL, a generative flow-based framework that models the semantic distribution of indoor environments by bridging observed regions with LLM-enriched full-scene semantic maps. During training, spatial priors inferred from large language models (LLMs) are encoded as two-dimensional Gaussian fields and injected into target maps, distilling rich contextual knowledge into the flow model and enabling more generalizable completions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GOAL achieves state-of-the-art performance on MP3D and Gibson, and shows strong generalization in transfer settings to HM3D.

paragraphs: Object Goal Navigation asks an agent to find a specified object in an unfamiliar environment. Doing so requires reasoning about parts of the scene it has not observed. The paper argues that deterministic approaches to completing semantic maps overlook uncertainty in indoor layouts, which can restrict how well navigation transfers to new environments.

GOAL addresses this with a generative flow model that learns a distribution over indoor semantic layouts. During training, large language models supply spatial priors, which are represented as two-dimensional Gaussian fields and added to full-scene target maps. The flow model learns to connect observed regions with these enriched maps, absorbing contextual knowledge into its map-completion process.

This design makes uncertainty in unseen regions part of the modeling problem while bringing language-model knowledge into spatial predictions. The reported experiments achieve state-of-the-art performance on MP3D and Gibson and strong transfer to HM3D. Together, those findings support the usefulness of training a generative map model with contextual spatial priors for navigation beyond the environments it originally encounters.
summary.tldr: GOAL trains a generative flow model with language-model spatial priors to improve unseen-scene completion and object navigation.

title: Distilling LLM Prior to Flow Model for Generalizable Agent’s Imagination in Object Goal Navigation

abstract: Floorplanning is the initial step in the physical design process of Electronic Design Automation (EDA), directly influencing subsequent placement, routing, and final power of the chip. However, the solution space in floorplanning is vast, and current algorithms often struggle to explore it sufficiently, making them prone to getting trapped in local optima. To achieve efficient floorplanning, we propose **CORE**, a general and effective solution optimization framework that synergizes Evolutionary Algorithms (EAs) and Reinforcement Learning (RL) for high-quality layout search and optimization. Specifically, we propose the Clustering-based Diversified Evolutionary Search that directly perturbs layouts and evolves them based on novelty and performance. Additionally, we model the floorplanning problem as a sequential decision problem with B*-Tree representation and employ RL for efficient learning. To efficiently coordinate EAs and RL, we propose the reinforcement-driven mechanism and evolution-guided mechanism. The former accelerates population evolution through RL, while the latter guides RL learning through EAs. The experimental results on the MCNC and GSRC benchmarks demonstrate that CORE outperforms other strong baselines in terms of wirelength and area utilization metrics, achieving a 12.9\% improvement in wirelength. CORE represents the first evolutionary reinforcement learning (ERL) algorithm for floorplanning, surpassing existing RL-based methods. The code is available at https://github.com/yeshenpy/CORE.

paragraphs: Chip floorplanning determines an initial layout that affects later placement, routing, and power. Its enormous search space makes it difficult for an optimizer to explore enough alternatives, and a search can settle on a locally attractive solution. CORE combines evolutionary search with reinforcement learning to improve exploration and layout quality.

The evolutionary component directly modifies layouts and develops a population using both novelty and performance. Clustering supports diversity within that search. The reinforcement-learning component treats floorplanning as a sequence of decisions using a B*-Tree representation. Two coordination mechanisms connect them: reinforcement learning helps accelerate population evolution, while the evolutionary search provides guidance for the learner. Each component therefore contributes to the other's optimization process.
