The authors also report that it surpasses existing reinforcement-learning approaches. These findings support combining population diversity with learned sequential decisions for the evaluated floorplanning problems.
summary.tldr: CORE coordinates evolutionary search and reinforcement learning to improve chip floorplans, reporting a 12.9% wirelength improvement.

title: CORE: Collaborative Optimization with Reinforcement Learning and Evolutionary Algorithm for Floorplanning

abstract: The widespread deployment of large language models (LLMs) allows users to access their capabilities via black-box APIs, but backdoor attacks pose serious security risks for API users by hijacking the model behavior. This highlights the importance of backdoor detection technologies to help users audit LLMs before use. However, most existing LLM backdoor defenses require white-box access or costly reverse engineering, limiting their practicality for resource-constrained users. Moreover, they mainly target classification tasks, leaving broader generative scenarios underexplored. To solve the problem, this paper introduces ICLScan, a lightweight framework that exploits targeted in-context learning (ICL) as illumination for backdoor detection in black-box LLMs, which effectively supports generative tasks without additional training or model modifications. ICLScan is based on our finding of backdoor susceptibility amplification: LLMs with pre-embedded backdoors are highly susceptible to new trigger implantation via ICL. Including only a small ratio of backdoor examples (containing ICL-triggered input and target output) in the ICL prompt can induce ICL trigger-specific malicious behavior in backdoored LLMs. ICLScan leverages this phenomenon to detect backdoored LLMs by statistically analyzing whether the success rate of new trigger injection via targeted ICL exceeds a threshold. It requires only multiple queries to estimate the backdoor success rate, overcoming black-box access and computational resource limitations. Extensive experiments across diverse LLMs and backdoor attacks demonstrate ICLScan's effectiveness and efficiency, achieving near-perfect detection performance (precision/recall/F1-score/ROC-AUC all approaching 1) with minimal additional overhead across all settings.

summary.tldr: ICLScan detects backdoored black-box language models by measuring their heightened susceptibility to new trigger behaviors introduced through prompts.

title: ICLScan: Detecting Backdoors in Black-Box Large Language Models via Targeted In-context Illumination

abstract: The synthesis of realistic Martian landscape videos, essential for mission rehearsal and robotic simulation, presents unique challenges. These primarily stem from the scarcity of high-quality Martian data and the significant domain gap relative to terrestrial imagery.To address these challenges, we introduce a holistic solution comprising two main components: 1) a data curation framework, Multimodal Mars Synthesis (M3arsSynth), which processes stereo navigation images to render high-fidelity 3D video sequences. 2) a video-based Martian terrain generator (MarsGen), that utilizes multimodal conditioning data to accurately synthesize novel, 3D-consistent frames. Our data are sourced from NASA’s Planetary Data System (PDS), covering diverse Martian terrains and dates, enabling the production of physics-accurate 3D surface models at metric-scale resolution. During inference, MarsGen is conditioned on an initial image frame and can be guided by specified camera trajectories or textual prompts to generate new environments.Experimental results demonstrate that our solution surpasses video synthesis approaches trained on terrestrial data, achieving superior visual quality and 3D structural consistency.

paragraphs: Generating realistic videos of Martian terrain is difficult because high-quality Mars imagery is scarce and differs substantially from terrestrial imagery. The paper addresses this problem with a combined data-curation and video-generation system intended to support mission rehearsal and robotic simulation. Its approach connects terrain reconstruction with controllable synthesis.

The first component, M3arsSynth, processes stereo navigation images into detailed 3D video sequences. The source imagery comes from NASA’s Planetary Data System and spans different terrains and dates. This supports physically accurate surface models at metric-scale resolution. The second component, MarsGen, uses multimodal conditioning to synthesize new frames with consistent three-dimensional structure.

At inference time, MarsGen starts from an initial image and accepts guidance through camera trajectories or text prompts. Experiments report better visual quality and 3D structural consistency than video synthesis approaches trained on terrestrial data. The contribution therefore addresses both the source-data mismatch and the generation process: reconstructed Martian geometry supplies a basis for videos that can be guided toward particular views or environments.
summary.tldr: A Mars-specific reconstruction and generation pipeline produces controllable terrain videos with improved visual and 3D consistency.

title: Martian World Model: Controllable Video Synthesis with Physically Accurate 3D Reconstructions

abstract: When building a world model, a common assumption is that the environment has a single, unchanging underlying causal rule, like applying Newton's laws to every situation. However, in truly open-ended environments, the apparent causal mechanism may drift over time because the agent continually encounters novel contexts and operates within a limited observational window. This brings about a problem that, when building a world model, even subtle shifts in policy or environment states can alter the very observed causal mechanisms. In this work, we introduce the Meta-Causal Graph as world models for open-ended environments, a minimal unified representation that efficiently encodes the transformation rules governing how causal structures shift across different latent world states. A single Meta-Causal Graph is composed of multiple causal subgraphs, each triggered by meta state, which is in the latent state space. Building on this representation, we introduce a Causality-Seeking Agent whose objectives are to (1) identify the meta states that trigger each subgraph, (2) discover the corresponding causal relationships by agent curiosity-driven intervention policy, and (3) iteratively refine the Meta-Causal Graph through ongoing curiosity-driven exploration and agent experiences. Experiments on both synthetic tasks and a challenging robot arm manipulation task demonstrate that our method robustly captures shifts in causal dynamics and generalizes effectively to previously unseen contexts.

In this work, we introduce the Meta-Causal Graph as world models for open-ended environments, a minimal unified representation that efficiently encodes the transformation rules governing how causal structures shift across different latent world states. A single Meta-Causal Graph is composed of multiple causal subgraphs, each triggered by meta state, which is in the latent state space. Building on this representation, we introduce a Causality-Seeking Agent whose objectives are to (1) identify the meta states that trigger each subgraph, (2) discover the corresponding causal relationships by agent curiosity-driven intervention policy, and (3) iteratively refine the Meta-Causal Graph through ongoing curiosity-driven exploration and agent experiences. Experiments on both synthetic tasks and a challenging robot arm manipulation task demonstrate that our method robustly captures shifts in causal dynamics and generalizes effectively to previously unseen contexts.

paragraphs: An agent exploring an open-ended environment may encounter different apparent cause-and-effect relationships as contexts change. The paper emphasizes that limited observations and shifts in policy or environment state can change the causal mechanisms the agent observes. A world model built around one fixed observed causal structure may therefore struggle to represent these experiences.

The proposed Meta-Causal Graph combines multiple causal subgraphs, each activated by a latent meta state. It represents both contextual causal relationships and the rules governing changes between them. The associated Causality-Seeking Agent tries to discover which meta states activate particular subgraphs and which causal relationships hold within each one.

Learning is driven by curiosity-based interventions and continued exploration, allowing the agent to refine its graph through experience. Experiments on synthetic tasks and robot arm manipulation show robust capture of changing causal dynamics and effective generalization to unseen contexts. These results support the usefulness of explicitly modeling context-dependent causal changes instead of treating every new observation as evidence about a single unchanging observed mechanism.
summary.tldr: A curiosity-driven agent learns context-dependent causal graphs and how they change, improving adaptation to unfamiliar situations in the reported experiments.

title: Curious Causality-Seeking Agents in Open-ended Worlds

abstract: Quantum noise constitutes a fundamental obstacle to realizing practical quantum technologies. To address the pivotal challenge of identifying quantum systems least affected by noise, we introduce the purest quantum state identification, which can be used to improve the accuracy of quantum computation and communication. We formulate a rigorous paradigm for identifying the purest quantum state among $K$ unknown $n$-qubit quantum states using total $N$ quantum state copies. For incoherent strategies, we derive the first adaptive algorithm achieving error probability $\exp\left(- \Omega\left(\frac{N H_1}{\log(K) 2^n }\right) \right)$, fundamentally improving quantum property learning through measurement optimization. By developing a coherent measurement protocol with error bound $\exp\left(- \Omega\left(\frac{N H_2}{\log(K) }\right) \right)$, we demonstrate a significant separation from incoherent strategies, formally quantifying the power of quantum memory and coherent measurement. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound by demonstrating that all strategies with fixed two-outcome incoherent POVM must suffer error probability exceeding $ \exp\left( - O\left(\frac{NH_1}{2^n}\right)\right)$. This research advances the characterization of quantum noise through efficient learning frameworks. Our results establish theoretical foundations for noise-adaptive quantum property learning while delivering practical protocols for enhancing the reliability of quantum hardware.

The contribution provides theoretical foundations and protocols aimed at improving noise-aware selection in quantum computing and communication.
summary.tldr: The paper develops purest-state identification algorithms and proves a significant advantage for coherent quantum measurements over incoherent strategies.

title: Purest Quantum State Identification

abstract: Human cognition typically involves thinking through abstract, fluid concepts rather than strictly using discrete linguistic tokens. Current Large Language Models (LLMs), however, are constrained to reasoning within the boundaries of human language, processing discrete token embeddings that represent fixed points in semantic space. This discrete constraint restricts the expressive power and upper potential of such reasoning models, often causing incomplete exploration of reasoning paths, as standard Chain-of-Thought (CoT) methods rely on sampling one token per step. In this work, we introduce Soft Thinking, a training-free method that emulates human-like ``soft'' reasoning by generating abstract concept tokens in a continuous concept space. These concept tokens are created by the probability-weighted mixture of token embeddings, which span the continuous concept space, enabling smooth transitions and richer representations that transcend traditional discrete boundaries. In essence, each generated concept token encapsulates multiple meanings from related discrete tokens, implicitly exploring various reasoning paths to converge effectively toward the correct answer. Empirical evaluations on diverse mathematical and coding benchmarks consistently demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of Soft Thinking, improving pass@1 accuracy by up to 2.48 points while simultaneously reducing token usage by up to 22.4\% compared to standard CoT. Qualitative analysis further reveals that Soft Thinking outputs remain highly interpretable and readable, highlighting the potential of Soft Thinking to break the inherent limits of discrete language-based reasoning.

paragraphs: Standard chain-of-thought reasoning selects a discrete token at each step. This paper argues that committing to one token can restrict exploration of possible reasoning paths. Soft Thinking introduces a training-free alternative in which intermediate concept tokens occupy a continuous space, allowing a representation to combine meanings associated with several discrete tokens.

Qualitative analysis also finds its outputs readable and interpretable. These results support continuous intermediate representations as a promising inference-time reasoning technique, with the reported gains representing maxima across the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Soft Thinking uses probability-weighted token embeddings for training-free reasoning, improving accuracy and reducing token usage in reported evaluations.

title: Soft Thinking: Unlocking the Reasoning Potential of LLMs in Continuous Concept Space

abstract: The scarcity of annotated medical imaging data has driven significant progress in semi-supervised learning to alleviate reliance on expensive expert labeling. While foundational vision models such as the Segment Anything Model (SAM) exhibit robust generalization in generic segmentation tasks, their direct application to medical images often results in suboptimal performance. To address this challenge, in this work, we propose a novel fully SAM-based semi-supervised medical image segmentation framework and develop the corresponding knowledge distillation-based learning strategy. Specifically, we first employ an efficient SAM variant as the backbone network of the semi‑supervised framework and update the default prompt embedding of SAM to unleash its full potential. Then, we utilize an original SAM, which is rich in prior knowledge, as the teacher to optimize our efficient student SAM backbone through hierarchical knowledge distillation and a dynamic loss weighting strategy. Extensive experiments on various medical datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art semi-supervised segmentation approaches. Especially, our model requires less than 10% of the parameter size of the original SAM, enabling substantially lower deployment and storage overhead in real-world clinical settings.

paragraphs: Medical image segmentation requires identifying relevant regions in images, but expert annotations are scarce and expensive. This paper develops a semi-supervised framework built entirely around SAM to address that mismatch.

An efficient SAM variant serves as the student network, and its default prompt embedding is updated during learning. The original SAM acts as a teacher, transferring prior knowledge to the smaller model through hierarchical knowledge distillation. Dynamic weighting adjusts the contributions of the training losses, combining these components into a strategy for learning with limited annotations.

Across several medical datasets, the authors report better performance than state-of-the-art semi-supervised segmentation approaches. The resulting model uses less than one-tenth of the original SAM’s parameter count, reducing storage and deployment overhead. The findings support using a large foundation model’s knowledge to train a compact medical segmentation model, while adapting the student rather than relying on direct application of the original model.
summary.tldr: A compact SAM student learns from the original SAM to improve semi-supervised medical segmentation with far fewer parameters.

title: Segment Anything Model Meets Semi-supervised Medical Image Segmentation: A Novel Perspective

abstract: Masked Graph Autoencoders (MGAEs) have gained significant attention recently. Their proxy tasks typically involve random corruption of input graphs followed by reconstruction. However, in the molecular domain, two main issues arise: the predetermined mask ratio and reconstruction objectives can lead to suboptimal performance or negative transfer due to overly simplified or complex tasks, and these tasks may deviate from chemical priors. To tackle these challenges, we propose Dynamic and Chemical Constraints (DyCC) for MGAEs. This includes a masking strategy called GIBMS, which preserves essential semantic information during graph masking while adaptively adjusting the mask ratio and content for each molecule. Additionally, we introduce a Soft Label Generator (SLG) that reconstructs masked tokens as learnable prototypes (soft labels) rather than hard labels. These components adhere to chemical constraints and allow dynamic variation of proxy tasks during training. We integrate the model-agnostic DyCC into various MGAEs and conduct comprehensive experiments, demonstrating significant performance improvements. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/forever-ly/DyCC}.

paragraphs: Masked graph autoencoders learn molecular representations by hiding parts of a molecular graph and reconstructing them. The paper identifies a problem with using a predetermined masking ratio and fixed reconstruction targets: the resulting exercise may be too easy, too difficult, or poorly matched to chemical knowledge. Such proxy tasks can produce weak learning or negative transfer.

Dynamic and Chemical Constraints, or DyCC, changes both what gets hidden and what the model predicts. Its GIBMS masking strategy adapts the amount and content of masking for each molecule while preserving essential semantic information. A Soft Label Generator replaces hard reconstruction labels with learnable prototypes. These two components allow the training exercise to change dynamically while following chemical constraints.

The framework is designed to work with different masked graph autoencoders, and the authors integrate it into several such models. Their experiments report significant performance improvements. The central finding is that molecular representation learning benefits from adapting the reconstruction task to the molecule and its chemical structure, rather than relying solely on a fixed corruption-and-reconstruction setup.
summary.tldr: DyCC improves molecular graph learning with molecule-specific masking and learnable reconstruction targets that follow chemical constraints.

title: Dynamic and Chemical Constraints to Enhance the Molecular Masked Graph Autoencoders

abstract: Unsupervised feature learning has emerged as a promising tool in learning representations from unlabeled data. However, it is still challenging to learn useful high-level features when the data contains a significant amount of irrelevant patterns. Although feature selection can be used for such complex data, it may fail when we have to build a learning system from scratch (i.e., starting from the lack of useful raw features). To address this problem, we propose a point-wise gated Boltzmann machine, a unified generative model that combines feature learning and feature selection. Our model performs not only feature selection on learned high-level features (i.e., hidden units), but also dynamic feature selection on raw features (i.e., visible units) through a gating mechanism. For each example, the model can adaptively focus on a variable subset of visible nodes corresponding to the task-relevant patterns, while ignoring the visible units corresponding to the task-irrelevant patterns. In experiments, our method achieves improved performance over state-of-the-art in several visual recognition benchmarks.

paragraphs: Learning representations from unlabeled data becomes difficult when many observed patterns are irrelevant to the task. Feature selection can help, but it may struggle when useful features have not yet been constructed. The paper addresses this interdependence by treating feature learning and feature selection as parts of one generative model.

The proposed point-wise gated Boltzmann machine selects information at two levels. It selects among learned high-level features represented by hidden units, and it dynamically selects raw features represented by visible units. A gating mechanism lets the chosen subset of visible inputs vary from one example to another.

This example-specific selection allows the model to focus on task-relevant patterns while ignoring irrelevant visible inputs. In experiments across several visual recognition benchmarks, the method improves on the state of the art used for comparison. The stated findings support combining representation learning with adaptive selection: the model can build useful features while also deciding which parts of each observation should contribute to them.
summary.tldr: A gated Boltzmann machine jointly learns features and selects relevant inputs for each example, improving performance on several visual recognition benchmarks.

title: Learning and Selecting Features Jointly with Point-wise Gated Boltzmann Machines

abstract: We present a Bayesian nonparametric framework for multilevel clustering which utilizes group-level context information to simultaneously discover low-dimensional structures of the group contents and partitions groups into clusters. Using the Dirichlet process as the building block, our model constructs a product base-measure with a nested structure to accommodate content and context observations at multiple levels. The proposed model possesses properties that link the nested Dirichlet processes (nDP) and the Dirichlet process mixture models (DPM) in an interesting way: integrating out all contents results in the DPM over contexts, whereas integrating out group-speciﬁc contexts results in the nDP mixture over content variables. We provide a Polya-urn view of the model and an efﬁcient collapsed Gibbs inference procedure. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate the advantage of utilizing context information via our model in both text and image domains.

The proposed model possesses properties that link the nested Dirichlet processes (nDP) and the Dirichlet process mixture models (DPM) in an interesting way: integrating out all contents results in the DPM over contexts, whereas integrating out group-speciﬁc contexts results in the nDP mixture over content variables. paragraphs: Grouped data can carry information at two levels: the observations inside each group and the context describing the group itself. This paper develops a Bayesian nonparametric model that uses both. It simultaneously discovers compact structure in group contents and clusters the groups, allowing contextual information to contribute to the organization of the data.

The construction uses Dirichlet processes with a nested product base measure to represent observations at multiple levels. Its relationship to established models helps explain what the combination accomplishes. Integrating out the contents leaves a Dirichlet process mixture over contexts; integrating out group-specific contexts leaves a nested Dirichlet process mixture over contents. Both views are therefore contained within one framework.

The authors provide a Polya-urn interpretation and an efficient collapsed Gibbs procedure for inference. Experiments on real-world text and image datasets demonstrate advantages from incorporating context through this model. The findings support treating group descriptions and internal observations as complementary evidence when learning both group clusters and the structure within them.
summary.tldr: A multilevel Bayesian clustering model combines group contents with contextual information and connects two established Dirichlet process constructions.

title: Bayesian Nonparametric Multilevel Clustering with Group-Level Contexts

abstract: Determinantal point processes (DPPs) offer an elegant tool for encoding probabilities over subsets of a ground set. Discrete DPPs are parametrized by a positive semidefinite matrix (called the DPP kernel), and estimating this kernel is key to learning DPPs from observed data. We consider the task of learning the DPP kernel, and develop for it a surprisingly simple yet effective new algorithm. Our algorithm offers the following benefits over previous approaches: (a) it is much simpler; (b) it yields equally good and sometimes even better local maxima; and (c) it runs an order of magnitude faster on large problems. We present experimental results on both real and simulated data to illustrate the numerical performance of our technique.

paragraphs: A determinantal point process assigns probabilities to subsets of a collection of items. In the discrete setting, these probabilities are controlled by a positive semidefinite matrix called the kernel. Learning a DPP from observed data therefore requires estimating that matrix. This paper focuses on making the kernel-learning step simpler and faster.

The authors introduce a fixed-point algorithm and compare it with earlier approaches. They report that the method is substantially simpler while reaching local maxima that are as good as, and sometimes better than, those found previously. The reference to local maxima is significant: the claimed improvement concerns the quality of the solutions obtained by the learning procedure.

Experiments on both real and simulated data illustrate the algorithm's numerical behavior. For large problems, the reported runtime improvement is an order of magnitude. Taken together, the findings suggest that a relatively simple update procedure can provide a favorable combination of computational speed and solution quality, making kernel estimation more practical without sacrificing the reported quality of the fitted DPP.
summary.tldr: A simple fixed-point method learns DPP kernels with comparable or better local maxima and much faster reported large-problem runtimes.

title: Fixed-point algorithms for learning determinantal point processes

abstract: We present efficient algorithms for the problem of contextual bandits with i.i.d. covariates, an arbitrary sequence of rewards, and an arbitrary class of policies. Our algorithm BISTRO requires d calls to the empirical risk minimization (ERM) oracle per round, where d is the number of actions. The method uses unlabeled data to make the problem computationally simple. When the ERM problem itself is computationally hard, we extend the approach by employing multiplicative approximation algorithms for the ERM. The integrality gap of the relaxation only enters in the regret bound rather than the benchmark. Finally, we show that the adversarial version of the contextual bandit problem is learnable (and efficient) whenever the full-information supervised online learning problem has a non-trivial regret bound (and efficient).

paragraphs: The paper studies contextual bandits, where a learner uses contextual information to select an action and learns from the reward of that choice. Its main setting assumes independently and identically distributed contexts, while allowing an arbitrary reward sequence and an arbitrary policy class. BISTRO addresses the computational problem of learning under these conditions.

On each round, BISTRO makes one call to an empirical risk minimization oracle for each available action. It uses unlabeled data to simplify the computation. When exact empirical risk minimization is itself difficult, the authors extend the approach to multiplicative approximation algorithms. The relaxation’s integrality gap affects the regret bound while leaving the comparison benchmark unchanged.

The paper also gives a conditional result for adversarial contextual bandits. Learnability follows whenever the corresponding full-information supervised online learning problem has a nontrivial regret bound, with efficiency when that problem is efficient. This connects learning from limited action feedback to a fuller-feedback problem and identifies a condition under which the harder feedback setting remains manageable.
summary.tldr: BISTRO uses unlabeled data and empirical risk minimization oracles to make contextual bandit learning computationally tractable under stated conditions.

title: BISTRO: An Efficient Relaxation-Based Method for Contextual Bandits

abstract: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and slice sampling are amongst the most widely used and studied classes of Markov Chain Monte Carlo samplers. We connect these two methods and present Hamiltonian slice sampling, which allows slice sampling to be carried out along Hamiltonian trajectories, or transformations thereof. Hamiltonian slice sampling clarifies a class of model priors that induce closed-form slice samplers. More pragmatically, inheriting properties of slice samplers, it offers advantages over Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, in that it has fewer tunable hyperparameters and does not require gradient information. We demonstrate the utility of Hamiltonian slice sampling out of the box on problems ranging from Gaussian process regression to Pitman-Yor based mixture models.

paragraphs: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and slice sampling are two established approaches to Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling. This paper connects them through Hamiltonian slice sampling, which performs slice sampling along Hamiltonian trajectories or transformations of those trajectories. The construction combines ideas from the two methods in a single sampling approach.

One theoretical contribution is to clarify a class of model priors that yield slice samplers with closed-form expressions. This identifies structure under which the sampling operation can be expressed directly. The connection is therefore useful both for constructing a sampler and for understanding which prior choices make particular sampling steps tractable.

The method also inherits practical properties from slice sampling: it has fewer tunable hyperparameters than Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and does not require gradient information. The authors demonstrate its out-of-the-box utility on problems ranging from Gaussian process regression to Pitman-Yor mixture models. These examples support its usefulness across different modeling settings, with reduced tuning and gradient requirements as the stated practical advantages.
summary.tldr: Hamiltonian slice sampling connects two sampling families while reducing tuning requirements and avoiding the need for gradients.

title: Slice Sampling on Hamiltonian Trajectories

abstract: Hierarchical Bayesian models often capture distributions over a very large number of distinct atoms. The need for these models arises when organizing huge amount of unsupervised data, for instance, features extracted using deep convnets that can be exploited to organize abundant unlabeled images. Inference for hierarchical Bayesian models in such cases can be rather nontrivial, leading to approximate approaches. In this work, we propose Canopy , a sampler based on Cover Trees that is exact, has guaranteed runtime logarithmic in the number of atoms, and is provably polynomial in the inherent dimensionality of the underlying parameter space. In other words, the algorithm is as fast as search over a hierarchical data structure. We provide theory for Canopy and demonstrate its effectiveness on both synthetic and real datasets, consisting of over 100 million images.

paragraphs: Hierarchical Bayesian models can organize large collections of unlabeled data, but their distributions may involve enormous numbers of distinct atoms. Sampling from these distributions then becomes a computational challenge. The paper motivates this setting with image collections represented through features extracted by deep convolutional networks.

Canopy addresses this challenge with an exact sampler built on cover trees, a hierarchical data structure. Its stated runtime guarantee grows logarithmically with the number of atoms and polynomially with the inherent dimensionality of the parameter space. These two dependencies distinguish the size of the collection from the dimensional complexity of the space in which its parameters live.

The authors provide theoretical analysis and evaluate Canopy on synthetic and real datasets, including a collection containing more than 100 million images. They report that the sampler is effective at this scale. The central significance is that exact sampling can have a runtime comparable to searching a hierarchy, making a difficult inference operation more manageable without replacing it with approximate sampling.
summary.tldr: Canopy uses cover trees for exact sampling with logarithmic dependence on the number of atoms and polynomial dependence on inherent dimensionality.

title: Canopy Fast Sampling with Cover Trees

abstract: A basic, and still largely unanswered, question in the context of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) is whether they are truly able to capture all the fundamental characteristics of the distributions they are trained on. In particular, evaluating the diversity of GAN distributions is challenging and existing methods provide only a partial understanding of this issue. In this paper, we develop quantitative and scalable tools for assessing the diversity of GAN distributions. Specifically, we take a classification-based perspective and view loss of diversity as a form of covariate shift introduced by GANs. We examine two specific forms of such shift: mode collapse and boundary distortion. In contrast to prior work, our methods need only minimal human supervision and can be readily applied to state-of-the-art GANs on large, canonical datasets. Examining popular GANs using our tools indicates that these GANs have significant problems in reproducing the more distributional properties of their training dataset.

paragraphs: A generator can produce convincing individual examples while still failing to represent the variety in its training data. This paper develops quantitative tools for examining that gap in generative adversarial networks. Its focus is distributional diversity: whether generated samples preserve important characteristics of the collection they are meant to reproduce.

The authors approach this question through classification, treating lost diversity as covariate shift between the training distribution and the generated distribution. They examine mode collapse and boundary distortion as two specific forms of this shift. This turns an elusive question about sample variety into a classification-based assessment that can be applied at scale with minimal human supervision.

Applying these tools to popular GANs reveals substantial difficulties in reproducing distributional properties of their training datasets. The finding concerns the models examined, rather than establishing that every GAN must fail. The contribution is therefore both a diagnostic method and evidence that evaluating realistic-looking samples alone provides an incomplete picture of what a generator has learned.
summary.tldr: Classification-based tools reveal diversity problems in popular GANs by measuring shifts between training and generated distributions.

title: A Classification-Based Study of Covariate Shift in GAN Distributions

abstract: We consider the problems of distribution estimation, and heavy hitter (frequency) estimation under privacy, and communication constraints. While the constraints have been studied separately, optimal schemes for one are sub-optimal for the other. We propose a sample-optimal $\eps$-locally differentially private (LDP) scheme for distribution estimation, where each user communicates one bit, and requires no public randomness. We also show that Hadamard Response, a recently proposed scheme for $\eps$-LDP distribution estimation is also utility-optimal for heavy hitters estimation. Our final result shows that unlike distribution estimation, without public randomness, any utility-optimal heavy hitter estimation algorithm must require $\Omega(\log n)$ bits of communication per user.

paragraphs: The paper studies statistical estimation when each user’s message must satisfy both privacy and communication constraints. It considers estimating a distribution and estimating heavy hitters, or frequent items. Methods optimized for either privacy or communication alone can perform poorly when both requirements apply at once.

For distribution estimation, the authors propose an epsilon-locally differentially private scheme that is sample-optimal, requires just one transmitted bit per user, and needs no public randomness. This establishes that strong communication economy can coexist with optimal sample requirements for this task. They also show that the existing Hadamard Response scheme is utility-optimal for heavy-hitter estimation.

summary.tldr: Private distribution estimation can be sample-optimal with one bit per user, while optimal heavy-hitter estimation needs more communication without public randomness.

title: Communication Complexity in Locally Private Distribution Estimation and Heavy Hitters

abstract: Computing Nash equilibrium (NE) of multi-player games has witnessed renewed interest due to recent advances in generative adversarial networks. However, computing equilibrium efficiently is challenging. To this end, we introduce the Gradient-based Nikaido-Isoda (GNI) function which serves: (i) as a merit function, vanishing only at the first-order stationary points of each player’s optimization problem, and (ii) provides error bounds to a stationary Nash point. Gradient descent is shown to converge sublinearly to a first-order stationary point of the GNI function. For the particular case of bilinear min-max games and multi-player quadratic games, the GNI function is convex. Hence, the application of gradient descent in this case yields linear convergence to an NE (when one exists). In our numerical experiments, we observe that the GNI formulation always converges to the first-order stationary point of each player’s optimization problem.

paragraphs: Finding a Nash equilibrium requires coordinating several players' optimization problems, which can be computationally difficult. This paper introduces the Gradient-based Nikaido-Isoda function to provide a single quantity for assessing progress. It is designed as a merit function whose vanishing indicates first-order stationarity for each player's optimization problem.

The function also provides error bounds relative to a stationary Nash point. The authors show that gradient descent converges sublinearly to a first-order stationary point of the GNI function. This general guarantee concerns stationarity of the combined function; it is distinct from a universal guarantee of reaching a Nash equilibrium in every multiplayer game.

There, the GNI function is convex, and gradient descent converges linearly to a Nash equilibrium when one exists. In the numerical experiments, the formulation consistently reaches first-order stationary points of the players' problems. The contribution therefore combines a general optimization construction with sharper equilibrium guarantees for particular game classes.
summary.tldr: The GNI function turns game optimization into a shared objective, with linear convergence to existing Nash equilibria for specified game classes.

title: Game Theoretic Optimization via Gradient-based Nikaido-Isoda Function

abstract: Over the past few years, neural networks were proven vulnerable to adversarial images: targeted but imperceptible image perturbations lead to drastically different predictions. We show that adversarial vulnerability increases with the gradients of the training objective when viewed as a function of the inputs. Surprisingly, vulnerability does not depend on network topology: for many standard network architectures, we prove that at initialization, the L1-norm of these gradients grows as the square root of the input dimension, leaving the networks increasingly vulnerable with growing image size. We empirically show that this dimension-dependence persists after either usual or robust training, but gets attenuated with higher regularization.

paragraphs: Small, deliberately chosen changes to an image can cause a neural network to make very different predictions. This paper studies that vulnerability through the gradient of the training objective with respect to the input. The gradient describes how sensitive the objective is to small input changes, and the authors connect larger input gradients with greater first-order adversarial vulnerability.

For many standard network architectures, they prove that at initialization the L1 norm of these gradients grows with the square root of the input dimension. In this analysis, the scaling does not depend on the particular network topology. The result links increasing image size to increasing vulnerability across the architectures covered by the theorem, with initialization being an essential part of the theoretical statement.

The authors also investigate trained networks empirically. They find that the dependence on input dimension persists after both ordinary and robust training, although stronger regularization attenuates it. This distinguishes the proven initialization result from the observed behavior after training. Together, the findings identify input dimensionality and gradient sensitivity as important factors in understanding adversarial vulnerability.
summary.tldr: Input-gradient scaling links larger input dimensions to greater adversarial vulnerability, with a proof at initialization and supporting observations after training.

title: First-Order Adversarial Vulnerability of Neural Networks and Input Dimension

abstract: We consider the problem of imitation learning from a finite set of expert trajectories, without access to reinforcement signals. The classical approach of extracting the expert’s reward function via inverse reinforcement learning, followed by reinforcement learning is indirect and may be computationally expensive. Recent generative adversarial methods based on matching the policy distribution between the expert and the agent could be unstable during training. We propose a new framework for imitation learning by estimating the support of the expert policy to compute a fixed reward function, which allows us to re-frame imitation learning within the standard reinforcement learning setting. We demonstrate the efficacy of our reward function on both discrete and continuous domains, achieving comparable or better performance than the state of the art under different reinforcement learning algorithms.

We propose a new framework for imitation learning by estimating the support of the expert policy to compute a fixed reward function, which allows us to re-frame imitation learning within the standard reinforcement learning setting. We demonstrate the efficacy of our reward function on both discrete and continuous domains, achieving comparable or better performance than the state of the art under different reinforcement learning algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper studies imitation learning from a finite collection of expert trajectories when no reinforcement signal is available. One traditional route first recovers an expert reward function and then performs reinforcement learning, which can be indirect and expensive. Adversarial approaches that match expert and agent policy distributions can instead face training instability.

The proposed framework estimates the support of the expert policy: the region of behavior represented by that policy. It uses this estimate to construct a fixed reward function. Once that reward is available, the imitation problem can be handled within a standard reinforcement-learning setup, giving the learning agent a stable reward definition to optimize.

Experiments in discrete and continuous domains demonstrate the usefulness of the reward function under different reinforcement-learning algorithms. Reported performance is comparable to or better than the state of the art. The central contribution is the conversion from demonstrations to a fixed training signal through support estimation, with the experiments showing that this signal can support effective imitation across the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Estimating expert-policy support turns demonstrations into a fixed reward for standard reinforcement learning, with competitive reported imitation performance.

title: Random Expert Distillation: Imitation Learning via Expert Policy Support Estimation

abstract: Kernel selection for kernel-based methods is prohibitively expensive due to the NP-hard nature of discrete optimization. Since gradient-based optimizers are not applicable due to the lack of a differentiable objective function, many state-of-the-art solutions resort to heuristic search or gradient-free optimization. These approaches, however, require imposing restrictive assumptions on the explorable space of structures such as limiting the active candidate pool, thus depending heavily on the intuition of domain experts. This paper instead proposes \textbf{DTERGENS}, a novel generative search framework that constructs and optimizes a high-performance composite kernel expressions generator. \textbf{DTERGENS} does not restrict the space of candidate kernels and is capable of obtaining flexible length expressions by jointly optimizing a generative termination criterion. We demonstrate that our framework explores more diverse kernels and obtains better performance than state-of-the-art approaches on many real-world predictive tasks.

We demonstrate that our framework explores more diverse kernels and obtains better performance than state-of-the-art approaches on many real-world predictive tasks.

paragraphs: Choosing a composite kernel involves searching over discrete expressions, making the optimization difficult and preventing direct use of gradient methods on the original objective. Existing search approaches often narrow the candidate space to make the problem manageable. This can leave the result heavily dependent on expert choices about which structures should be considered.

DTERGENS approaches the problem by constructing and optimizing a generator of composite kernel expressions. The framework does not impose the candidate-space restrictions described for earlier approaches. It also jointly learns a termination criterion, allowing generated expressions to have flexible lengths instead of requiring a fixed expression size.

On many real-world prediction tasks, the authors report that the framework explores more diverse kernels and achieves better performance than the compared state-of-the-art approaches. The contribution is to make the production of candidate structures itself an optimization target. Learning both expression generation and when generation stops provides a way to search structures whose complexity can vary during the process.
summary.tldr: DTERGENS learns a generator and stopping rule for variable-length composite kernels, improving search diversity and prediction in the reported tasks.

title: Optimizing Dynamic Structures with Bayesian Generative Search

abstract: Deep neural networks have dramatically transformed machine learning, but their memory and energy demands are substantial. The requirements of real biological neural networks are rather modest in comparison, and one feature that might underlie this austerity is their sparse connectivity. In deep learning, trainable sparse networks that perform well on a specific task are usually constructed using label-dependent pruning criteria. In this article, we introduce Neural Tangent Transfer, a method that instead finds trainable sparse networks in a label-free manner. Specifically, we find sparse networks whose training dynamics, as characterized by the neural tangent kernel, mimic those of dense networks in function space. Finally, we evaluate our label-agnostic approach on several standard classification tasks and show that the resulting sparse networks achieve higher classification performance while converging faster.

paragraphs: Dense neural networks can demand substantial memory and energy, motivating methods that retain fewer connections while remaining trainable. Many approaches select those connections using labels from a particular task. Neural Tangent Transfer instead seeks sparse networks without using labels to decide which network structure to retain.

The method matches aspects of a sparse network's training behavior to those of a dense network. It characterizes that behavior through the neural tangent kernel, which describes training dynamics in the space of functions represented by the network. The selection target is therefore how the sparse model learns, rather than a label-dependent pruning score.

Evaluations on several standard classification tasks report higher classification performance and faster convergence for the resulting sparse networks. The label-free claim concerns finding the sparse networks; the paper still evaluates them on classification tasks. Its contribution is to use similarity in learning dynamics as a criterion for sparsification, connecting structural compression to the ability to train effectively.
summary.tldr: Neural Tangent Transfer finds sparse networks without labels by matching dense-network training dynamics.

title: Finding trainable sparse networks through Neural Tangent Transfer

abstract: Max-margin methods for binary classification such as the support vector machine (SVM) have been extended to the structured prediction setting under the name of max-margin Markov networks ($M^3N$), or more generally structural SVMs. Unfortunately, these methods are statistically inconsistent when the relationship between inputs and labels is far from deterministic. We overcome such limitations by defining the learning problem in terms of a “max-min” margin formulation, naming the resulting method max-min margin Markov networks ($M^4N$). We prove consistency and finite sample generalization bounds for $M^4N$ and provide an explicit algorithm to compute the estimator. The algorithm achieves a generalization error of $O(1/\sqrt{n})$ for a total cost of $O(n)$ projection-oracle calls (which have at most the same cost as the max-oracle from $M^3N$). Experiments on multi-class classification, ordinal regression, sequence prediction and ranking demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

paragraphs: Structured prediction extends classification to outputs with internal organization, such as sequences or rankings. Existing max-margin Markov networks apply the support vector machine idea to this setting. The paper identifies a statistical problem with these methods when inputs do not nearly determine their labels: their learning objective can be inconsistent.

The authors replace the usual margin formulation with a max-min version, producing max-min margin Markov networks, or M4N. They prove consistency and finite-sample generalization bounds, and give an explicit algorithm for computing the estimator. These results connect the choice of training objective with both statistical reliability and an implementable learning procedure.

The algorithm achieves a generalization error rate of order one over the square root of the sample count using a number of projection-oracle calls linear in that count. Each call costs at most as much as the corresponding maximization oracle used by M3N. Experiments on multiclass classification, ordinal regression, sequence prediction, and ranking demonstrate effectiveness. Together, the results show that addressing inconsistency can be compatible with controlled computational cost.
summary.tldr: M4N replaces the structured max-margin objective with a max-min formulation that has consistency guarantees and an efficient learning algorithm.

title: Consistent Structured Prediction with Max-Min Margin Markov Networks

abstract: A well-known first-order method for sampling from log-concave probability distributions is the Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm (ULA). This work proposes a new annealing step-size schedule for ULA, which allows to prove new convergence guarantees for sampling from a smooth log-concave distribution, which are not covered by existing state-of-the-art convergence guarantees. To establish this result, we derive a new theoretical bound that relates the Wasserstein distance to total variation distance between any two log-concave distributions that complements the reach of Talagrand $T_2$ inequality. Moreover, applying this new step size schedule to an existing constrained sampling algorithm, we show state-of-the-art convergence rates for sampling from a constrained log-concave distribution, as well as improved dimension dependence.

To establish this result, we derive a new theoretical bound that relates the Wasserstein distance to total variation distance between any two log-concave distributions that complements the reach of Talagrand $T_2$ inequality. paragraphs: The Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm is a first-order method for drawing samples from log-concave probability distributions. This paper changes its step-size schedule through annealing. The contribution centers on how that schedule enables convergence guarantees for smooth log-concave distributions that are not covered by the existing guarantees discussed by the authors.

To prove these results, the authors establish a new relationship between Wasserstein distance and total variation distance for any two log-concave distributions. These are different ways to measure how far probability distributions are from one another. Connecting them supplies a theoretical tool for the sampling analysis and complements the range of situations addressed by Talagrand’s T2 inequality.

The authors also apply the schedule to an existing algorithm for sampling under constraints. In that setting, they obtain state-of-the-art convergence rates and improve how the guarantees depend on dimension. The significance is both algorithmic and analytical: a step-size choice expands the available convergence results, while the new distance bound helps justify them. The stated guarantees concern the specified log-concave sampling settings.
summary.tldr: A new annealing schedule for Langevin sampling yields additional convergence guarantees and improves dimension dependence for constrained log-concave sampling.

title: Double-Loop Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm

abstract: In this paper, we propose a bootstrap method applied to massive data processed distributedly in a large number of machines. This new method is computationally efficient in that we bootstrap on the master machine without over-resampling, typically required by existing methods (Kleiner et al., 2014; Sengupta et al., 2016), while provably achieving optimal statistical efficiency with minimal communication. Our method does not require repeatedly re-fitting the model but only applies multiplier bootstrap in the master machine on the gradients received from the worker machines. Simulations validate our theory.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we propose a bootstrap method applied to massive data processed distributedly in a large number of machines. This new method is computationally efficient in that we bootstrap on the master machine without over-resampling, typically required by existing methods (Kleiner et al., 2014; Sengupta et al., 2016), while provably achieving optimal statistical efficiency with minimal communication. Our method does not require repeatedly re-fitting the model but only applies multiplier bootstrap in the master machine on the gradients received from the worker machines. Simulations validate our theory.

paragraphs: Bootstrap methods assess statistical uncertainty, but applying them to massive data spread across many machines creates computational and communication burdens. This paper proposes a distributed bootstrap procedure designed to retain statistical efficiency while reducing that work. Its central choice is to carry out the bootstrap on a coordinating master machine using information received from workers.

The workers supply gradients, and the master applies a multiplier bootstrap to those gradients. The procedure does not require fitting the model repeatedly. It also avoids the over-resampling that the abstract identifies as typical of existing approaches. These choices concentrate the uncertainty calculation at the master rather than repeatedly distributing model-fitting work across the data.

The authors prove optimal statistical efficiency with minimal communication for their method, and simulations support the theoretical results. The significance is that reducing computation and data exchange need not sacrifice the statistical efficiency established by the analysis. The method specifically achieves this through gradient-based bootstrap computation, connecting distributed learning information with uncertainty estimation.
summary.tldr: A master-side multiplier bootstrap uses worker gradients to achieve optimal statistical efficiency without repeated model fitting or over-resampling.

title: Simultaneous Inference for Massive Data: Distributed Bootstrap

abstract: We study reinforcement learning (RL) with no-reward demonstrations, a setting in which an RL agent has access to additional data from the interaction of other agents with the same environment. However, it has no access to the rewards or goals of these agents, and their objectives and levels of expertise may vary widely. These assumptions are common in multi-agent settings, such as autonomous driving. To effectively use this data, we turn to the framework of successor features. This allows us to disentangle shared features and dynamics of the environment from agent-specific rewards and policies. We propose a multi-task inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) algorithm, called \emph{inverse temporal difference learning} (ITD), that learns shared state features, alongside per-agent successor features and preference vectors, purely from demonstrations without reward labels. We further show how to seamlessly integrate ITD with learning from online environment interactions, arriving at a novel algorithm for reinforcement learning with demonstrations, called $\Psi \Phi$-learning (pronounced ‘Sci-Fi’). We provide empirical evidence for the effectiveness of $\Psi \Phi$-learning as a method for improving RL, IRL, imitation, and few-shot transfer, and derive worst-case bounds for its performance in zero-shot transfer to new tasks.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning from demonstrations made by other agents in the same environment when their rewards and goals are unavailable. These agents may pursue different objectives and have very different skill levels. The challenge is to extract useful shared knowledge without treating every demonstration as evidence of the learner’s own objective.

The approach uses successor features to separate shared environmental features and dynamics from agent-specific rewards and policies. Its inverse temporal difference learning algorithm learns shared state features together with each demonstrator’s successor features and preference vector, using demonstrations without reward labels. This creates a representation of both common structure and differences between agents.

Combining that algorithm with online interaction produces PsiPhi-learning. Experiments provide evidence of improvements in reinforcement learning, inverse reinforcement learning, imitation, and transfer with few examples. The authors also derive worst-case performance bounds for transfer to new tasks without additional examples. The contribution connects learning from diverse demonstrations with learning through direct interaction, using a shared representation to bridge the two sources of experience.
summary.tldr: PsiPhi-learning combines reward-free demonstrations and online interaction by separating shared environmental structure from individual agents’ preferences.

title: PsiPhi-Learning: Reinforcement Learning with Demonstrations using Successor Features and Inverse Temporal Difference Learning

abstract: Self-attention mechanisms have been widely adopted in many machine learning areas, including Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Graph Representation Learning (GRL), etc. However, existing works heavily rely on hand-crafted design to obtain customized attention mechanisms. In this paper, we automate Key, Query and Value representation design, which is one of the most important steps to obtain effective self-attentions. We propose an automated self-attention representation model, AutoAttend, which can automatically search powerful attention representations for downstream tasks leveraging Neural Architecture Search (NAS). In particular, we design a tailored search space for attention representation automation, which is flexible to produce effective attention representation designs. Based on the design prior obtained from attention representations in previous works, we further regularize our search space to reduce the space complexity without the loss of expressivity. Moreover, we propose a novel context-aware parameter sharing mechanism considering special characteristics of each sub-architecture to provide more accurate architecture estimations when conducting parameter sharing in our tailored search space. Experiments show the superiority of our proposed AutoAttend model over previous state-of-the-arts on eight text classification tasks in NLP and four node classification tasks in GRL.

paragraphs: Self-attention depends on key, query, and value representations, whose design influences how a model uses information. These representations are often customized by hand for particular tasks. AutoAttend treats their design as a search problem, using neural architecture search to find attention representations suited to a downstream task.

The authors construct a search space specifically for attention representations. They then use design knowledge from earlier attention mechanisms to constrain this space, reducing its complexity while preserving its expressivity. This matters because an architecture search must explore useful alternatives without becoming overwhelmed by the number of possible designs.

AutoAttend also introduces context-aware parameter sharing that accounts for characteristics of each candidate sub-architecture. Its purpose is to make architecture estimates more accurate when candidates share parameters during search. Experiments cover eight text classification tasks and four graph node classification tasks, where the authors report improvements over previous leading methods. Together, these results support automated representation design across both language and graph applications in the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: AutoAttend searches for task-specific attention representations and reports improvements on text and graph node classification tasks.

title: AutoAttend: Automated Attention Representation Search

abstract: Deep learning has made revolutionary advances to diverse applications in the presence of large-scale labeled datasets. However, it is prohibitively time-costly and labor-expensive to collect sufficient labeled data in most realistic scenarios. To mitigate the requirement for labeled data, semi-supervised learning (SSL) focuses on simultaneously exploring both labeled and unlabeled data, while transfer learning (TL) popularizes a favorable practice of fine-tuning a pre-trained model to the target data. A dilemma is thus encountered: Without a decent pre-trained model to provide an implicit regularization, SSL through self-training from scratch will be easily misled by inaccurate pseudo-labels, especially in large-sized label space; Without exploring the intrinsic structure of unlabeled data, TL through fine-tuning from limited labeled data is at risk of under-transfer caused by model shift. To escape from this dilemma, we present Self-Tuning to enable data-efficient deep learning by unifying the exploration of labeled and unlabeled data and the transfer of a pre-trained model, as well as a Pseudo Group Contrast (PGC) mechanism to mitigate the reliance on pseudo-labels and boost the tolerance to false labels. Self-Tuning outperforms its SSL and TL counterparts on five tasks by sharp margins, e.g. it doubles the accuracy of fine-tuning on Cars with $15%$ labels.

paragraphs: Learning from few labels creates difficulties for both semi-supervised learning and transfer learning. Self-training from scratch can be misled by incorrect pseudo-labels, especially when many classes are possible. Fine-tuning a pretrained model on limited labeled data can also transfer poorly when it does not exploit the structure in available unlabeled examples.

Self-Tuning combines these two sources of help: transferring a pretrained model and learning from both labeled and unlabeled target data. It also introduces Pseudo Group Contrast, a mechanism designed to reduce dependence on pseudo-labels and increase tolerance to incorrect ones. The approach tackles unreliable inferred labels while bringing unlabeled-data structure into the transfer process.

The reported evaluation finds substantial improvements over semi-supervised and transfer-learning counterparts across five tasks. On Cars with 15% of the labels available, Self-Tuning doubles the accuracy of fine-tuning. This result illustrates the potential value of combining pretraining with unlabeled-data learning, while the broader contribution is a unified training approach designed to address weaknesses of either strategy used alone.
summary.tldr: Self-Tuning combines pretrained-model transfer with labeled and unlabeled data, using Pseudo Group Contrast to tolerate inaccurate pseudo-labels.

title: Self-Tuning for Data-Efficient Deep Learning

abstract: A number of variational autoencoders (VAEs) have recently emerged with the aim of modeling multimodal data, e.g., to jointly model images and their corresponding captions. Still, multimodal VAEs tend to focus solely on a subset of the modalities, e.g., by fitting the image while neglecting the caption. We refer to this limitation as modality collapse. In this work, we argue that this effect is a consequence of conflicting gradients during multimodal VAE training. We show how to detect the sub-graphs in the computational graphs where gradients conflict (impartiality blocks), as well as how to leverage existing gradient-conflict solutions from multitask learning to mitigate modality collapse. That is, to ensure impartial optimization across modalities. We apply our training framework to several multimodal VAE models, losses and datasets from the literature, and empirically show that our framework significantly improves the reconstruction performance, conditional generation, and coherence of the latent space across modalities.
originalAbstract: A number of variational autoencoders (VAEs) have recently emerged with the aim of modeling multimodal data, e.g., to jointly model images and their corresponding captions. Still, multimodal VAEs tend to focus solely on a subset of the modalities, e.g., by fitting the image while neglecting the caption. We refer to this limitation as modality collapse. In this work, we argue that this effect is a consequence of conflicting gradients during multimodal VAE training. We show how to detect the sub-graphs in the computational graphs where gradients conflict (impartiality blocks), as well as how to leverage existing gradient-conflict solutions from multitask learning to mitigate modality collapse. That is, to ensure impartial optimization across modalities. We apply our training framework to several multimodal VAE models, losses and datasets from the literature, and empirically show that our framework significantly improves the reconstruction performance, conditional generation, and coherence of the latent space across modalities.

paragraphs: A multimodal variational autoencoder aims to learn related data types together, such as images and their captions. During training, however, it can concentrate on some modalities while neglecting others. The paper calls this modality collapse. A model that reconstructs images well while largely ignoring captions has failed to learn the intended joint representation.

The authors argue that conflicting gradients during training cause this imbalance. Gradients specify how parameters should change, and different modalities can push shared computation in competing directions. The proposed framework identifies the portions of the computational graph where those conflicts occur, called impartiality blocks, and applies existing gradient-conflict techniques from multitask learning at those locations.

This makes optimization across modalities the focus of the intervention. The authors apply the framework to several existing multimodal VAE models, objectives, and datasets. They report significant improvements in reconstruction, generation conditioned on another modality, and coherence of the shared latent space. These findings support addressing training conflicts as a practical way to mitigate modality collapse across the evaluated multimodal systems.
summary.tldr: Detecting and resolving conflicting training gradients helps multimodal VAEs learn modalities more evenly and improves their reported generation and reconstruction results.

title: Mitigating Modality Collapse in Multimodal VAEs via Impartial Optimization

abstract: The tremendous recent progress in analyzing the training dynamics of overparameterized neural networks has primarily focused on wide networks and therefore does not sufficiently address the role of depth in deep learning. In this work, we present the first trainability guarantee of infinitely deep but narrow neural networks. We study the infinite-depth limit of a multilayer perceptron (MLP) with a specific initialization and establish a trainability guarantee using the NTK theory. We then extend the analysis to an infinitely deep convolutional neural network (CNN) and perform brief experiments.

paragraphs: Much theoretical progress on neural network training has focused on networks with very large width. That emphasis leaves depth less directly addressed. This paper instead studies narrow networks as their depth grows without bound, asking whether training can be guaranteed in a regime where depth is the central source of overparameterization.

The authors begin with a multilayer perceptron under a specific initialization. They analyze its infinite-depth limit using neural tangent kernel theory and establish a trainability guarantee. The initialization is part of the stated setting, so the result provides a guarantee for this construction rather than an unrestricted claim about every deep, narrow network.

The analysis is then extended to an infinitely deep convolutional network, accompanied by brief experiments. The authors present the work as the first trainability guarantee for infinitely deep but narrow networks. Its main contribution is to expand the theoretical study of training beyond the wide-network regime, showing that a depth-focused limit can also support a mathematical guarantee.
summary.tldr: Neural tangent kernel analysis establishes trainability for infinitely deep, narrow networks under a specific initialization.

title: Neural Tangent Kernel Analysis of Deep Narrow Neural Networks

abstract: The Lipschitz constant of neural networks has been established as a key quantity to enforce the robustness to adversarial examples. In this paper, we tackle the problem of building $1$-Lipschitz Neural Networks. By studying Residual Networks from a continuous time dynamical system perspective, we provide a generic method to build $1$-Lipschitz Neural Networks and show that some previous approaches are special cases of this framework. Then, we extend this reasoning and show that ResNet flows derived from convex potentials define $1$-Lipschitz transformations, that lead us to define the Convex Potential Layer (CPL). A comprehensive set of experiments on several datasets demonstrates the scalability of our architecture and the benefits as an $\ell_2$-provable defense against adversarial examples. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/MILES-PSL/Convex-Potential-Layer}

Then, we extend this reasoning and show that ResNet flows derived from convex potentials define $1$-Lipschitz transformations, that lead us to define the Convex Potential Layer (CPL). A comprehensive set of experiments on several datasets demonstrates the scalability of our architecture and the benefits as an $\ell_2$-provable defense against adversarial examples. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/MILES-PSL/Convex-Potential-Layer}

paragraphs: The paper studies how to build neural networks whose outputs cannot change more than their inputs, as measured by a Lipschitz constant of one. Controlling this sensitivity matters for adversarial robustness: small changes to an input should have a bounded effect on the network. The contribution concerns architectures designed to satisfy that mathematical constraint.

The authors view residual networks through continuous-time dynamical systems. This perspective provides a general construction for 1-Lipschitz networks and places some earlier approaches inside the same framework. They then show that residual-network flows derived from convex potentials produce 1-Lipschitz transformations. This result motivates a building block called the Convex Potential Layer.

Experiments across several datasets demonstrate that the resulting architecture can scale and provide benefits for provable defenses against adversarial perturbations measured with the Euclidean norm. The theoretical construction and empirical evaluation serve different purposes: the construction establishes controlled sensitivity, while the experiments investigate its usefulness in practical networks. The result connects architectural design to a mathematically grounded form of robustness.
summary.tldr: A dynamical-systems view of residual networks yields 1-Lipschitz architectures and convex-potential layers for provable adversarial defense.

title: A Dynamical System Perspective for Lipschitz Neural Networks

abstract: We study the inference of mean-variance robustness measures to quantify input uncertainty under the Gaussian Process (GP) framework. These measures are widely used in applications where the robustness of the solution is of interest, for example, in engineering design. While the variance is commonly used to characterize the robustness, Bayesian inference of the variance using GPs is known to be challenging. In this paper, we propose a Spectral Representation of Robustness Measures based on the GP’s spectral representation, i.e., an analytical approach to approximately infer both robustness measures for normal and uniform input uncertainty distributions. We present two approximations based on different Fourier features and compare their accuracy numerically. To demonstrate their utility and efficacy in robust Bayesian Optimization, we integrate the analytical robustness measures in three standard acquisition functions for various robust optimization formulations. We show their competitive performance on numerical benchmarks and real-life applications.

paragraphs: When an input is uncertain, a useful solution should account for both its average outcome and how much that outcome varies. This paper studies inference of those mean and variance measures within a Gaussian process framework. Variance is especially relevant to robustness, but Bayesian inference of it using Gaussian processes is challenging.

The authors use the Gaussian process’s spectral representation to derive analytical approximations for both measures. Their approach handles normal and uniform distributions of input uncertainty. They present two approximations based on different Fourier features and compare their numerical accuracy, making the representation choice part of the study rather than assuming a single approximation is sufficient.

To connect the inference method with decision-making, they incorporate the approximate robustness measures into three standard acquisition functions for different robust Bayesian optimization formulations. Numerical benchmarks and real-life applications show competitive performance. The contribution is a way to carry approximate mean and variance information into the optimization process, so uncertainty in the inputs can influence which solution is sought and which evaluations are selected.
summary.tldr: Spectral Gaussian process approximations estimate mean and variance under normal or uniform input uncertainty and support competitive robust Bayesian optimization.

title: Spectral Representation of Robustness Measures for Optimization Under Input Uncertainty

abstract: Incomplete multi-view clustering is a significant but challenging task. Although jointly imputing incomplete samples and conducting clustering has been shown to achieve promising performance, learning from both complete and incomplete data may be worse than learning only from complete data, particularly when imputed views are semantic inconsistent with missing views. To address this issue, we propose a novel framework to reduce the clustering performance degradation risk from semantic inconsistent imputed views. Concretely, by the proposed bi-level optimization framework, missing views are dynamically imputed from the learned semantic neighbors, and imputed samples are automatically selected for training. In theory, the empirical risk of the model is no higher than learning only from complete data, and the model is never worse than learning only from complete data in terms of expected risk with high probability. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior performance and efficient safe incomplete multi-view clustering.
