paragraphs: Multi-view clustering groups examples using several forms of information, some of which may be missing. Filling in missing views can make more examples available for training. However, an imputed view can convey the wrong meaning, and adding such examples can produce worse clustering than using complete examples alone.

The paper proposes a bilevel optimization framework that addresses both imputation and selection. It dynamically fills missing views using learned semantic neighbors and automatically selects which imputed samples enter training. These coupled decisions aim to reduce the harm caused by semantically inconsistent replacements, rather than assuming every completed example should be used.

The theoretical results compare the method directly with learning only from complete data. Its empirical risk is no higher, and its expected risk is no worse with high probability. The probability qualification applies to the expected-risk result. Comprehensive experiments also report superior performance and efficient clustering. The work makes the complete-data-only approach an explicit safety reference for using incomplete examples.
summary.tldr: Jointly imputing and selecting incomplete samples enables clustering with risk guarantees relative to training only on complete data.

title: Deep Safe Incomplete Multi-view Clustering: Theorem and Algorithm

abstract: In distributionally robust Bayesian optimization (DRBO), an exact computation of the worst-case expected value requires solving an expensive convex optimization problem. We develop a fast approximation of the worst-case expected value based on the notion of worst-case sensitivity that caters to arbitrary convex distribution distances. We provide a regret bound for our novel DRBO algorithm with the fast approximation, and empirically show it is competitive with that using the exact worst-case expected value while incurring significantly less computation time. In order to guide the choice of distribution distance to be used with DRBO, we show that our approximation implicitly optimizes an objective close to an interpretable risk-sensitive value.

paragraphs: Distributionally robust Bayesian optimization evaluates decisions against uncertainty about the underlying distribution. Computing the exact worst-case expected value requires solving an expensive convex optimization problem. This paper targets that computational burden, which is part of evaluating robust choices rather than simply evaluating a single assumed distribution.

The authors develop a fast approximation based on worst-case sensitivity. The approximation accommodates arbitrary convex distances between distributions, giving it scope across different ways of defining distributional uncertainty. They incorporate it into a new optimization algorithm and provide a regret bound, supplying theoretical support for using the approximation in the decision process.

Experiments show performance competitive with an approach that computes the exact worst-case expected value, while requiring significantly less computation time. The authors also show that the approximation implicitly optimizes something close to an interpretable risk-sensitive value. This interpretation helps guide the choice of distribution distance: that choice affects the risk-related objective the approximation effectively favors.
summary.tldr: A worst-case-sensitivity approximation makes distributionally robust Bayesian optimization faster while retaining a regret bound and competitive empirical performance.

title: Efficient Distributionally Robust Bayesian Optimization with Worst-case Sensitivity

abstract: Instrumental variable (IV) methods are used to estimate causal effects in settings with unobserved confounding, where we cannot directly experiment on the treatment variable. Instruments are variables which only affect the outcome indirectly via the treatment variable(s). Most IV applications focus on low-dimensional treatments and crucially require at least as many instruments as treatments. This assumption is restrictive: in the natural sciences we often seek to infer causal effects of high-dimensional treatments (e.g., the effect of gene expressions or microbiota on health and disease), but can only run few experiments with a limited number of instruments (e.g., drugs or antibiotics). In such under-specified problems, the full treatment effect is not identifiable in a single experiment even in the linear case. We show that one can still reliably recover the projection of the treatment effect onto the instrumented subspace and develop techniques to consistently combine such partial estimates from different sets of instruments. We then leverage our combined estimators in an algorithm that iteratively proposes the most informative instruments at each round of experimentation to maximize the overall information about the full causal effect.

paragraphs: Instrumental-variable methods estimate causal effects when hidden confounding is present and direct treatment experiments are unavailable. Instruments affect the outcome only through the treatment variables. Standard applications typically require at least as many instruments as treatments, which becomes restrictive when many treatment dimensions must be studied using only a few experimental instruments.

With too few instruments, a single experiment cannot identify the complete treatment effect, even in a linear setting. The paper shows that useful information can still be recovered: the projection of the effect onto the instrumented subspace. This is the component of the overall effect accessible through the available instruments, giving a precise target for partial estimation.

The authors develop techniques to combine partial estimates consistently across different instrument sets. They then use those combined estimators in a sequential algorithm that proposes informative instruments for the next experimental round. The goal is to maximize accumulated information about the full causal effect. The contribution makes incomplete experiments useful and coordinates their information, without claiming that any single underspecified experiment identifies the entire effect.
summary.tldr: Partial causal effects from limited instruments can be combined across experiments to guide more informative instrument selection.

title: Sequential Underspecified Instrument Selection for Cause-Effect Estimation

abstract: Variational auto-encoders are powerful probabilistic models in generative tasks but suffer from generating low-quality samples which are caused by the holes in the prior. We propose the Coupled Variational Auto-Encoder (C-VAE), which formulates the VAE problem as one of Optimal Transport (OT) between the prior and data distributions. The C-VAE allows greater flexibility in priors and natural resolution of the prior hole problem by enforcing coupling between the prior and the data distribution and enables flexible optimization through the primal, dual, and semi-dual formulations of entropic OT. Simulations on synthetic and real data show that the C-VAE outperforms alternatives including VAE, WAE, and InfoVAE in fidelity to the data, quality of the latent representation, and in quality of generated samples.

The C-VAE allows greater flexibility in priors and natural resolution of the prior hole problem by enforcing coupling between the prior and the data distribution and enables flexible optimization through the primal, dual, and semi-dual formulations of entropic OT. paragraphs: This paper addresses poor generated samples in variational autoencoders by focusing on holes in the prior. The issue concerns how the distribution used to draw latent samples relates to the data distribution. The authors propose the Coupled Variational Autoencoder, which treats that relationship as an optimal transport problem.

Optimal transport provides a way to formulate a coupling between two distributions. C-VAE explicitly enforces such a coupling between the prior and the data, giving greater freedom in choosing the prior and providing a natural resolution of the prior-hole problem. Its use of entropic optimal transport also offers several optimization routes through primal, dual, and semi-dual formulations.

Experiments on synthetic and real data compare C-VAE with VAE, WAE, and InfoVAE alternatives. The reported improvements cover fidelity to the data, latent representation quality, and generated sample quality. These findings suggest that explicitly organizing the relationship between the prior and data can benefit both generation and representation learning in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: C-VAE uses optimal transport to couple prior and data distributions, improving latent representations and generated samples in the reported experiments.

title: Coupled Variational Autoencoder

abstract: We formalize the problem of contextual optimization through the lens of Bayesian experimental design and propose CO-BED—a general, model-agnostic framework for designing contextual experiments using information-theoretic principles. After formulating a suitable information-based objective, we employ black-box variational methods to simultaneously estimate it and optimize the designs in a single stochastic gradient scheme. In addition, to accommodate discrete actions within our framework, we propose leveraging continuous relaxation schemes, which can naturally be integrated into our variational objective. As a result, CO-BED provides a general and automated solution to a wide range of contextual optimization problems. We illustrate its effectiveness in a number of experiments, where CO-BED demonstrates competitive performance even when compared to bespoke, model-specific alternatives.

After formulating a suitable information-based objective, we employ black-box variational methods to simultaneously estimate it and optimize the designs in a single stochastic gradient scheme. paragraphs: Contextual optimization concerns choosing actions while accounting for the context in which they are used. This paper approaches that problem through Bayesian experimental design: experiments are selected according to an information-based objective. CO-BED turns this perspective into a general framework intended to work across different models, reducing the need to design a separate experimental strategy for each one.

The computational challenge is that the information objective must be estimated while the experiment design is being optimized. CO-BED uses black-box variational methods to perform both operations within one stochastic-gradient scheme. For discrete actions, it introduces continuous relaxations that fit into the same objective, allowing gradient-based design machinery to accommodate choices that are originally discrete.

Experiments show competitive performance against alternatives tailored to particular models. That finding supports the usefulness of a general, automated approach even when specialized methods are available. The contribution combines a formulation of contextual optimization with a practical optimization procedure, linking what an experiment should teach the learner to how its design is computed.
summary.tldr: CO-BED uses an information-based objective and joint variational optimization to automate contextual experiment design across models.

title: CO-BED: Information-Theoretic Contextual Optimization via Bayesian Experimental Design

abstract: Plasticity, the ability of a neural network to quickly change its predictions in response to new information, is essential for the adaptability and robustness of deep reinforcement learning systems. Deep neural networks are known to lose plasticity over the course of training even in relatively simple learning problems, but the mechanisms driving this phenomenon are still poorly understood. This paper conducts a systematic empirical analysis into plasticity loss, with the goal of understanding the phenomenon mechanistically in order to guide the future development of targeted solutions. We find that loss of plasticity is deeply connected to changes in the curvature of the loss landscape, but that it often occurs in the absence of saturated units. Based on this insight, we identify a number of parameterization and optimization design choices which enable networks to better preserve plasticity over the course of training. We validate the utility of these findings on larger-scale RL benchmarks in the Arcade Learning Environment.

paragraphs: Plasticity is a neural network’s ability to change its predictions quickly when new information arrives. That adaptability matters in deep reinforcement learning, yet networks can lose it during training even on relatively simple problems. This paper systematically investigates the mechanisms behind that loss to help guide more targeted solutions.

The empirical analysis finds a strong connection between declining plasticity and changes in the curvature of the loss landscape. Curvature describes how the training objective bends as parameters change. The authors also observe plasticity loss without saturated units, showing that this phenomenon often occurs even when that possible explanation is absent.

Using these findings, the authors identify parameterization and optimization choices that help networks retain their ability to adapt throughout training. They validate the usefulness of those choices on larger reinforcement learning benchmarks in the Arcade Learning Environment. The study links a mechanistic investigation to practical design decisions, while its empirical findings support a connection with loss geometry rather than establishing one universal cause of plasticity loss.
summary.tldr: Plasticity loss is empirically linked to loss-landscape curvature, guiding network and optimization choices that better preserve adaptability.

title: Understanding Plasticity in Neural Networks

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved great success in solving difficult tasks across many domains, but such success comes with a high computation cost, and inference latency. As developers and third parties customize these models, the need to provide efficient inference has increased. Many efforts have attempted to reduce inference cost through model compression techniques such as pruning and distillation. However, these techniques either require labeled data, or are time-consuming as they require the compressed model to be retrained to regain accuracy. In this paper, we propose a gradient-free structured pruning framework that uses only unlabeled data. An evaluation on the GLUE and SQuAD benchmarks using BERT$_{BASE}$ and DistilBERT illustrates the effectiveness of the proposed approach. By only using the weights of the pre-trained model and unlabeled data, in a matter of a few minutes on a single GPU, up to 40% of the original FLOP count can be reduced with less than a $4%$ accuracy loss across all tasks considered.

paragraphs: Language models can be expensive to run, creating demand for compression methods that reduce computation and inference latency. Existing pruning and distillation approaches may require labeled examples or time-consuming retraining to recover accuracy. This paper proposes a structured pruning framework that operates without gradients and uses only pretrained model weights and unlabeled data.

The approach aims to make compression practical when labeled downstream data is unavailable and the time available for adapting a model is limited. Its required inputs are the existing model and unlabeled examples, so the pruning procedure does not depend on obtaining task annotations. The reported process takes only a few minutes on a single GPU.

The authors evaluate BERT_BASE and DistilBERT on GLUE and SQuAD. Across the tasks considered, they report reductions of up to 40% in the original floating-point operation count with less than 4% accuracy loss. These findings demonstrate a favorable computation–accuracy tradeoff in the tested settings. The reported savings concern operation counts; the abstract does not claim an identical percentage reduction in inference latency.
summary.tldr: Gradient-free pruning uses pretrained weights and unlabeled data to reduce tested language models' FLOPs by up to 40% with less than 4% accuracy loss.

title: Gradient-Free Structured Pruning with Unlabeled Data

abstract: With the introduction of data protection and privacy regulations, it has become crucial to remove the lineage of data on demand from a machine learning (ML) model. In the last few years, there have been notable developments in machine unlearning to remove the information of certain training data efficiently and effectively from ML models. In this work, we explore unlearning for the regression problem, particularly in deep learning models. Unlearning in classification and simple linear regression has been considerably investigated. However, unlearning in deep regression models largely remains an untouched problem till now. In this work, we introduce deep regression unlearning methods that generalize well and are robust to privacy attacks. We propose the Blindspot unlearning method which uses a novel weight optimization process. A randomly initialized model, partially exposed to the retain samples and a copy of the original model are used together to selectively imprint knowledge about the data that we wish to keep and scrub off the information of the data we wish to forget. We also propose a Gaussian fine tuning method for regression unlearning. The existing unlearning metrics for classification are not directly applicable to regression unlearning. Therefore, we adapt these metrics for the regression setting. We conduct regression unlearning experiments for computer vision, natural language processing and forecasting applications. Our methods show excellent performance for all these datasets across all the metrics. Source code: https://github.com/ayu987/deep-regression-unlearning

paragraphs: Machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of selected training examples from an already trained model. This paper addresses deep regression, where models predict numerical values. The authors identify this as a less explored setting than classification or simple linear regression and develop methods specifically for its learning and evaluation requirements.

Their Blindspot method uses a new weight optimization procedure involving two models: a randomly initialized model partially exposed to retained examples, and a copy of the original trained model. Together, these guide the selective preservation of knowledge about retained data and removal of information about examples designated for forgetting. The paper also introduces a Gaussian fine-tuning method.

Because classification unlearning metrics do not transfer directly to regression, the authors adapt those metrics to this setting. Experiments span computer vision, natural language processing, and forecasting. The reported results show strong performance across the evaluated datasets and metrics, including generalization and robustness to privacy attacks. These findings support the proposed methods across several kinds of deep regression application.
summary.tldr: Blindspot and Gaussian fine-tuning extend machine unlearning to deep regression while aiming to retain useful knowledge and resist privacy attacks.

title: Deep Regression Unlearning

abstract: Large pretrained language models (LMs) have shown impressive In-Context Learning (ICL) ability, where the model learns to do an unseen task simply by conditioning on a prompt consisting of input-output examples as demonstration, without any parameter updates. The performance of ICL is highly dominated by the quality of the selected in-context examples. However, previous selection methods are mostly based on simple heuristics, leading to sub-optimal performance. In this work, we systematically formulate in-context example selection as a subset selection problem, and optimize it in an end-to-end fashion. We propose CEIL (Compositional Exemplars for In-context Learning), which is instantiated by Determinantal Point Processes (DPPs) to model the interaction between the given input and in-context examples, and optimized through carefully-designed contrastive learning to obtain preference from LMs. We validate CEIL on 12 classification and generation datasets from 7 distinct NLP tasks, including sentiment analysis, phraphrase detection, natural language inference, commonsense reasoning, open-domain question answering, code generation and semantic parsing. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness, transferability, compositionality of CEIL, shedding new lights on in-context leaning. Our code is released at https://github.com/HKUNLP/icl-ceil.
originalAbstract: Large pretrained language models (LMs) have shown impressive In-Context Learning (ICL) ability, where the model learns to do an unseen task simply by conditioning on a prompt consisting of input-output examples as demonstration, without any parameter updates. The performance of ICL is highly dominated by the quality of the selected in-context examples. However, previous selection methods are mostly based on simple heuristics, leading to sub-optimal performance. In this work, we systematically formulate in-context example selection as a subset selection problem, and optimize it in an end-to-end fashion. We propose CEIL (Compositional Exemplars for In-context Learning), which is instantiated by Determinantal Point Processes (DPPs) to model the interaction between the given input and in-context examples, and optimized through carefully-designed contrastive learning to obtain preference from LMs. We validate CEIL on 12 classification and generation datasets from 7 distinct NLP tasks, including sentiment analysis, phraphrase detection, natural language inference, commonsense reasoning, open-domain question answering, code generation and semantic parsing. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness, transferability, compositionality of CEIL, shedding new lights on in-context leaning. Our code is released at https://github.com/HKUNLP/icl-ceil.

paragraphs: A language model can perform an unfamiliar task by reading input-output demonstrations in its prompt, without changing its parameters. Which demonstrations it sees strongly affects performance. This paper studies how to choose those examples systematically, treating the prompt’s demonstration set as something to optimize rather than assemble through simple heuristics.

The proposed method, CEIL, formulates example selection as a subset-selection problem. It uses determinantal point processes to model interactions involving the current input and candidate demonstrations. A contrastive learning procedure draws preference information from language models to train the selection process. The central idea is to account for how examples work together within a set.

The authors evaluate CEIL on 12 datasets covering seven language tasks, including classification, question answering, code generation, and semantic parsing. They report evidence of effectiveness, transferability, and compositionality. These findings support learning a demonstration-selection strategy that captures relationships among examples, making the composition of the prompt an explicit part of improving in-context learning.
summary.tldr: CEIL learns to select demonstration sets for language-model prompts by modeling how examples work together.

title: Compositional Exemplars for In-context Learning

abstract: We study the impact of the batch size $n_b$ on the iteration time $T$ of training two-layer neural networks with one-pass stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on multi-index target functions of isotropic covariates. We characterize the optimal batch size minimizing the iteration time as a function of the hardness of the target, as characterized by the information exponents. We show that performing gradient updates with large batches $n_b \lesssim d^{\frac{\ell}{2}}$ minimizes the training time without changing the total sample complexity, where $\ell$ is the information exponent of the target to be learned and $d$ is the input dimension. However, larger batch sizes than $n_b \gg d^{\frac{\ell}{2}}$ are detrimental for improving the time complexity of SGD. We provably overcome this fundamental limitation via a different training protocol, Correlation loss SGD, which suppresses the auto-correlation terms in the loss function. We show that one can track the training progress by a system of low-dimensional ordinary differential equations (ODEs). Finally, we validate our theoretical results with numerical experiments.

paragraphs: Larger training batches can reduce the number of gradient updates needed, but the benefit depends on the target being learned. This paper studies that tradeoff for two-layer neural networks trained with one-pass stochastic gradient descent on multi-index targets with isotropic covariates. Target difficulty is described using information exponents.

The authors characterize the batch size that minimizes iteration time. Batches up to roughly the input dimension raised to half the target’s information exponent can minimize training time without changing total sample complexity. Batches much larger than this scale become detrimental to improving SGD’s time complexity. The result identifies a problem-dependent boundary for useful batch growth in the analyzed setting.

The paper then introduces Correlation loss SGD, a different training protocol that suppresses auto-correlation terms in the loss. It provably overcomes the identified limitation of the original protocol. A low-dimensional system of ordinary differential equations tracks training progress, and numerical experiments validate the theoretical findings. The contribution distinguishes iteration efficiency from sample efficiency and shows that changing the training objective can alter the batch-size tradeoff.
summary.tldr: Theory identifies a target-dependent useful batch-size scale for one-pass SGD and a modified loss that overcomes its time-complexity limitation.

title: Online Learning and Information Exponents: The Importance of Batch size & Time/Complexity Tradeoffs

abstract: We study how to best spend a budget of noisy labels to compare the accuracy of two binary classifiers. It’s common practice to collect and aggregate multiple noisy labels for a given data point into a less noisy label via a majority vote. We prove a theorem that runs counter to conventional wisdom. If the goal is to identify the better of two classifiers, we show it’s best to spend the budget on collecting a single label for more samples. Our result follows from a non-trivial application of Cramér’s theorem, a staple in the theory of large deviations. We discuss the implications of our work for the design of machine learning benchmarks, where they overturn some time-honored recommendations. In addition, our results provide sample size bounds superior to what follows from Hoeffding’s bound.

paragraphs: When labels are noisy, collecting several judgments for each example and taking a majority vote seems like a natural way to improve an evaluation. This paper asks whether that is the best use of a fixed labeling budget when the specific goal is to determine which of two binary classifiers is more accurate.

The authors prove that, in the comparison problem they study, the budget is better spent obtaining one label for each of more examples. The distinction is between improving an individual example’s label and improving the overall decision about which classifier wins. Spending labels repeatedly on the same example can sacrifice the broader coverage that helps make that comparison.

The proof uses Cramér’s theorem from large-deviation theory to analyze the comparison. It also yields sample-size bounds that improve on those obtained from Hoeffding’s bound. These findings challenge familiar recommendations for benchmark construction: when the objective is ranking two binary classifiers, the most useful labeling strategy need not be the one that produces the cleanest labels for individual examples.
summary.tldr: For the studied task of comparing two binary classifiers, labeling more examples once is better than spending the same budget on repeated labels.

title: Don’t Label Twice: Quantity Beats Quality when Comparing Binary Classifiers on a Budget

abstract: We introduce a method to generate 3D scenes that are disentangled into their component objects. This disentanglement is unsupervised, relying only on the knowledge of a large pretrained text-to-image model. Our key insight is that objects can be discovered by finding parts of a 3D scene that, when rearranged spatially, still produce valid configurations of the same scene. Concretely, our method jointly optimizes multiple NeRFs—each representing its own object—along with a set of layouts that composite these objects into scenes. We then encourage these composited scenes to be in-distribution according to the image generator. We show that despite its simplicity, our approach successfully generates 3D scenes decomposed into individual objects, enabling new capabilities in text-to-3D content creation.

paragraphs: Generating a three-dimensional scene as distinct objects makes its internal structure available for content creation. This paper develops an unsupervised method for obtaining that decomposition using the knowledge of a pretrained text-to-image model. Its central idea is that meaningful objects should remain parts of plausible scenes when their spatial arrangement changes.

The method jointly optimizes several neural radiance fields, or NeRFs, with each field representing an individual object. It also optimizes a collection of layouts that combine these objects into complete scenes. The composed scenes are encouraged to remain within the kinds of images supported by the pretrained generator, providing guidance for both object discovery and arrangement.

Learning across multiple arrangements is important because the proposed signal for identifying objects comes from their ability to participate in valid configurations of the same scene. The authors demonstrate scenes that separate into individual objects despite the absence of supervised disentanglement. The result supports text-to-3D creation in which component objects and their layouts are represented explicitly as part of the generated scene.
summary.tldr: Jointly learning object NeRFs and multiple plausible layouts enables unsupervised generation of 3D scenes with separate component objects.

title: Disentangled 3D Scene Generation with Layout Learning

abstract: Although pre-trained models such as Contrastive Language-Image Pre-Training (CLIP) show impressive generalization results, their robustness is still limited under Out-of-Distribution (OOD) scenarios. Instead of undesirably leveraging human annotation as commonly done, it is possible to leverage the visual understanding power of Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs). However, MLLMs struggle with vision problems due to task incompatibility, thus hindering their effectiveness. In this paper, we propose to effectively leverage MLLMs via Machine Vision Therapy which aims to rectify erroneous predictions of specific vision models. By supervising vision models using MLLM predictions, visual robustness can be boosted in a nearly unsupervised manner. Moreover, we propose a Denoising In-Context Learning (DICL) strategy to solve the incompatibility issue. Concretely, by examining the noise probability of each example through a transition matrix, we construct an instruction containing a correct exemplar and a probable erroneous one, which enables MLLMs to detect and rectify the incorrect predictions of vision models. Under mild assumptions, we theoretically show that our DICL method is guaranteed to find the ground truth. Through extensive experiments on various OOD datasets, our method demonstrates powerful capabilities for enhancing visual robustness under many OOD scenarios.

paragraphs: Machine Vision Therapy uses multimodal language models to help correct the predictions of vision models under distribution shifts. Models such as CLIP can generalize well yet remain unreliable on unfamiliar data. The proposed approach uses multimodal-model predictions as supervision, aiming to improve robustness with very little reliance on human annotation.

A key obstacle is that a multimodal language model may not naturally handle the vision task in the required way. Denoising In-Context Learning addresses this mismatch by estimating examples’ noise probabilities through a transition matrix. It constructs an instruction containing a correct example and a likely incorrect one, helping the model identify and repair erroneous vision-model predictions.

The paper proves that this procedure can find the ground truth under assumptions described as mild. That guarantee remains conditional on those assumptions. Experiments across several out-of-distribution datasets show improvements in visual robustness in many settings. The approach therefore combines a method for eliciting useful corrections with a training strategy that transfers those corrections back to the vision model.
summary.tldr: Machine Vision Therapy uses carefully constructed multimodal prompts to correct vision-model predictions and improve robustness under distribution shifts.

title: Machine Vision Therapy: Multimodal Large Language Models Can Enhance Visual Robustness via Denoising In-Context Learning

abstract: Deep kernel learning (DKL) marries the uncertainty quantification of Gaussian processes (GPs) and the representational power of deep neural networks. However, training DKL is challenging and often leads to overfitting. Most notably, DKL often learns “non-local” kernels — incurring spurious correlations. To remedy this issue, we propose using amortized inducing points and a parameter-sharing scheme, which ties together the amortization and DKL networks. This design imposes an explicit dependency between the ELBO’s model fit and capacity terms. In turn, this prevents the former from dominating the optimization procedure and incurring the aforementioned spurious correlations. Extensive experiments show that our resulting method, amortized varitional DKL (AVDKL), i) consistently outperforms DKL and standard GPs for tabular data; ii) achieves significantly higher accuracy than DKL in node classification tasks; and iii) leads to substantially better accuracy and negative log-likelihood than DKL on CIFAR100.

paragraphs: Deep kernel learning combines neural networks’ ability to learn representations with Gaussian processes’ uncertainty estimates. Training this combination can nevertheless lead to overfitting. The paper focuses on a particular failure: learned kernels can connect observations through spurious correlations, producing relationships that the model should not rely on.

The proposed method, amortized variational deep kernel learning, uses amortized inducing points together with shared parameters between the amortization and deep kernel networks. This links two parts of the training objective: the term rewarding agreement with observations and the term controlling model capacity. According to the authors, that dependency prevents the fit term from dominating optimization and creating the unwanted correlations.

Experiments cover tabular data, graph node classification, and image classification. The method consistently outperforms conventional deep kernel learning and standard Gaussian processes on the reported tabular tasks. It also improves node classification accuracy over deep kernel learning and improves both accuracy and negative log-likelihood on CIFAR100. These findings support the proposed training design across the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Sharing parameters between inducing-point amortization and deep kernel learning helps prevent spurious correlations and improves results across several evaluated tasks.

title: Amortized Variational Deep Kernel Learning

abstract: In large deep neural networks that seem to perform surprisingly well on many tasks, we also observe a few failures related to accuracy, social biases, and alignment with human values, among others. Therefore, before deploying these models, it is crucial to characterize this failure landscape for engineers to debug and legislative bodies to audit models. Nevertheless, it is infeasible to exhaustively test for all possible combinations of factors that could lead to a model’s failure. In this paper, we introduce a post-hoc method that utilizes deep reinforcement learning to explore and construct the landscape of failure modes in pre-trained discriminative and generative models. With the aid of limited human feedback, we then demonstrate how to restructure the failure landscape to be more desirable by moving away from the discovered failure modes. We empirically show the effectiveness of the proposed method across common Computer Vision, Natural Language Processing, and Vision-Language tasks.

paragraphs: Strong performance on many tasks can coexist with failures involving accuracy, social bias, or alignment with human values. Understanding where these failures occur matters for debugging and auditing a model before deployment. The difficulty is that testing every possible combination of contributing factors is infeasible, leaving a need for methods that actively search for problematic behavior.

The authors introduce a method applied after model training that uses deep reinforcement learning to explore failure modes. Its aim is to construct a picture of where pretrained models go wrong, covering both discriminative models and generative models. This connects failure discovery to a search process rather than requiring exhaustive enumeration of possible test conditions.

The method then uses limited human feedback to shift behavior away from discovered failures, making the resulting failure landscape more desirable. Experiments across vision, language, and combined vision-language tasks demonstrate effectiveness. The contribution therefore combines characterization and mitigation: discovering failure patterns supplies targets for subsequent improvement, without implying that every possible failure has been found or eliminated.
summary.tldr: A reinforcement-learning method searches pretrained models for failures and uses limited human feedback to reduce discovered unwanted behaviors.

title: Failures Are Fated, But Can Be Faded: Characterizing and Mitigating Unwanted Behaviors in Large-Scale Vision and Language Models

abstract: Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP) has achieved remarkable success, leading to rapid advancements in multimodal studies. However, CLIP faces a notable challenge in terms of inefficient data utilization. It relies on a single contrastive supervision for each image-text pair during representation learning, disregarding a substantial amount of valuable information that could offer richer supervision. Additionally, the retention of non-informative tokens leads to increased computational demands and time costs, particularly in CLIP’s ViT image encoder. To address these issues, we propose Multi-Perspective Language-Image Pretraining (MLIP). In MLIP, we leverage the frequency transform’s sensitivity to both high and low-frequency variations, which complements the spatial domain’s sensitivity limited to low-frequency variations only. By incorporating frequency transforms and token-level alignment, we expand CILP’s single supervision into multi-domain and multi-level supervision, enabling a more thorough exploration of informative image features. Additionally, we introduce a token merging method guided by comprehensive semantics from the frequency and spatial domains. This allows us to merge tokens to multi-granularity tokens with a controllable compression rate to accelerate CLIP. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of our design.

paragraphs: CLIP learns image and text representations from paired examples, but this paper argues that a single contrastive training signal leaves useful information unused. It also identifies computational waste from retaining uninformative image tokens. MLIP addresses both problems by enriching the supervision available from each pair and compressing the image-token representation.

The method adds frequency-domain information to spatial image information. The authors use frequency transforms for their sensitivity to both high- and low-frequency variations, complementing the spatial sensitivity described in the paper. Token-level alignment adds finer-grained supervision. Together, these changes provide learning signals across multiple domains and levels, giving the model more ways to extract informative image features from each training pair.

For efficiency, MLIP merges tokens using semantic information from both frequency and spatial domains. It produces tokens at multiple granularities with a controllable compression rate, allowing the amount of compression to be adjusted. Extensive experiments support the design’s effectiveness. The overall contribution connects richer use of training examples with selective reduction of the tokens that the visual encoder must process.
summary.tldr: MLIP enriches image-text supervision with frequency information and token alignment while merging tokens to accelerate CLIP.

title: MLIP: Efficient Multi-Perspective Language-Image Pretraining with Exhaustive Data Utilization

abstract: With the rise of social media and the proliferation of facial recognition surveillance, concerns surrounding privacy have escalated significantly. While numerous studies have concentrated on safeguarding users against unauthorized face recognition, a new and often overlooked issue has emerged due to advances in facial restoration techniques: traditional methods of facial obfuscation may no longer provide a secure shield, as they can potentially expose anonymous information to human perception. Our empirical study shows that blind face restoration (BFR) models can restore obfuscated faces with high probability by simply retraining them on obfuscated (e.g., pixelated) faces. To address it, we propose a transferable adversarial obfuscation method for privacy protection against BFR models. Specifically, we observed a common characteristic among BFR models, namely, their capability to approximate an inverse mapping of a transformation from a high-quality image domain to a low-quality image domain. Leveraging this shared model attribute, we have developed a domain-consistent adversarial method for generating obfuscated images. In essence, our method is designed to minimize overfitting to surrogate models during the perturbation generation process, thereby enhancing the generalization of adversarial obfuscated facial images. Extensive experiments on various BFR models demonstrate the effectiveness and transferability of the proposed method.

paragraphs: Obscuring a face through methods such as pixelation may leave information that restoration models can recover. The paper empirically finds that blind face restoration models can restore obfuscated faces with high probability after retraining on such images. This raises a privacy concern involving information visible to people, beyond protection against automated face recognition.

The proposed defense generates adversarially obfuscated images that transfer across restoration models. It builds on a shared characteristic of those models: they approximate the inverse of a transformation from high-quality images to low-quality images. The method uses that common domain relationship to shape adversarial obfuscation, with the aim of reducing dependence on the particular surrogate model used to generate perturbations.

Reducing surrogate overfitting is intended to make the obfuscation effective against other restoration models as well. Extensive experiments across multiple blind face restoration models support both effectiveness and transferability. The contribution addresses the specific risk that restoration can undermine conventional obfuscation, and demonstrates a defense based on shared restoration behavior across the tested models rather than solely on one model’s response.
summary.tldr: The paper develops adversarial face obfuscation that transfers across restoration models by targeting their shared mapping between image-quality domains.

title: Transferable Facial Privacy Protection against Blind Face Restoration via Domain-Consistent Adversarial Obfuscation

abstract: In this work, we study statistical learning with dependent data and square loss in a hypothesis class with tail decay in Orlicz space: $\mathscr{F}\subset L_{\Psi_p}$. Our inquiry is motivated by the search for a sharp noise interaction term, or variance proxy, in learning with dependent (e.g. $\beta$-mixing) data. Typical non-asymptotic results exhibit variance proxies that are deflated multiplicatively in the mixing time of the underlying covariates process. We show that whenever the topologies of $L^2$ and $\Psi_p$ are comparable on our hypothesis class $\mathscr{F}$, the empirical risk minimizer achieves a rate that only depends on the complexity of the class and second order statistics in its leading term. We refer to this as a near mixing-free rate, since direct dependence on mixing is relegated to an additive higher order term. Our approach, reliant on mixed tail generic chaining, allows us to obtain sharp, instance-optimal rates. Examples that satisfy our framework include for instance sub-Gaussian linear regression and bounded smoothness classes.

paragraphs: Learning theory often studies independent observations, but this paper considers dependent data and squared prediction loss. Existing finite-sample bounds commonly penalize the variance term through the mixing time, which measures how dependence persists. Such penalties can make a dataset behave, in the bound, as though it contained substantially fewer useful observations.

The authors study hypothesis classes with controlled tail behavior in an Orlicz space. When the L2 and Orlicz topologies are comparable on the class, they show that empirical risk minimization achieves a leading error term governed by class complexity and second-order statistics. Direct dependence on mixing moves into an additive higher-order term instead of multiplying the leading term.

Their proof uses mixed-tail generic chaining and yields sharp, instance-optimal rates within the framework. Applicable examples include sub-Gaussian linear regression and bounded smoothness classes. The result is described as nearly mixing-free because mixing still appears in the bound, but its direct role is restricted. The comparability assumption is central to obtaining this more precise account of learning from dependent observations.
summary.tldr: Under a comparability condition on the hypothesis class, squared-loss learning bounds avoid a direct mixing penalty in their leading term.

title: Sharp Rates in Dependent Learning Theory: Avoiding Sample Size Deflation for the Square Loss

abstract: Formal logic enables computers to reason in natural language by representing sentences in symbolic forms and applying rules to derive conclusions. However, in what our study characterizes as "rulebreaker" scenarios, this method can lead to conclusions that are typically not inferred or accepted by humans given their common sense and factual knowledge. Inspired by works in cognitive science, we create RULEBREAKERS, the first dataset for rigorously evaluating the ability of large language models (LLMs) to recognize and respond to rulebreakers (versus non-rulebreakers) in a knowledge-informed and human-like manner. Evaluating seven LLMs, we find that most models achieve mediocre accuracy on RULEBREAKERS and exhibit some tendency to over-rigidly apply logical rules, unlike what is expected from typical human reasoners. Further analysis suggests that this apparent failure is potentially associated with the models’ poor utilization of their world knowledge and their attention distribution patterns. Whilst revealing a limitation of current LLMs, our study also provides a timely counterbalance to a growing body of recent works that propose methods relying on formal logic to improve LLMs’ general reasoning capabilities, highlighting their risk of further increasing divergence between LLMs and human-like reasoning.

paragraphs: Applying formal inference rules to natural-language statements can produce conclusions that people would not normally accept given common sense or factual knowledge. The paper calls these cases rulebreakers. It introduces RULEBREAKERS, a dataset designed to test whether language models distinguish them from ordinary cases and respond in a knowledge-informed, human-like way.

The authors evaluate seven language models and find that most achieve mediocre accuracy. The models also show some tendency to apply logical rules too rigidly compared with typical human reasoning. The evaluation thus probes whether a model can recognize when the surrounding knowledge changes what constitutes a reasonable conclusion.

Further analysis suggests that the failures may be associated with weak use of world knowledge and with attention distribution patterns. These are proposed associations, rather than established causes. The study also raises a concern for methods that use formal logic to strengthen general reasoning: increasing rule adherence could widen the gap from human-like judgments in these scenarios. The dataset makes that tension available for systematic evaluation.
summary.tldr: RULEBREAKERS tests when language models should temper formal inference with world knowledge and finds that many models apply rules too rigidly.

title: RULEBREAKERS: Challenging LLMs at the Crossroads between Formal Logic and Human-like Reasoning

abstract: Diffusion models have transformed generative modeling but suffer from scalability limitations due to computational overhead and inflexible architectures that process all generative stages and tokens uniformly. In this work, we introduce Diff-MoE, a novel framework that combines Diffusion Transformers with Mixture-of-Experts to exploit both temporarily adaptability and spatial flexibility. Our design incorporates expert-specific timestep conditioning, allowing each expert to process different spatial tokens while adapting to the generative stage, to dynamically allocate resources based on both the temporal and spatial characteristics of the generative task. Additionally, we propose a globally-aware feature recalibration mechanism that amplifies the representational capacity of expert modules by dynamically adjusting feature contributions based on input relevance. Extensive experiments on image generation benchmarks demonstrate that Diff-MoE significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Our work demonstrates the potential of integrating diffusion models with expert-based designs, offering a scalable and effective framework for advanced generative modeling.

paragraphs: Diffusion models face computational costs that make scaling difficult, particularly when their architectures treat every generation stage and spatial token uniformly. Diff-MoE combines Diffusion Transformers with a mixture of experts to make processing responsive to both the current stage of generation and the spatial content being handled.

Each expert receives its own timestep conditioning, allowing it to adapt to the generative stage while processing different spatial tokens. The framework can therefore allocate resources according to temporal and spatial characteristics together. It also introduces a globally informed feature recalibration mechanism, which adjusts the contributions of features according to their relevance to the input.

Experiments on image-generation benchmarks report significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The stated findings support the potential of expert-based architectures to provide a more flexible foundation for diffusion generation. The main architectural contribution is the combination of stage-aware experts, spatially adaptive processing, and feature recalibration, all directed toward improving representation and resource allocation within the generative model.
summary.tldr: Diff-MoE improves diffusion image generation with experts that adapt to generation timesteps, spatial tokens, and input-relevant features.

title: Diff-MoE: Diffusion Transformer with Time-Aware and Space-Adaptive Experts

abstract: Maximal Update Parameterization ($\mu$P) has shown significant promise in allowing zero-shot hyperparameter transfer across neural network scales, reducing the prohibitive cost of hyperparameter tuning for large models. However, the theoretical foundation behind the observed approximate transferability of hyperparameters remains underexplored. Relying on a width-dominance regime, which ensures that as width grows, certain terms of the learning dynamics dominate, we establish the first fundamental separation of scales in $\mu$P between macro-variables (e.g. loss landscapes) and micro-variables (e.g. individual weights). Our formulation explains why hyperparameter tuning can be effectively performed in early training stages, i.e., early statistics effectively approximate global hyperparameter optima, implying the potential to further reduce the training costs required for searching optimal hyperparameters. We further apply our main theory to explain an empirical deep learning phenomenon discovered independently by prior work.

paragraphs: Maximal Update Parameterization, or μP, has shown promise for transferring hyperparameters across neural-network sizes without repeating the full tuning process. This could reduce the cost of developing large models. The paper investigates the theoretical structure behind that observed approximate transferability, focusing on how different kinds of training variables behave as network width grows.

The analysis assumes a width-dominance regime, in which certain terms increasingly dominate the learning dynamics. Under that regime, the authors establish a separation of scales between macro-variables, such as loss landscapes, and micro-variables, such as individual weights. This distinction gives a way to reason about overall training behavior separately from changes to particular parameters.

The resulting formulation explains why early training statistics can approximate global hyperparameter optima, supporting the possibility of shorter tuning runs. The authors also apply the theory to explain a previously observed empirical phenomenon. The practical implication is potential additional savings in hyperparameter search, grounded in the specified regime rather than an unrestricted guarantee for every neural network or training setup.
summary.tldr: Under a width-dominance assumption, a scale-separation theory for μP explains why early training can inform hyperparameter selection.

title: On the Provable Separation of Scales in Maximal Update Parameterization

abstract: Out-Of-Domain (OOD) generalization is a significant challenge in learning dynamical systems, especially when they exhibit bifurcation, a sudden topological transition triggered by a model parameter crossing a critical threshold. A prevailing belief is that machine learning models, unless equipped with strong priors, struggle to generalize across bifurcations due to the abrupt changes in data characteristics. Contrary to this belief, we demonstrate that context-dependent Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (NODEs), trained solely on localized, pre-bifurcation, symmetric data and without physics-based priors, can still identify post-bifurcation, symmetry-breaking behaviors, even in a zero-shot manner. We interpret this capability to the model’s implicit utilization of topological invariants, particularly the Poincaré index, and offer a formal explanation based on the Poincaré–Hopf theorem. We derive the conditions under which NODEs can recover—or erroneously hallucinate—broken symmetries without explicit training. Building on this insight, we showcase a topological regularizer inspired by the Poincaré–Hopf theorem and validate it empirically on phase transitions of systems described by the Landau–Khalatnikov equation.

paragraphs: A dynamical system can change qualitatively when a parameter crosses a critical threshold, a phenomenon called bifurcation. Predicting behavior beyond that threshold is difficult because the new regime can differ sharply from the training data. This paper asks whether context-dependent neural ordinary differential equations can nevertheless identify symmetry breaking beyond such a transition.

The authors demonstrate that models trained only on localized, symmetric data before a bifurcation can identify symmetry-breaking behavior afterward, including without examples from the new regime. These models do not require physics-based priors for the demonstrated behavior. The authors interpret this ability through implicit use of topological invariants, particularly the Poincaré index.

A formal explanation based on the Poincaré–Hopf theorem gives conditions under which these models can recover broken symmetries or incorrectly predict them. Thus, the finding is conditional rather than a general guarantee of extrapolation. The authors also develop a topology-based regularizer inspired by the theorem and validate it on phase transitions described by the Landau–Khalatnikov equation.
summary.tldr: Context-dependent neural ODEs can identify unseen symmetry breaking, with topology explaining conditions for both successful extrapolation and erroneous predictions.

title: Context-Informed Neural ODEs Unexpectedly Identify Broken Symmetries: Insights from the Poincaré–Hopf Theorem

abstract: Image AutoRegressive generation has emerged as a new powerful paradigm with image autoregressive models (IARs) matching state-of-the-art diffusion models (DMs) in image quality (FID: 1.48 vs. 1.58) while allowing for a higher generation speed. However, the privacy risks associated with IARs remain unexplored, raising concerns regarding their responsible deployment. To address this gap, we conduct a comprehensive privacy analysis of IARs, comparing their privacy risks to the ones of DMs as reference points. Concretely, we develop a novel membership inference attack (MIA) that achieves a remarkably high success rate in detecting training images (with a True Positive Rate at False Positive Rate = 1% of 86.38% vs. 6.38% for DMs with comparable attacks). We leverage our novel MIA to provide dataset inference (DI) for IARs, and show that it requires as few as 6 samples to detect dataset membership (compared to 200 for DI in DMs), confirming a higher information leakage in IARs. Finally, we are able to extract hundreds of training data points from an IAR (e.g., 698 from VAR-d30). Our results suggest a fundamental privacy-utility trade-off: while IARs excel in image generation quality and speed, they are empirically significantly more vulnerable to privacy attacks compared to DMs that achieve similar performance. We release the code at https://github.com/sprintml/privacy_attacks_against_iars for reproducibility.

paragraphs: Image autoregressive models can match leading diffusion models in image quality while generating faster, but those benefits leave a separate question about training-data privacy. This paper compares their privacy exposure through attacks that detect training membership, infer dataset membership, and extract training examples. The analysis uses diffusion models as reference points.

The new membership attack identifies training images with an 86.38% true-positive rate at a 1% false-positive rate, compared with 6.38% for comparable diffusion-model attacks. Building on that attack, dataset inference can detect membership with as few as six samples, versus 200 in the diffusion comparison. These results show substantially more detectable training information in the evaluated autoregressive models.

The authors also extract hundreds of training examples, including 698 from VAR-d30. Together, the findings suggest a privacy-utility trade-off: strong quality and speed accompany greater empirical vulnerability in these comparisons. The evidence establishes a substantial concern for the tested models, while the abstract frames the broader trade-off as suggested by the results rather than as a universal theorem.
summary.tldr: The evaluated image autoregressive models leak substantially more training information than comparable diffusion models through membership inference and training-example extraction.

title: Privacy Attacks on Image AutoRegressive Models

abstract: Causal machine learning (ML) promises to provide powerful tools for estimating individual treatment effects. While causal methods have placed some emphasis on heterogeneity in treatment response, it is of paramount importance to clarify the nature of this heterogeneity, by highlighting which variables drive it. We propose PermuCATE, an algorithm based on the Conditional Permutation Importance (CPI) method, for statistically rigorous global variable importance assessment in the estimation of the Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE). Theoretical analysis of the finite sample regime and empirical studies show that PermuCATE has lower variance than the Leave-One-Covariate-Out (LOCO) method and provides a reliable measure of variable importance. This property increases statistical power, which is crucial for causal inference applications with finite sample sizes. We empirically demonstrate the benefits of PermuCATE in simulated and real datasets, including complex settings with high-dimensional, correlated variables.

paragraphs: A treatment can have different effects for people with different characteristics. Estimating those differences is only part of the task; researchers also want to know which measured variables matter for the variation. This paper develops a statistically rigorous way to assess global variable importance when estimating conditional average treatment effects.

The proposed algorithm, PermuCATE, builds on Conditional Permutation Importance. It evaluates variable importance for the treatment-effect estimation problem, helping characterize heterogeneity across the population. The authors compare it with Leave-One-Covariate-Out, an alternative importance method, using both finite-sample theoretical analysis and empirical studies. Their results show that PermuCATE has lower variance and provides a reliable importance measure.

Lower variance increases statistical power, making relevant differences easier to detect when the available sample is finite. Experiments on simulated and real datasets demonstrate the benefits, including settings with many correlated variables. The contribution is a more statistically effective assessment of which variables matter to treatment-effect heterogeneity, complementing the estimation of how treatment responses vary across individuals.
summary.tldr: PermuCATE measures variable importance in treatment-effect heterogeneity with lower variance and greater statistical power than Leave-One-Covariate-Out.

title: Measuring Variable Importance in Heterogeneous Treatment Effects with Confidence

abstract: Detecting AI-generated images is a challenging yet essential task. A primary difficulty arises from the detector’s tendency to rely on spurious patterns, such as compression artifacts, which can influence its decisions. These issues often stem from specific patterns that the detector associates with the real data distribution, making it difficult to isolate the actual generative traces. We argue that an image should be classified as fake if and only if it contains artifacts introduced by the generative model. Based on this premise, we propose Stay-Positive, an algorithm designed to constrain the detector’s focus to generative artifacts while disregarding those associated with real data. Experimental results demonstrate that detectors trained with Stay-Positive exhibit reduced susceptibility to spurious correlations, leading to improved generalization and robustness to post-processing. Additionally, unlike detectors that associate artifacts with real images, those that focus purely on fake artifacts are better at detecting inpainted real images.

paragraphs: A detector of AI-generated images can learn misleading shortcuts, including compression patterns associated with its real-image training data. Such patterns can influence decisions without identifying traces left by an image generator. This paper examines how reliance on features associated with real images interferes with learning the evidence needed for fake-image detection.

The authors propose a design premise: an image should be labeled fake exactly when it contains artifacts introduced by a generative model. Stay-Positive implements this premise by constraining the detector to focus on generative artifacts and disregard artifacts associated with real data. The aim is to make the detector's evidence more closely match the phenomenon being detected.

Experiments show reduced susceptibility to spurious correlations, better generalization, and greater robustness to post-processing. The resulting detectors are also better at recognizing real images that have been inpainted. That finding fits the method's focus on detecting generative traces within an image, including images that also retain substantial real content. The results support the training strategy empirically.
summary.tldr: Stay-Positive focuses fake-image detectors on generative artifacts, improving generalization, post-processing robustness, and inpainting detection.

title: Stay-Positive: A Case for Ignoring Real Image Features in Fake Image Detection

abstract: In this manuscript, we study the learning of deep attention neural networks, defined as the composition of multiple self-attention layers, with tied and low-rank weights. We first establish a mapping of such models to sequence multi-index models, a generalization of the widely studied multi-index model to sequential covariates, for which we establish a number of general results. In the context of Bayes-optimal learning, in the limit of large dimension $D$ and proportionally large number of samples $N$, we derive a sharp asymptotic characterization of the optimal performance as well as the performance of the best-known polynomial-time algorithm for this setting –namely approximate message-passing–, and characterize sharp thresholds on the minimal sample complexity required for better-than-random prediction performance. Our analysis uncovers, in particular, how the different layers are learned sequentially. Finally, we discuss how this sequential learning can also be observed in a realistic setup.

paragraphs: This paper studies fundamental learning limits for deep attention networks composed of multiple self-attention layers with tied, low-rank weights. The authors connect these networks to sequence multi-index models, extending a model family used to study learning to inputs that are sequences. That connection provides a mathematical setting for analyzing the attention networks.

The analysis considers Bayes-optimal learning as input dimension and sample count both become large in proportion. Within this regime, the authors characterize optimal prediction performance and the performance of approximate message-passing, identified as the best-known polynomial-time algorithm for the setting. They also determine sharp sample thresholds for achieving predictions better than random.

One finding is that the network’s different layers are learned sequentially. This adds an account of how learning unfolds across layers to the results about how much data is needed. The paper also discusses observing this sequential behavior in a realistic setup. Its sharp theoretical characterizations apply to the stated weight structure and high-dimensional learning regime.
summary.tldr: For a structured class of deep attention networks, the paper derives asymptotic performance and sample thresholds and reveals sequential learning across layers.

title: Fundamental limits of learning in sequence multi-index models and deep attention networks: high-dimensional asymptotics and sharp thresholds

abstract: Multi-view Diffusion has greatly advanced the development of 3D content creation by generating multiple images from distinct views, achieving remarkable photorealistic results. However, existing works are still vulnerable to inconsistent 3D geometric structures (commonly known as Janus Problem) and severe artifacts. In this paper, we introduce MIRROR, a versatile plug-and-play method that rectifies such inconsistencies in a training-free manner, enabling the acquisition of high-fidelity, realistic structures without compromising diversity. Our key idea focuses on tracing the motion trajectory of physical points across adjacent viewpoints, enabling rectifications based on neighboring observations of the same region. Technically, MIRROR comprises two core modules: Trajectory Tracking Module (TTM) for pixel-wise trajectory tracking that labels identical points across views, and Feature Rectification Module (FRM) for explicitly adjustment of each pixel embedding on noisy synthesized images by minimizing the distance to corresponding block features in neighboring views, thereby achieving consistent outputs. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that MIRROR can seamlessly integrate with a diverse range of off-the-shelf object-level multi-view diffusion models, significantly enhancing both the consistency and the fidelity in an efficient way.

paragraphs: Generating realistic images of an object from several viewpoints does not automatically produce a coherent three-dimensional object. Multi-view diffusion models can generate conflicting geometry and severe artifacts, including inconsistencies described as the Janus problem. MIRROR addresses these failures through a correction procedure that can be added to existing models without further training.

The method tracks the apparent trajectories of physical points across neighboring viewpoints. Its Trajectory Tracking Module identifies pixels that correspond to the same point across views. A Feature Rectification Module then adjusts pixel embeddings in noisy generated images, bringing them closer to corresponding regional features in adjacent views. Neighboring observations therefore provide evidence for correcting each view.

Evaluations across a range of existing object-level multi-view diffusion models show improvements in consistency and fidelity, with efficient integration. The authors also report preserving generation diversity. The contribution is a reusable correction mechanism that makes corresponding parts of different views agree more closely, improving the structural coherence of the generated object.
summary.tldr: MIRROR improves multi-view object generation without training by tracking corresponding points and correcting features across neighboring views.

title: MIRROR: Make Your Object-Level Multi-View Generation More Consistent with Training-Free Rectification

abstract: While state-of-the-art LLMs have demonstrated great promise of using long Chains-of-Thought (CoT) to boost reasoning, scaling it up to more challenging problems is fundamentally limited by suboptimal memory usage — intermediate computations accumulate indefinitely in context even no longer needed for future thoughts. We introduce PENCIL, which incorporates a novel reduction mechanism into the autoregressive generation process that recursively clean up intermediate thoughts based on patterns learned from training. By alternately generating and erasing, PENCIL can think deeper to solve harder problems using shorter context and less computes. Empirically, for example, we demonstrate PENCIL with a small 25M-parameter transformer and 2048 context length solves Einstein’s puzzle — a task that challenges much larger models like GPT-4. Theoretically, we prove PENCIL can perform universal efficient computation by simulating any Turing machines with optimal time and space complexity, and thus can solve arbitrary computable tasks that are otherwise intractable for vanilla CoT.

paragraphs: Long chains of thought can help language models reason, but they also accumulate intermediate computations in the context. Some of that material is no longer needed for later reasoning. PENCIL addresses this memory problem by changing autoregressive generation so that intermediate thoughts can be removed according to patterns learned during training.

The method alternates generation with a recursive reduction mechanism that cleans up the working context. This allows reasoning to continue without retaining every previous intermediate step. The authors report that the resulting process can solve harder problems with shorter context and less computation. As an empirical example, a 25-million-parameter Transformer with a context length of 2,048 solves Einstein's puzzle, which the paper describes as challenging for much larger models.

The theoretical contribution concerns computational capacity: PENCIL can simulate any Turing machine with optimal time and space complexity. This supports universal efficient computation and the ability to express computable tasks that are intractable for vanilla chain-of-thought processing. That capacity result is distinct from showing that a particular trained model has learned to solve every such task.
summary.tldr: PENCIL alternates generating and erasing intermediate thoughts to support deeper reasoning with shorter working context.

title: PENCIL: Long Thoughts with Short Memory

abstract: Spatial Transcriptomics (ST) is a method that captures gene expression profiles aligned with spatial coordinates. The discrete spatial distribution and the super-high dimensional sequencing results make ST data challenging to be modeled effectively. In this paper, we manage to model ST in a continuous and compact manner by the proposed tool, SUICA, empowered by the great approximation capability of Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) that can enhance both the spatial density and the gene expression. Concretely within the proposed SUICA, we incorporate a graph-augmented Autoencoder to effectively model the context information of the unstructured spots and provide informative embeddings that are structure-aware for spatial mapping. We also tackle the extremely skewed distribution in a regression-by-classification fashion and enforce classification-based loss functions for the optimization of SUICA. By extensive experiments of a wide range of common ST platforms under varying degradations, SUICA outperforms both conventional INR variants and SOTA methods regarding numerical fidelity, statistical correlation, and bio-conservation. The prediction by SUICA also showcases amplified gene signatures that enriches the bio-conservation of the raw data and benefits subsequent analysis.

paragraphs: Spatial transcriptomics records gene expression together with spatial coordinates, producing measurements that are discrete in space and extremely high-dimensional. SUICA models these data through a compact, continuous implicit neural representation. The goal is to enhance spatial density and gene-expression representation while accounting for the structure of the observed sampling locations.

A graph-augmented autoencoder captures contextual information among unstructured spots and produces structure-aware embeddings for spatial mapping. To handle the highly skewed expression distribution, SUICA treats regression through a classification-based formulation and uses classification losses during optimization. These components address different aspects of the problem: spatial relationships among measurements and the uneven distribution of expression values.

Across common spatial transcriptomics platforms and varying degradations, experiments show better numerical fidelity, statistical correlation, and biological conservation than conventional implicit representations and state-of-the-art methods. The predictions also amplify gene signatures in ways reported to enrich biological conservation and help subsequent analysis. The findings support combining spatial structure with distribution-aware learning for continuous representations of these data.
summary.tldr: SUICA combines graph-aware embeddings and classification-based learning to create compact, continuous representations of spatial gene-expression data.

title: SUICA: Learning Super-high Dimensional Sparse Implicit Neural Representations for Spatial Transcriptomics

abstract: Multiple kernel learning (MKL) combines several base kernels in the spirit of ensemble learning, yet existing methods rarely model kernel diversity—a known cornerstone of ensembles—and most traditional kernels weight all features uniformly, ignoring feature-level discriminability. We address both gaps with DARFMMKL: a data-driven kernel family (Recursive Feature Machine kernels) that learns feature importance directly from data, paired with a kernel selection method that jointly optimizes diversity and quality. The resulting NP-hard binary quadratic program is reformulated via Glover linearization and continuous relaxation into a linear program, and accelerated by Nyström sketching, yielding a selector whose cost is decoupled from the sample size. We provide a covering-number generalization bound that explicitly relates kernel diversity to estimation error. Experiments on 12 benchmark datasets show that DARFMMKL consistently outperforms 9 state-of-the-art MKL methods.
