paragraphs: Multiple kernel learning combines several ways of measuring similarity between examples. As with an ensemble, a collection can benefit from members that contribute different information. This paper targets two weaknesses in existing approaches: insufficient attention to diversity among kernels and the tendency of traditional kernels to treat all input features as equally important.

DARFMMKL combines Recursive Feature Machine kernels, which learn feature importance from data, with a selection procedure that considers both kernel quality and diversity. Selecting the collection leads to a difficult binary optimization problem. The authors use Glover linearization and continuous relaxation to obtain a linear program, then apply Nyström sketching to accelerate the procedure and decouple the selector’s cost from sample size.

A generalization bound explicitly connects kernel diversity with estimation error, giving diversity a role in the theoretical account as well as the selection objective. Across 12 benchmark datasets, the method consistently outperforms nine state-of-the-art multiple kernel learning methods. The results support jointly improving the individual similarity measures and the complementarity of the collection selected for learning.
summary.tldr: DARFMMKL learns feature-sensitive kernels and selects them for both quality and diversity, improving results across 12 benchmark datasets.

title: Diversity-Aware Recursive Feature Multiple Kernel Learning

abstract: Tool-integrated (TI) reinforcement learning (RL) enables large language models (LLMs) to perform multi-step reasoning by interacting with external tools such as search engines and retrievers. Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), exemplified by the recent Search-R1, offers fast convergence and a value-free formulation that makes it appealing for this setting, yet consistently suffers from training collapse. We identify Lazy Likelihood Displacement (LLD), a systematic reduction or stagnation in the likelihood of both correct and incorrect responses, as the core mechanism driving this failure. LLD emerges early and triggers a self-reinforcing LLD Death Spiral, where declining likelihood leads to low-confidence responses, inflating gradients, and ultimately causing collapse. We empirically characterize this process across models on a Search-R1-style, search-integrated question answering task, revealing a consistent three-phase trajectory: early stagnation, steady decay, and accelerated collapse. To address this, we propose a likelihood-preserving regularization LLDS that activates only when a response action’s likelihood decreases, and regularizes only the tokens responsible. This fine-grained structure mitigates LLD with minimal interference. Our method stabilizes training, prevents gradient explosion, and yields substantial performance improvements across seven benchmarks, including relative improvements of +45.2% on Qwen2.5-3B and +37.1% on Qwen2.5-7B over vanilla GRPO training. Our results establish LLD as a previously overlooked bottleneck in GRPO- based TIRL and provide a practical path toward stable, scalable training of tool-integrated RL.

paragraphs: Group Relative Policy Optimization is attractive for training tool-using language models because it converges quickly and does not require a value model. This paper investigates its training collapse in search-integrated question answering. The authors identify Lazy Likelihood Displacement: the probabilities of both correct and incorrect responses stagnate or decline early in training.

Their experiments describe a reinforcing failure process in which falling response likelihood produces low-confidence outputs, increasingly large gradients, and eventual collapse. Across the models studied, this follows three phases: initial stagnation, steady deterioration, and accelerated failure. The diagnosis connects an early change in response probabilities to the later instability of the optimization process.

The proposed LLDS regularizer activates only when a response action loses likelihood and targets only the responsible tokens. This selective intervention aims to preserve likelihood with minimal interference elsewhere. The authors report stable training, prevention of gradient explosion, and improvements across seven benchmarks, including relative gains of 45.2% for Qwen2.5-3B and 37.1% for Qwen2.5-7B over unmodified GRPO training.
summary.tldr: The paper traces search-agent GRPO collapse to declining response likelihood and introduces selective regularization that stabilizes the evaluated training runs.

title: On Group Relative Policy Optimization Collapse in Agent Search: The Lazy Likelihood-Displacement

abstract: Despite remarkable progress in text-to-image diffusion models, accurately generating the specified number of objects remains a persistent challenge. We identify the initial noise as a primary determinant of spatial layout formation, with early-stage cross-attention serving as the key mechanism that mediates the propagation of noise-induced structures throughout the denoising process. We characterize this phenomenon as Noise-Induced Layout Prior. Leveraging this insight, we propose a novel training-free framework for object counting in diffusion models. Our approach consists of two key components: (1) a Count-Aware Noise Adjustment Strategy, which explicitly manipulates the initial latent noise to align layout formation with the target object count, and (2) an Attention-Guided Layout Consistency Strategy, which performs test-time optimization on early-stage cross-attention to further stabilize layout formation during denoising. Extensive experiments on both single-category and multi-category benchmarks demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms strong diffusion baselines and state-of-the-art object count control methods in terms of counting accuracy and image quality. Code Release: https://github.com/lxlong1201/Mitigate_Noise_Prior.

paragraphs: Text-to-image diffusion models can produce convincing images while missing the requested number of objects. This paper identifies initial noise as a primary influence on the spatial layout that emerges during generation. It further identifies early cross-attention as the mechanism that carries these noise-induced structures through denoising, calling the phenomenon a Noise-Induced Layout Prior.

The proposed framework intervenes at both points in that process. A count-aware noise adjustment changes the initial latent noise to encourage a layout compatible with the requested object count. An attention-guided consistency strategy then optimizes early cross-attention at test time to stabilize that layout as denoising proceeds. The framework does not require model training, although it does perform optimization during generation.

Experiments cover benchmarks with one object category and multiple categories. The authors report consistent improvements in counting accuracy and image quality over strong diffusion baselines and state-of-the-art count-control methods. The findings connect counting errors to layout formation and show the value of coordinating the initial spatial conditions with the early attention behavior that propagates them.
summary.tldr: Adjusting initial noise and stabilizing early cross-attention improves object counts and image quality without training the diffusion model.

title: Mitigating Noise-Induced Layout Priors for Object Counting in Diffusion Models

abstract: Literature reveals that a Large Language Model’s (LLM) behavior is not only conditioned by its original weights but also its instance-level parameters, such as instructional prompt, sampling configuration or quantization. A model that generates safe outputs under one configuration may produce toxic content under another. However, current LLM identification techniques (such as fingerprinting) focus on intellectual property protection, and their design favors robustness to changes in these instance-level parameters. This poses a critical challenge for AI regulation in which compliance assessments target actual deployed behaviors, not model provenance. In this paper, we introduce instance-level fingerprinting, a regulator-oriented paradigm that distinguishes configurations of the same LLM. Our method FLIPS, exploits biases in generated binary random sequences to reach 96% (closed-set) and 90% (open-set, where some targets are unknown) identification accuracy across 237 model instances, versus 35% for the adapted LLMmap baseline. This shows that instance-level fingerprinting is both necessary for regulation and practically feasible. Code available at https://github.com/GurvanR/FLIPS-LLM-Instance-Fingerprinting.

paragraphs: The same language model can behave differently when its instructions, sampling settings, or quantization change. A configuration that produces safe responses does not establish that another configuration behaves similarly. This paper argues that regulatory identification should distinguish deployed model instances, whereas existing fingerprints often emphasize recognizing model provenance despite configuration changes.

FLIPS identifies instances through biases in binary sequences that models generate as supposedly random outputs. Those biases provide a behavioral signal for distinguishing configurations of the same underlying model. This changes the identification target from the original model alone to the particular setup through which users interact with it.

Across 237 instances, FLIPS reports 96% identification accuracy in a closed-set setting and 90% in an open-set setting, where some targets are unknown. The adapted LLMmap baseline reaches 35%. These results demonstrate practical instance identification in the evaluated settings. The regulatory relevance follows from configuration-dependent behavior: identifying a model’s origin alone may not identify the behavior assessed in deployment.
summary.tldr: FLIPS uses biases in generated binary sequences to distinguish deployed LLM configurations, achieving high identification accuracy across 237 instances.

title: FLIPS: Instance-Fingerprinting for LLMs via Pseudo-random Sequences

abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) suffer from sycophantic behavior, where models tend to agree with users’ incorrect beliefs and follow misinformation rather than maintain independent reasoning. This behavior undermines model reliability and poses societal risks. Mitigating LRM sycophancy requires monitoring how this sycophancy emerges during the reasoning trajectory; however, current methods mainly focus on judging based on final answers and correcting them, without understanding how sycophancy develops during reasoning processes. To address this limitation, we propose MONICA, a novel Monitor-guided Calibration framework that monitors and mitigates sycophancy during model inference at the level of reasoning steps, without requiring the model to finish generating its complete answer. MONICA integrates a sycophantic monitor that provides real-time monitoring of sycophantic drift scores during response generation with a calibrator that dynamically suppresses sycophantic behavior when scores exceed predefined thresholds. Extensive experiments across 12 datasets and 3 LRMs demonstrate that our method effectively reduces sycophantic behavior in both intermediate reasoning steps and final answers, yielding robust performance improvements.

paragraphs: Sycophancy occurs when a reasoning model follows a user’s incorrect beliefs or misinformation instead of maintaining independent reasoning. The paper argues that judging and correcting only completed answers misses how this behavior develops along the reasoning trajectory. MONICA moves monitoring and intervention into the generation process itself.

The framework combines a monitor with a calibrator. As the model generates reasoning steps, the monitor assigns scores describing sycophantic drift. When those scores exceed predefined thresholds, the calibrator dynamically suppresses the behavior. The intervention therefore does not require waiting for a complete answer, allowing the framework to respond to problematic drift during intermediate reasoning.

Experiments across 12 datasets and three large reasoning models show reductions in sycophancy in both intermediate steps and final answers, alongside robust performance improvements. The contribution is the coupling of step-level observation with immediate calibration. These findings support treating sycophancy as behavior that can emerge during a response and be addressed before generation finishes, rather than evaluating only its final expression.
summary.tldr: MONICA monitors sycophantic drift during reasoning and triggers calibration before the model finishes its answer.

title: Real-Time Monitoring and Calibration of Chain-of-Thought Sycophancy in Large Reasoning Models

abstract: Accurately modeling complex temporal and topological dependencies and depth information is critical for monocular 3D human pose estimation, yet existing Mamba-based approaches struggle to fulfill these demands, suffering from internal state update confusion induced by forced sequence flattening and depth modeling confusion inherent to single-view observations. To address this confusion, we propose a StructMamPose framework equipped with Identity Anchoring Mechanism (IAM) and View Transformation Hub (VTH). The IAM injects spatiotemporal identities into the parameter generation network to anchor the selectivity of state update matrices, suppressing spurious connections to enforce feature propagation along valid topological dependencies. The VTH performs internal coordinate rotation to transform implicit depth inference into observable planar features, endowing the model with explicit spatial understanding and multi-view constraints. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework achieves SOTA performance on most datasets.

To address this confusion, we propose a StructMamPose framework equipped with Identity Anchoring Mechanism (IAM) and View Transformation Hub (VTH). The IAM injects spatiotemporal identities into the parameter generation network to anchor the selectivity of state update matrices, suppressing spurious connections to enforce feature propagation along valid topological dependencies. paragraphs: StructMamPose estimates three-dimensional human pose from a single camera view. The paper identifies two difficulties for Mamba-based approaches: flattening structured pose information into a sequence can confuse internal state updates, and a single view makes depth difficult to infer. Both problems interfere with modeling the body’s spatial and temporal relationships.

The Identity Anchoring Mechanism introduces spatial and temporal identities into the network that generates state-update parameters. This anchors which information the model selects, suppressing spurious connections and encouraging propagation along valid structural relationships. The mechanism therefore ties sequential processing more directly to the organization of the pose data.

The View Transformation Hub addresses depth through internal coordinate rotations that expose depth-related information as planar features. This supplies explicit spatial understanding and multiple-view constraints within the model’s representation. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on most evaluated datasets. Together, the two components support the paper’s shift toward structural reasoning: state updates respect meaningful relationships, while transformed internal views help organize the depth information needed for three-dimensional pose estimation.
summary.tldr: StructMamPose improves monocular 3D pose estimation by anchoring state updates to pose structure and using internal coordinate rotations to support depth reasoning.

title: StructMamPose: From Sequential Perception to Structural Reasoning for 3D Human Pose Estimation

abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) such as CLIP achieve strong zero-shot recognition but remain highly fragile under adversarial perturbations. Recent test-time adaptation defenses improve robustness by leveraging many augmented views, but this leads to impractical slowdown and a clear robustness-throughput trade-off. To address this challenge, we present Stability and Suitability-guided Test-time Prompt Tuning (SS-TPT), evaluating the quality of each augmented view via two complementary scores: (1) stability, measuring prediction invariance to weak augmentations, and (2) suitability, measuring feature-space density among views. These stability and suitability (SS) scores guide both adaptation and inference through an SS-guided consistency loss and an SS-weighted prediction, amplifying trustworthy views while suppressing corrupted ones. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SS-TPT significantly outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods, achieving superior robustness-throughput trade-offs across diverse datasets and varying numbers of views, thereby demonstrating both strong practicality and generality. Our code is available at https://github.com/sunoh-kim/SS-TPT.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can recognize new categories without task-specific training, yet adversarial perturbations can still disrupt their predictions. Test-time defenses often adapt using many augmented versions of an image. Those extra views can improve robustness, but processing them creates a substantial speed cost and makes the quality of each view important.

SS-TPT evaluates views using two complementary signals. Stability measures whether predictions remain consistent under weak augmentations. Suitability measures how densely a view's features sit among the features of other views. These scores guide a consistency loss during prompt adaptation and determine how predictions are weighted at inference.

The method therefore uses view quality both to update the prompts and to combine the resulting predictions, emphasizing trustworthy views while reducing the influence of corrupted ones. Across diverse datasets and different numbers of views, the authors report significant improvements over prior state-of-the-art methods and a better robustness-throughput tradeoff. The results support quality-aware use of augmented views as a practical test-time defense.
summary.tldr: SS-TPT scores augmented image views for stability and suitability, improving adversarial robustness relative to inference throughput in the reported evaluations.

title: SS-TPT: Stability and Suitability-Guided Test-Time Prompt Tuning for Adversarially Robust Vision-Language Models

abstract: Many real-world optimization problems are guided by complex, subjective preferences that are difficult to express as explicit closed-form objectives. In response, we introduce Language-in-the-Loop Optimization (LILO), a Bayesian optimization (BO) framework that employs a large language model (LLM) to translate free-form natural language feedback and prior knowledge from a decision maker into structured preference signals, going beyond the restrictive scalar or pairwise feedback formats typically assumed in preferential BO. The LLM-derived preferences are integrated by a Gaussian process proxy model, enabling principled acquisition-driven exploration with calibrated uncertainty. By placing the LLM in a supporting role rather than as the optimizer itself, LILO preserves the sample efficiency and stability of BO while providing a flexible and expressive feedback interface. Across synthetic and real-world benchmarks, LILO consistently outperforms both conventional preference-based BO methods and LLM-only optimizers, with particularly strong gains in feedback-limited regimes. The code for reproducing our experimental results is available at: https://github.com/facebookresearch/lilo.

paragraphs: Many optimization tasks depend on preferences that are difficult to reduce to a numerical score or a choice between two candidates. A decision maker may express several considerations in ordinary language, along with relevant prior knowledge. LILO brings this richer feedback into Bayesian optimization while retaining a statistical model for choosing what to explore next.

An LLM translates free-form feedback and prior knowledge into structured preference signals. A Gaussian process proxy model incorporates those signals, represents uncertainty, and supports acquisition-driven exploration. The language model handles interpretation, while the Bayesian optimization machinery remains responsible for the search process.

This division is designed to preserve Bayesian optimization's sample efficiency and stability while expanding the ways people can communicate preferences. Across synthetic and real-world benchmarks, LILO consistently outperforms conventional preference-based Bayesian optimization and LLM-only optimizers. Its strongest reported gains occur when feedback is limited, supporting the value of extracting richer guidance from the interactions available.
summary.tldr: LILO translates natural-language preferences into signals for Bayesian optimization, improving results especially when decision-maker feedback is limited.

title: LILO: Bayesian Optimization with Natural Language Feedback

abstract: Estimating Individual Treatment Effects (ITE) in multi-treatment scenarios faces two critical challenges: the Hyperparameter Selection Dilemma for balancing weights and the Curse of Dimensionality in computational scalability. This paper derives a novel multi-treatment generalization bound and proposes a theoretical estimator for the optimal balancing weight $\alpha$, eliminating expensive heuristic tuning. We investigate three balancing strategies: Pairwise, One-vs-All (OVA), and Treatment Aggregation. While OVA achieves superior precision in low-dimensional settings, our proposed Treatment Aggregation ensures both accuracy and $\mathcal{O}(1)$ scalability as the treatment space expands. Furthermore, we extend our framework to a generative architecture, Multi-Treatment CausalEGM, which preserves the Wasserstein geodesic structure of the treatment manifold. Experiments on semi-synthetic and image datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms traditional models in estimation accuracy and efficiency, particularly in large-scale intervention scenarios.

paragraphs: Estimating how different treatments affect an individual becomes harder as the number and complexity of treatment options increase. This paper addresses two obstacles: choosing the weight used to balance treatment representations and keeping that balancing process computationally manageable. Both affect whether a method can handle a large intervention space.

The authors derive a generalization bound for multiple treatments and use it to construct a theoretical estimator for the balancing weight. This replaces expensive heuristic tuning. They compare pairwise balancing, one-versus-all balancing, and treatment aggregation. One-versus-all is more precise in low-dimensional settings, while treatment aggregation is reported to maintain accuracy with constant-order scalability as the treatment space grows.

The framework also extends to Multi-Treatment CausalEGM, a generative architecture designed to preserve Wasserstein geodesic structure in the treatment manifold. This retains a particular geometric relationship among treatments during representation learning. Experiments on semi-synthetic and image datasets report improvements over traditional models in estimation accuracy and efficiency, especially for large intervention scenarios. The results make the choice of balancing strategy consequential to both precision and scaling.
summary.tldr: A theoretically selected balancing weight and treatment aggregation improve the accuracy and scalability of multi-treatment effect estimation.

title: Causal Representation Learning with Optimal Compression under Complex Treatments

abstract: While explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) equips Large Language Models (LLMs) with strong reasoning capabilities, it constrains the model’s thoughts to a discrete vocabulary space. Recently, reasoning in continuous latent space has emerged as a promising alternative, but current paradigms suffer from feature collapse and instability due to distribution mismatch when recurrently reusing hidden states, or alignment issues when relying on assistant models. To address this, we propose $\textbf{Latent Thoughts Tuning (\textit{LT-Tuning})}$, a post-training framework that redefines how latent thoughts are constructed and deployed. Instead of relying solely on raw hidden states, our method introduces a $\textbf{Context-Prediction-Fusion}$ mechanism that jointly leverages contextual hidden states and predictive semantic guidance from the vocabulary embedding space. Combined with a progressive three-stage curriculum learning pipeline, $\textit{LT-Tuning}$ also enables dynamic switching between latent and explicit thinking modes. Experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms existing latent reasoning baselines, effectively mitigating feature collapse and achieving robust reasoning accuracy.

paragraphs: Continuous latent reasoning offers an alternative to expressing every intermediate thought as a token. But repeatedly feeding raw hidden states back into a model can cause distribution mismatch, unstable behavior, and collapsed features. LT-Tuning changes how latent thoughts are constructed to address those problems.

Its Context-Prediction-Fusion mechanism combines contextual hidden states with predictive semantic guidance from vocabulary embeddings. A progressive three-stage curriculum trains the system to use this representation. The resulting model can also switch dynamically between latent and explicit reasoning modes instead of committing to one form throughout the computation.

Experiments outperform existing latent-reasoning baselines and show reduced feature collapse with robust accuracy. The contribution is a post-training framework that connects continuous reasoning states to semantic predictions. The abstract does not give numerical gains or establish that latent reasoning always saves computation, so its evidence primarily concerns representation stability and reasoning quality in the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: LT-Tuning fuses context and vocabulary-based predictive information to stabilize latent reasoning and support switching to explicit thoughts.

title: Latent Thoughts Tuning: Bridging Context and Reasoning with Fused Information in Latent Tokens

abstract: Low-bit model quantization for image super-resolution (SR) is a longstanding task that is renowned for its surprising compression and acceleration ability. However, accuracy degradation is inevitable when compressing the full-precision (FP) model to ultra-low bit widths ($2\sim4$ bits). Experimentally, we observe that the degradation of quantization is mainly attributed to the quantization of activation instead of model weights. Considering that the activation quantization error is hard to minimize, minimizing the impact of the error emerges as a good choice, which is described by the condition number. Therefore, we propose CondiQuant, a condition number-based low-bit post-training quantization for image super-resolution. Specifically, we formulate the quantization error of activation as the condition number of weight metrics. By decoupling the representation ability and the quantization sensitivity, we design an efficient proximal gradient descent algorithm to iteratively minimize the condition number and maintain the output. With comprehensive experiments, we demonstrate that CondiQuant outperforms existing state-of-the-art post-training quantization methods in accuracy without computation overhead and gains the theoretically optimal compression ratio in model parameters. Our code will be released soon.

paragraphs: Image super-resolution models can become smaller and faster when their numerical values use fewer bits, but reducing precision to two through four bits degrades accuracy. The authors experimentally attribute much of this degradation to quantizing activations, the intermediate values produced during computation, rather than model weights. This observation motivates controlling how strongly activation errors affect the output.

CondiQuant uses condition numbers to characterize that sensitivity. Its formulation connects activation quantization error to the conditioning of weight matrices, separating the model’s ability to represent an image transformation from its sensitivity to numerical perturbations. An iterative proximal gradient method then reduces the condition number while maintaining the output. The procedure is designed for post-training quantization.

Experiments report higher accuracy than existing state-of-the-art post-training quantization methods without computational overhead, alongside a theoretically optimal parameter compression ratio. The central finding is that reducing error amplification can improve low-bit super-resolution even when activation quantization errors themselves are difficult to minimize.
summary.tldr: CondiQuant improves low-bit image super-resolution by reducing the model’s sensitivity to activation quantization errors.

title: Condition Number Based Low-Bit Quantization for Image Super-Resolution

abstract: Socially intelligent AI systems must reason across diverse human behavioral tasks and generalize to new social contexts. However, behavioral data is inherently heterogeneous, comprising diverse modalities and prediction targets that produce uneven training signals across samples, creating imbalanced learning dynamics that challenge existing AI models. To address this, we develop OmniSapiens-7B 2.0, a foundation model for social behavior processing that explicitly addresses learning from heterogeneous behavioral data. This is enabled through Heterogeneity-Aware Relative Policy Optimization, a new RL method that rebalances learning signals across samples by approximating each sample’s contribution to the policy update and using these estimates to drive geometrically centered, inertially smoothed advantage modulation for stable training. OmniSapiens-7B 2.0 achieves the best and most consistent performance across 10 behavioral tasks, while also attaining the best performance on all five held-out benchmarks, with gains of up to +12.02% and +9.37% respectively. Furthermore, it demonstrates more consistent and interpretable reasoning traces, supporting reliable real-world behavioral applications. Our model is available at https://github.com/MIT-MI/human_behavior_atlas.

To address this, we develop OmniSapiens-7B 2.0, a foundation model for social behavior processing that explicitly addresses learning from heterogeneous behavioral data. This is enabled through Heterogeneity-Aware Relative Policy Optimization, a new RL method that rebalances learning signals across samples by approximating each sample’s contribution to the policy update and using these estimates to drive geometrically centered, inertially smoothed advantage modulation for stable training. OmniSapiens-7B 2.0 achieves the best and most consistent performance across 10 behavioral tasks, while also attaining the best performance on all five held-out benchmarks, with gains of up to +12.02% and +9.37% respectively. Furthermore, it demonstrates more consistent and interpretable reasoning traces, supporting reliable real-world behavioral applications. Our model is available at https://github.com/MIT-MI/human_behavior_atlas.

paragraphs: Social behavior data spans different modalities and prediction targets, producing uneven learning signals across examples. A model trained across these tasks can therefore experience imbalanced updates. OmniSapiens-7B 2.0 addresses this challenge with a reinforcement-learning method designed explicitly for heterogeneous behavioral data.

Heterogeneity-Aware Relative Policy Optimization estimates how much each sample contributes to a policy update. It uses those estimates to adjust the advantages that guide learning, applying geometric centering and inertial smoothing for stability. The purpose is to rebalance how examples influence training while supporting a shared model across diverse behavioral tasks.

The authors report the best and most consistent performance across ten behavioral tasks, with gains up to +12.02%. They also report the best performance on all five held-out benchmarks, with gains up to +9.37%. More consistent and interpretable reasoning traces accompany these results. Together, the findings support accounting for unequal sample contributions when building behavioral models intended to transfer across social contexts, rather than treating heterogeneous training signals as interchangeable.
summary.tldr: OmniSapiens rebalances heterogeneous behavioral training signals through a new policy optimizer, improving performance across evaluated tasks and held-out benchmarks.

title: OmniSapiens: A Foundation Model for Social Behavior Processing via Heterogeneity-Aware Relative Policy Optimization

abstract: To cope with uncertain changes of the external world, intelligent systems must continually learn from complex, evolving environments and respond in real time. This ability, collectively known as general continual learning (GCL), encapsulates practical challenges such as online datastreams and blurry task boundaries. Although leveraging pretrained models (PTMs) has greatly advanced conventional continual learning (CL), these methods remain limited in reconciling the diverse and temporally mixed information along a single pass, resulting in sub-optimal GCL performance. Inspired by meta-plasticity and reconstructive memory in neuroscience, we introduce here an innovative approach named Meta Post-Refinement (MePo) for PTMs-based GCL. This approach constructs pseudo task sequences from pretraining data and develops a bi-level meta-learning paradigm to refine the pretrained backbone, which serves as a prolonged pretraining phase but greatly facilitates rapid adaptation of representation learning to downstream GCL tasks. MePo further initializes a meta covariance matrix as the reference geometry of pretrained representation space, enabling GCL to exploit second-order statistics for robust output alignment. MePo serves as a plug-in strategy that achieves significant performance gains across a variety of GCL benchmarks and pretrained checkpoints in a rehearsal-free manner (e.g., 15.10%, 13.36%, and 12.56% on CIFAR-100, ImageNet-R, and CUB-200 under Sup-21/1K). Our source code is available at https://github.com/SunGL001/MePo.

paragraphs: MePo prepares pretrained models for continual learning from streams where task boundaries are unclear and information from different tasks can be mixed over time. In this setting, a single pass through incoming data must support adaptation. The paper argues that conventional uses of pretrained models do not adequately reconcile this varied, temporally mixed information.

The method constructs artificial task sequences from pretraining data and uses a two-level meta-learning procedure to refine the pretrained backbone. This acts as an extended pretraining phase designed to make later representation learning adapt more quickly. It also initializes a meta covariance matrix that supplies a reference geometry for the representation space, enabling output alignment using second-order statistics.

Experiments show gains across multiple benchmarks and pretrained checkpoints, including reported improvements of 15.10%, 13.36%, and 12.56% on CIFAR-100, ImageNet-R, and CUB-200 under Sup-21/1K. title: MePo: Meta Post-Refinement for Rehearsal-Free General Continual Learning

abstract: Continuous prediction in complex environments is critical for Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV). However, the existing Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) models follows the dead-reckoning, which iteratively predicts the next waypoint and updates its position, thereby constructing the complete trajectory. Then, such stepwise manner will inevitably lead to accumulated errors of position over time, resulting in misalignment between internal belief and objective coordinates, which is known as “state drift” and ultimately compromises the subsequent trajectory prediction. Drawing inspiration from classical control theory, we propose to correct for errors by formulating the continuous prediction as a recursive Bayesian state estimation problem. In this paper, we design NeuroKalman, a novel framework that decouples navigation into two complementary processes: a Prior Prediction, based on motion dynamic,s and a Likelihood Correction, from historical observation. We first mathematically associate Kernel Density Estimation of the measurement likelihood with the attention-based retrieval mechanism, which then allows the system to rectify the latent representation using retrieved historical anchors without gradient updates. Comprehensive experiments on TravelUAV benchmark demonstrate that, with only 10% of the full training data fine-tuning, our method clearly outperforms strong baselines and regulates drift accumulation.

paragraphs: Continuous vision-language navigation predicts successive waypoints while updating the agent’s estimated position. Errors in those updates accumulate, allowing the internal position estimate to drift away from the actual coordinates. That mismatch then affects later trajectory predictions, creating a persistent problem for navigation in complex environments.

NeuroKalman recasts this process as recursive Bayesian state estimation. It separates a prediction based on motion dynamics from a correction based on historical observations. The authors mathematically connect kernel density estimation of measurement likelihoods with attention-based retrieval. This connection allows retrieved historical anchors to correct the model’s latent state without gradient updates during that correction.

Memory therefore supplies evidence for revising the current estimate as navigation proceeds. On the TravelUAV benchmark, the method clearly outperforms strong baselines after fine-tuning with only 10% of the full training data, while controlling drift accumulation. The result supports combining learned trajectory prediction with explicit state correction, and distinguishes training the navigator from correcting its state during use.
summary.tldr: NeuroKalman uses retrieved historical observations to correct navigation-state drift, outperforming strong TravelUAV baselines with 10% of the training data.

title: Mitigating Error Accumulation in Continuous Navigation via Memory-Augmented Kalman Filtering

abstract: Scaling laws provide a fundamental framework for understanding the performance of Language Models (LMs), yet deriving them requires prohibitively expensive evaluations across thousands of checkpoints or millions of inference samples. To address this, we introduce Item Response Scaling Laws (IRSL), a unified framework that integrates Item Response Theory (IRT) within the scaling law framework. Unlike traditional approaches that treat each model-benchmark pair in isolation, IRSL disentangles latent model ability from question characteristics, factorizing the scaling law estimation for $M$ models and $N$ questions to significantly reduce parameter complexity from $O(M \times N)$ to $O(M + N)$. We instantiate IRSL with Beta-IRT, which leverages the empirical probability responses of LMs—such as token probabilities in pre-training and pass rates in test-time sampling—to capture richer signals than binary responses. We validate our approach across two prevalent scaling paradigms: (1) pre-training downstream scaling, using 6,612 LM checkpoints and 37,682 questions from 10 benchmarks; and (2) test-time scaling, using 12 LMs and 120 questions from 4 benchmarks with up to 2,500 samples per question. Given a one-time calibration on existing model responses, IRSL yields more reliable scaling estimates using only 50 questions per benchmark (a 99.9% reduction), achieving comparable or superior decision accuracy to traditional approaches. Furthermore, we show that the estimated latent model abilities are generalizable, enabling accurate performance forecasting across benchmarks that share the same measurement objective.

paragraphs: Estimating how language-model performance scales can require evaluating many checkpoints or drawing many generated samples. Item Response Scaling Laws reduce this burden by separating a model’s latent ability from the characteristics of the questions used to measure it. This lets information be shared across evaluations instead of treating every model-question combination independently.

The framework integrates Item Response Theory with scaling laws, reducing parameter complexity for M models and N questions from a product, O(M × N), to a sum, O(M + N). Its Beta-IRT implementation uses probability-valued responses, including token probabilities and sampled pass rates. These carry more information than recording only a binary success or failure.

After a one-time calibration using existing responses, they report reliable estimates with just 50 questions per benchmark and comparable or better decision accuracy than traditional approaches. Estimated abilities also support performance forecasting across benchmarks, provided those benchmarks share the same measurement objective. That condition defines the reported scope of cross-benchmark generalization.
summary.tldr: Item Response Scaling Laws separate model ability from question characteristics to estimate scaling efficiently after one-time calibration.

title: Item Response Scaling Laws: A Measurement Theory Approach for Efficient and Generalizable Neural Scaling Estimation

abstract: Federated Learning (FL) often suffers from sacrificing global model accuracy when improving client-level fairness due to data heterogeneity, which often leads to inconsistent performance of the globally trained models, resulting in unfair outcomes among users. Existing fair FL algorithms face a bottleneck: they either sacrifice global model accuracy to promote fairness or fall short of achieving optimal fairness. In this paper, we propose a novel framework that effectively improves fairness while preserving global accuracy by integrating information-theoretic principles with model alignment. Specifically, we leverage the Maximum Entropy Principle to derive an analytic, closed-form solution for fair aggregation weights, ensuring significant fairness enhancements. We further employ a step-wise model alignment strategy that synchronizes gradient directions across heterogeneous clients, effectively mitigating the drift induced by local updates. Theoretical analysis proves that our method guarantees convergence even in non-convex settings. Importantly, we push the theoretical frontier of federated fairness by extending performance variance analysis to generalized regression, providing broader guarantees. Extensive experiments on five datasets demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving superior fairness without sacrificing global accuracy. Our code is available at https://github.com/T-Lab-CUHKSZ/FedEBA-Plus.

paragraphs: Federated learning combines updates from clients whose data can differ substantially. A shared model may consequently work well for some clients and poorly for others. FedEBA+ addresses the difficulty of reducing these performance disparities while preserving the accuracy of the global model.

The framework combines two mechanisms. First, it uses the maximum entropy principle to derive a closed-form expression for aggregation weights, determining how client contributions are combined to promote fairness. Second, a step-wise alignment procedure synchronizes gradient directions across clients. This alignment targets the drift caused by local training on heterogeneous data, complementing the fairness-oriented weighting.

The paper provides convergence analysis covering non-convex settings and extends its analysis of performance variation to generalized regression. Experiments on five datasets show better fairness than the compared state-of-the-art methods without sacrificing global accuracy. The contribution therefore joins an aggregation rule, a mechanism for coordinating local updates, and theoretical analysis, with empirical evidence that fairness and accuracy can improve together in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: FedEBA+ combines entropy-derived aggregation weights and client-update alignment to improve fairness while preserving global accuracy.

title: FedEBA+: Towards Fair and Effective Federated Learning via Entropy-Based Model

abstract: Multilingual documents encapsulate rich regional cultures, scientific discoveries, and historical records. Parsing this content into structured, machine-readable formats is critical for unlocking global knowledge. However, existing benchmarks predominantly focus on high-resource languages like English and Chinese, creating an $\textit{evaluation blind spot}$ concerning model performance on other languages. While recent Vision-Language Models (VLMs) claim support for hundreds of languages, the lack of ground truth makes it impossible to empirically verify these capabilities. To bridge this gap, we introduce $\textbf{MORE}$, a large-scale benchmark designed for multilingual document parsing evaluation. MORE distinguishes itself through three key dimensions: (1) $\textbf{Unprecedented Scale}$: It covers $\textbf{149 languages}$, making it the most linguistically diverse benchmark to date; (2) $\textbf{Structural Complexity}$: Unlike previous works, it extends evaluation beyond plain text to include structural elements such as code blocks, tables, and catalogs; and (3) $\textbf{Data Authenticity}$: All samples are curated from real-world documents via a model-assisted, human-refined annotation pipeline. We evaluate state-of-the-art models using MORE, establishing new performance baselines for long-tail languages and validating the benchmark’s effectiveness in diagnosing model capabilities in realistic, diverse scenarios. The MORE dataset will be available at https://github.com/zimoqingfeng/MORE.

paragraphs: Document parsing converts pages into structured information that software can use. Existing evaluations concentrate heavily on languages such as English and Chinese, leaving many claimed multilingual capabilities difficult to verify. MORE addresses this evaluation gap by providing reference annotations across 149 languages.

The benchmark evaluates document structure as well as ordinary text. It includes elements such as tables, code blocks, and catalogs, so systems must handle more than the words appearing on a page. Its samples come from real documents, and annotations are produced through a process that combines model assistance with human refinement. This connects the evaluation to the variety of material encountered outside narrowly controlled examples.

The authors evaluate leading models on MORE and establish performance baselines for languages that receive less attention in existing benchmarks. They report that the benchmark helps diagnose model capabilities in realistic, linguistically diverse settings. Its main contribution is a broader basis for measuring document understanding, making multilingual support more directly testable across both language coverage and structural complexity.
summary.tldr: MORE evaluates parsing of real documents across 149 languages, including structural elements beyond plain text.

title: MORE: A Multilingual Document Parsing Benchmark and Evaluation

abstract: Existing dimensionality reduction methods all perform dimensionality reduction by preserving some invariant in the space before and after dimensionality reduction. This paper proposes a new dimensionality reduction invariant: preserving the invariant of the point-distributions similarity. We also design a linear and efficient method to achieve dimensionality reduction while preserving this invariant. We theoretically prove the feasibility of our method for dimensionality reduction. Furthermore, our results on benchmark datasets and single-cell expression data demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed method.
originalAbstract: Existing dimensionality reduction methods all perform dimensionality reduction by preserving some invariant in the space before and after dimensionality reduction. This paper proposes a new dimensionality reduction invariant: preserving the invariant of the point-distributions similarity. We also design a linear and efficient method to achieve dimensionality reduction while preserving this invariant. We theoretically prove the feasibility of our method for dimensionality reduction. Furthermore, our results on benchmark datasets and single-cell expression data demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed method.

paragraphs: Dimensionality reduction represents data using fewer dimensions while trying to retain a meaningful property of the original representation. The choice of what to preserve determines the method’s objective. This paper proposes preserving similarity between point distributions, making that relationship the invariant that should survive the move from the original space to a lower-dimensional one.

The authors develop a linear method designed around this invariant and describe it as computationally efficient. Their contribution therefore includes both a preservation principle and a concrete way to pursue it. They also provide a theoretical proof of feasibility for dimensionality reduction, connecting the proposed objective to a mathematically supported construction rather than presenting only an empirical procedure.

Evaluation covers benchmark datasets and single-cell expression data. The reported results support the method’s effectiveness and efficiency in those settings. Taken together, the theory and experiments establish point-distribution similarity as a usable basis for dimensionality reduction, with a linear implementation that makes the proposed principle operational.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces an efficient linear dimensionality-reduction method designed to preserve similarity between point distributions.

title: Dimensionality Reduction with Point-Distribution Similarity Invariant

abstract: Large vision-language models can produce object hallucinations in image descriptions, highlighting the need for effective detection and mitigation strategies. Prior work commonly relies on the model’s attention weights on visual tokens as a detection signal. We reveal that coarse-grained attention-based analysis is unreliable due to hidden confounders, specifically token position and object repetition in a description. This leads to Simpson’s paradox: the attention trends reverse or disappear when statistics are aggregated. Based on this observation, we introduce HaloProbe, a Bayesian framework that factorizes external description statistics and internal decoding signals to estimate token-level hallucination probabilities. HaloProbe uses balanced training to encourage learning from internal evidence and combines it with a learned prior over external features to recover the true posterior. While intervention-based mitigation methods often degrade utility or fluency by modifying models’ internals, we use HaloProbe as an external scoring signal for non-invasive mitigation. Our experiments show that HaloProbe-guided decoding reduces hallucinations more effectively than state-of-the-art intervention-based methods while preserving caption utility and linguistic fluency.

paragraphs: Attention to image tokens might appear to reveal whether a vision-language model is describing a real object. This paper finds that coarse attention statistics can be misleading because token position and repeated object mentions affect the signal. Aggregating these cases can reverse or erase trends, producing Simpson’s paradox and undermining a simple attention-based detector.

HaloProbe separates external description features from internal decoding evidence in a Bayesian framework. Balanced training encourages its detector to learn from internal signals, while a learned prior captures external features. Combining the two produces token-level estimates of hallucination probability. The separation is designed to account for confounding factors rather than letting them dominate the detection signal.

In the reported experiments, HaloProbe-guided decoding reduces hallucinations more effectively than state-of-the-art intervention-based methods while preserving caption usefulness and fluency. Its contribution joins a diagnosis of misleading detection statistics with a practical way to use corrected estimates.
summary.tldr: HaloProbe accounts for confounded attention signals to estimate hallucination probabilities and guide decoding while preserving caption utility and fluency.

title: HaloProbe: Bayesian Detection and Mitigation of Object Hallucinations in Vision-Language Models

abstract: Autoformalization translates informal natural language into formal, machine-verifiable languages. While most work focuses on individual statements, real formalization efforts are inherently theory-level: they require an entire web of axioms, definitions, and lemmas before target theorems can even be stated. In this position paper, we argue for theory-level autoformalization: formalizing complete theories, including all their inter-dependencies, as structured libraries. We examine the significance of this shift, address alternative views, identify open challenges, and propose three promising paths forward. Our survey of autoformalization is available at https://github.com/marcusm117/Awesome-Autoformalization.

paragraphs: Autoformalization converts informal language into a formal language that machines can verify. Much existing work treats an individual statement as the unit of translation. This position paper argues that real formalization operates at a larger scale because a theorem depends on a surrounding network of definitions, assumptions, and supporting results.

The authors propose making complete theories the target of autoformalization. The desired output is a structured library that represents both its constituent statements and their dependencies. This matters because the surrounding mathematical structure is needed before a target theorem can even be expressed formally. Translating an isolated sentence therefore captures only part of the work involved in building formal knowledge.

The paper examines the significance of this change in scope, considers alternative views, identifies open challenges, and proposes three promising research directions. Its contribution is to reframe what an autoformalization system should aim to produce. Success at the theory level would concern an interconnected body of machine-verifiable knowledge, with the relationships between statements treated as part of the formalization task.
summary.tldr: Autoformalization should build connected formal theories, including their definitions and dependencies, rather than focus only on individual statements.

abstract: The majority of the existing algorithms for learning decision trees are greedy-a tree is induced top-down, making locally optimal decisions at each node. In most cases, however, the constructed tree is not globally optimal. Furthermore, the greedy algorithms require a fixed amount of time and are not able to generate a better tree if additional time is available. To overcome this problem, we present two lookahead-based algorithms for anytime induction of decision trees, thus allowing tradeoff between tree quality and learning time. The first one is depth-k lookahead, where a larger time allocation permits larger k. The second algorithm uses a novel strategy for evaluating candidate splits; a stochastic version of ID3 is repeatedly invoked to estimate the size of the tree in which each split results, and the one that minimizes the expected size is preferred. Experimental results indicate that for several hard concepts, our proposed approach exhibits good anytime behavior and yields significantly better decision trees when more time is available.

paragraphs: Greedy decision-tree learners choose a locally attractive split at each node, but those choices often do not produce a globally optimal tree. They also cannot necessarily turn extra available computation into a better result. This paper introduces two lookahead methods designed to trade additional learning time for improved trees.

The first method looks ahead to depth k, increasing that depth when more time is available. The second evaluates candidate splits through repeated calls to a stochastic version of ID3. These calls estimate the size of the tree that would follow each split, and the algorithm prefers the split with the smallest expected resulting tree.

Both approaches evaluate consequences beyond the immediate split, giving extra computation a specific role in the search. Experiments on several hard concepts indicate good anytime behavior and significantly better decision trees when more time is provided. The reported improvement concerns those tested concepts; the abstract does not claim that either method always finds a globally optimal tree.
summary.tldr: Two lookahead tree learners use extra computation to evaluate future splits and produce better trees on several hard concepts.

title: Lookahead-based algorithms for anytime induction of decision trees

abstract: Predictive state representations (PSRs) are a recently proposed way ofmodeling controlled dynamical systems. PSR-based models use predictions ofobservable outcomes of tests that could be done on the system as their staterepresentation, and have model parameters that define how the predictive staterepresentation changes over time as actions are taken and observations noted.Learning PSR-based models requires solving two subproblems: 1) discovery ofthe tests whose predictions constitute state, and 2) learning the modelparameters that define the dynamics. So far, there have been no resultsavailable on the discovery subproblem while for the learning subproblem anapproximate-gradient algorithm has been proposed (Singh et al., 2003) withmixed results (it works on some domains and not on others). In this paper, weprovide the first discovery algorithm and a new learning algorithm for linearPSRs for the special class of controlled dynamical systems that have a resetoperation. We provide experimental verification of our algorithms. Finally,we also distinguish our work from prior work by Jaeger (2000) on observableoperator models (OOMs).

paragraphs: Predictive state representations describe a controlled dynamical system using predictions about observable outcomes of tests that could be performed on it. Their parameters specify how those predictions change as actions are taken and observations arrive. Learning such a model involves choosing the tests that define state as well as estimating the dynamics.

This paper addresses both problems for linear predictive state representations in systems with a reset operation. The authors present the first discovery algorithm for selecting the tests and a new algorithm for learning model parameters. The reset requirement is part of the stated scope of these methods.

The paper reports experimental verification of the algorithms. It also distinguishes the approach from prior work on observable operator models. Against earlier parameter-learning work with mixed results and the absence of discovery results, the contribution supplies methods for both defining the predictive state and learning its evolution within the specified class of resettable systems.
summary.tldr: The paper provides discovery and learning algorithms for linear predictive state representations in controlled systems that support resetting.

title: Learning and discovery of predictive state representations in dynamical systems with reset

abstract: Entropy-type measures for the heterogeneity of clusters have been used for a long time. This paper studies the entropy-based criterion in clustering categorical data. It first shows that the entropy-based criterion can be derived in the formal framework of probabilistic clustering models and establishes the connection between the criterion and the approach based on dissimilarity coefficients. An iterative Monte-Carlo procedure is then presented to search for the partitions minimizing the criterion. Experiments are conducted to show the effectiveness of the proposed procedure.
