An iterative Monte-Carlo procedure is then presented to search for the partitions minimizing the criterion. Experiments are conducted to show the effectiveness of the proposed procedure.

paragraphs: This paper examines an entropy-based objective for clustering categorical data. Entropy-type measures have long been used to describe how heterogeneous a cluster is. The authors investigate the mathematical basis of such a criterion and how it can guide the search for a partition of the data into clusters.

They show that the criterion can be derived within a formal probabilistic clustering framework. They also establish a connection with clustering approaches based on dissimilarity coefficients. These results relate the entropy objective to two ways of describing clustering: through a probability model and through measures of differences between observations.

The paper then presents an iterative Monte Carlo procedure for searching for partitions that minimize the criterion. Experiments show the effectiveness of the proposed procedure. The contribution combines an explanation of why the objective arises with a method for pursuing it computationally, linking the interpretation of cluster heterogeneity to an operational search over possible groupings.
summary.tldr: The paper grounds entropy-based categorical clustering in probabilistic models and proposes a Monte Carlo procedure to optimize the criterion.

title: Entropy-based criterion in categorical clustering

abstract: When monitoring spatial phenomena, which are often modeled as Gaussian Processes (GPs), choosing sensor locations is a fundamental task. A common strategy is to place sensors at the points of highest entropy (variance) in the GP model. We propose a mutual information criteria, and show that it produces better placements. Furthermore, we prove that finding the configuration that maximizes mutual information is NP-complete. To address this issue, we describe a polynomial-time approximation that is within (1 − 1/e) of the optimum by exploiting the submodularity of our criterion. This algorithm is extended to handle local structure in the GP, yielding significant speedups. We demonstrate the advantages of our approach on two real-world data sets.
originalAbstract: When monitoring spatial phenomena, which are often modeled as Gaussian Processes (GPs), choosing sensor locations is a fundamental task. A common strategy is to place sensors at the points of highest entropy (variance) in the GP model. We propose a mutual information criteria, and show that it produces better placements. Furthermore, we prove that finding the configuration that maximizes mutual information is NP-complete. To address this issue, we describe a polynomial-time approximation that is within (1 − 1/e) of the optimum by exploiting the submodularity of our criterion. This algorithm is extended to handle local structure in the GP, yielding significant speedups. We demonstrate the advantages of our approach on two real-world data sets.

paragraphs: When sensors monitor a spatial phenomenon modeled by a Gaussian process, their locations determine how informative the observations will be. A common placement strategy chooses locations with the highest uncertainty, measured by variance or entropy. This paper proposes a mutual-information criterion and shows that it produces better sensor placements.

The authors prove that finding a configuration that maximizes mutual information is NP-complete. They address that computational difficulty through a polynomial-time approximation that exploits the criterion's submodularity. The resulting objective value is guaranteed to be at least a fraction 1 − 1/e of the optimum, providing a precise sense in which the placement is near optimal.

The algorithm is also extended to use local structure in the Gaussian process, producing significant speedups. Experiments on two real-world datasets demonstrate advantages of the approach. The paper thus links an information-based placement objective, a computational approximation guarantee, and an efficiency improvement, giving both theoretical and empirical reasons to consider the method for spatial monitoring.
summary.tldr: A mutual-information sensor-placement method achieves a 1 − 1/e approximation guarantee and gains speed by exploiting local Gaussian-process structure.

title: Near-optimal sensor placements in Gaussian processes

abstract: A geometric construction is presented which is shown to be an effective tool for understanding and implementing multi-category support vector classification. It is demonstrated how this construction can be used to extend many other existing two-class kernel-based classification methodologies in a straightforward way while still preserving attractive properties of individual algorithms. Reducing training times through incorporating the results of pairwise classification is also discussed and experimental results presented.
originalAbstract: A geometric construction is presented which is shown to be an effective tool for understanding and implementing multi-category support vector classification. It is demonstrated how this construction can be used to extend many other existing two-class kernel-based classification methodologies in a straightforward way while still preserving attractive properties of individual algorithms. Reducing training times through incorporating the results of pairwise classification is also discussed and experimental results presented.

paragraphs: Methods built to choose between two classes do not automatically explain how to choose among many. This paper presents a geometric construction for understanding and implementing support vector classification with multiple categories. The construction provides a way to connect the multiclass problem to the geometry underlying existing binary classification methods.

The authors show how this construction can extend many other kernel-based two-class approaches in a straightforward manner. A central aim is to retain attractive properties of the individual algorithms as they are adapted. The contribution therefore goes beyond a single multiclass classifier: it offers a shared route for extending a collection of existing methods.

The paper also discusses using results from pairwise classification to reduce training time and presents experimental results. Pairwise classification handles categories two at a time, making those results relevant to the larger multicategory task. Together, the geometric construction and training discussion address both how to formulate these extensions and how to make their implementation computationally practical.
summary.tldr: A geometric construction extends binary kernel classifiers to multiple classes while preserving attractive properties of the original methods.

title: Adapting two-class support vector classification methods to many class problems

abstract: By the term “quantization”, we refer to the process of using quantum mechanics in order to improve a classical algorithm, usually by making it go faster. In this paper, we initiate the idea of quantizing clustering algorithms by using variations on a celebrated quantum algorithm due to Grover. After having introduced this novel approach to unsupervised learning, we illustrate it with a quantized version of three standard algorithms: divisive clustering, k-medians and an algorithm for the construction of a neighbourhood graph. We obtain a significant speedup compared to the classical approach.
originalAbstract: By the term “quantization”, we refer to the process of using quantum mechanics in order to improve a classical algorithm, usually by making it go faster. In this paper, we initiate the idea of quantizing clustering algorithms by using variations on a celebrated quantum algorithm due to Grover. After having introduced this novel approach to unsupervised learning, we illustrate it with a quantized version of three standard algorithms: divisive clustering, k-medians and an algorithm for the construction of a neighbourhood graph. We obtain a significant speedup compared to the classical approach.

paragraphs: This paper explores how quantum computation can accelerate clustering algorithms. It uses the term quantization to mean adapting a classical algorithm through quantum mechanics, usually with speed as the objective. The focus is on bringing this idea to unsupervised learning by developing quantum versions of established computational procedures.

The proposed approach uses variations of Grover's quantum algorithm. The authors illustrate it with three procedures: divisive clustering, k-medians, and the construction of a neighborhood graph. These examples span algorithms that directly create clusters and a procedure that builds relationships among data points. Together, they demonstrate how the proposed quantum approach can be applied to several tasks relevant to clustering.

The paper reports a significant speedup over the classical approach. The stated gain concerns computation, rather than a reported improvement in the quality of the resulting clusters. Its contribution is an initial framework for quantizing clustering procedures, supported by concrete versions of the three algorithms and the speed advantage obtained for the proposed approach.
summary.tldr: Quantum variants of Grover's algorithm accelerate divisive clustering, k-medians, and neighborhood-graph construction.

title: Quantum clustering algorithms

abstract: We show that the Brier game of prediction is mixable and find the optimal learning rate and substitution function for it. The resulting prediction algorithm is applied to predict results of football and tennis matches. The theoretical performance guarantee turns out to be rather tight on these data sets, especially in the case of the more extensive tennis data.
originalAbstract: We show that the Brier game of prediction is mixable and find the optimal learning rate and substitution function for it. The resulting prediction algorithm is applied to predict results of football and tennis matches. The theoretical performance guarantee turns out to be rather tight on these data sets, especially in the case of the more extensive tennis data.

paragraphs: The paper studies prediction with expert advice in the setting called the Brier game. The central question is how to construct a prediction algorithm with a theoretical performance guarantee. Rather than presenting only an application, the authors establish a mathematical property of the prediction game and use it to derive an algorithm.

They prove that the Brier game is mixable and identify its optimal learning rate and substitution function. These are the ingredients used to form the resulting prediction procedure. The optimality claim applies to those ingredients in this setting, giving the algorithm a principled specification rather than merely reporting a successful choice from an application.

The algorithm is applied to football and tennis match prediction. On these datasets, the theoretical guarantee is reported to be fairly tight, especially on the larger tennis dataset. This means the guarantee closely reflects the observed performance in those applications. The empirical contribution is therefore evidence about the practical informativeness of the theory, not just an example of deploying the algorithm.
summary.tldr: The Brier game's mixability yields a prediction algorithm whose theoretical guarantee is fairly tight on football and especially tennis data.

title: Prediction with expert advice for the Brier game

abstract: We describe a method for inferring linear causal relations among multi-dimensional variables. The idea is to use an asymmetry between the distributions of cause and effect that occurs if the covariance matrix of the cause and the structure matrix mapping the cause to the effect are independently chosen.The method applies to both stochastic and deterministic causal relations, provided that the dimensionality is sufficiently high (in some experiments, 5 was enough). It is applicable to Gaussian as well as non-Gaussian data.
originalAbstract: We describe a method for inferring linear causal relations among multi-dimensional variables. The idea is to use an asymmetry between the distributions of cause and effect that occurs if the covariance matrix of the cause and the structure matrix mapping the cause to the effect are independently chosen.The method applies to both stochastic and deterministic causal relations, provided that the dimensionality is sufficiently high (in some experiments, 5 was enough). It is applicable to Gaussian as well as non-Gaussian data.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a method for identifying the direction of a linear causal relationship between multidimensional variables. Its central idea is that cause and effect can have different distributional properties. The method uses this asymmetry to help determine which variable is the cause.

The asymmetry arises under a specific assumption: the covariance matrix of the cause and the structure matrix mapping cause to effect are chosen independently. This assumption links the distribution of the cause to the mechanism producing the effect without coordinating their structures. It is the stated basis for the directional signal, so the result is conditional on this setup.

The method applies to stochastic and deterministic causal relationships, and to Gaussian and non-Gaussian data, provided the dimensionality is sufficiently high. In some experiments, five dimensions were enough; that observation does not establish a universal threshold. The contribution is a route to causal-direction inference that draws on high-dimensional structure and the stated independence assumption across several types of linear relationships.
summary.tldr: A causal-direction method exploits high-dimensional asymmetry when the cause covariance and linear causal mapping are independently chosen.

title: Telling cause from effect based on high-dimensional observations

abstract: In this work, inspired by (Buhler and Hein, 2009), (Strang, 1983), and (Zhang et al., 2009),we give a continuous relaxation of the Cheeger cut problem on a weighted graph. We show that the relaxation is actually equivalent to the original problem. We then describe an algorithm for finding good cuts suggested by the similarities of the energy of the relaxed problem and various well studied energies in image processing. Finally we provide experimental validation of the proposed algorithm, demonstrating its efficiency in finding high quality cuts.
originalAbstract: In this work, inspired by (Buhler and Hein, 2009), (Strang, 1983), and (Zhang et al., 2009),we give a continuous relaxation of the Cheeger cut problem on a weighted graph. We show that the relaxation is actually equivalent to the original problem. We then describe an algorithm for finding good cuts suggested by the similarities of the energy of the relaxed problem and various well studied energies in image processing. Finally we provide experimental validation of the proposed algorithm, demonstrating its efficiency in finding high quality cuts.

paragraphs: The paper studies the Cheeger cut problem on a weighted graph, where the goal is to find a useful partition of connected objects. Its first contribution is a continuous relaxation: the discrete partitioning problem is expressed through an optimization problem with continuous variables, opening the door to a different set of computational methods.

The authors prove that this relaxation is equivalent to the original problem. That is a stronger statement than simply presenting a continuous surrogate that resembles the graph-cut objective. The equivalence establishes that the relaxed formulation retains the underlying optimization problem, making its mathematical structure directly relevant to finding cuts.

The algorithm is motivated by similarities between the relaxed objective and energies studied in image processing. This connection supplies a practical route from the formulation to a procedure for finding good cuts. Experiments demonstrate efficient discovery of high-quality cuts. The theoretical equivalence and the empirical algorithm results play distinct roles: one validates the formulation, while the other supports the usefulness of the proposed computation.
summary.tldr: An equivalent continuous formulation of Cheeger cuts motivates an image-processing-inspired algorithm that efficiently finds high-quality cuts in experiments.

title: Total Variation, Cheeger Cuts

abstract: Deep Belief Networks (DBNs) are hierarchical generative models which have been used successfully to model high dimensional visual data. However, they are not robust to common variations such as occlusion and random noise. We explore two strategies for improving the robustness of DBNs. First, we show that a DBN with sparse connections in the first layer is more robust to variations that are not in the training set. Second, we develop a probabilistic denoising algorithm to determine a subset of the hidden layer nodes to unclamp. We show that this can be applied to any feed forward network classifier with localized first layer connections. Recognition results after denoising are significantly better over the standard DBN implementations for various sources of noise.
originalAbstract: Deep Belief Networks (DBNs) are hierarchical generative models which have been used successfully to model high dimensional visual data. However, they are not robust to common variations such as occlusion and random noise. We explore two strategies for improving the robustness of DBNs. First, we show that a DBN with sparse connections in the first layer is more robust to variations that are not in the training set. Second, we develop a probabilistic denoising algorithm to determine a subset of the hidden layer nodes to unclamp. We show that this can be applied to any feed forward network classifier with localized first layer connections. Recognition results after denoising are significantly better over the standard DBN implementations for various sources of noise.

paragraphs: Deep belief networks can model high-dimensional visual data, yet ordinary implementations can struggle when images contain occlusion or random noise. This paper explores two ways to improve their robustness. Both concern how the network handles visual information when the input differs from what it encountered during training.

The first strategy changes the network's connections: a sparsely connected first layer is shown to improve robustness to variations absent from the training set. The second strategy introduces probabilistic denoising. It selects a subset of hidden-layer nodes to unclamp, allowing those internal quantities to be reconsidered during denoising instead of keeping them fixed.

The denoising method applies beyond deep belief networks to feed-forward classifiers with localized first-layer connections. That architectural requirement is part of the stated scope of the method. Across various sources of noise, recognition after denoising is significantly better than with standard deep belief network implementations. Together, the findings show how first-layer structure and selective adjustment of hidden representations can improve recognition under corrupted inputs.
summary.tldr: Sparse first-layer connections and probabilistic hidden-node denoising improve visual recognition robustness in the reported experiments.

title: Deep networks for robust visual recognition

abstract: We present the infinite dynamic Bayesian network model (iDBN), a nonparametric, factored state-space model that generalizes dynamic Bayesian networks (DBNs). The iDBN can infer every aspect of a DBN: the number of hidden factors, the number of values each factor can take, and (arbitrarily complex) connections and conditionals between factors and observations. In this way, the iDBN generalizes other nonparametric state space models, which until now generally focused on binary hidden nodes and more restricted connection structures. We show how this new prior allows us to find interesting structure in benchmark tests and on two real-world datasets involving weather data and neural information flow networks.
originalAbstract: We present the infinite dynamic Bayesian network model (iDBN), a nonparametric, factored state-space model that generalizes dynamic Bayesian networks (DBNs). The iDBN can infer every aspect of a DBN: the number of hidden factors, the number of values each factor can take, and (arbitrarily complex) connections and conditionals between factors and observations. In this way, the iDBN generalizes other nonparametric state space models, which until now generally focused on binary hidden nodes and more restricted connection structures. We show how this new prior allows us to find interesting structure in benchmark tests and on two real-world datasets involving weather data and neural information flow networks.

paragraphs: The infinite dynamic Bayesian network is a nonparametric model for systems with evolving hidden state. Its state is factored into hidden components, and the model can infer the number of those components rather than requiring that aspect of the structure to be fixed. It generalizes the dynamic Bayesian network formulation.

The flexibility extends beyond the number of hidden factors. The model can infer how many values each factor takes, connections among factors and observations, and their conditional relationships. The abstract allows arbitrarily complex connections and conditionals. This expands on earlier nonparametric state-space approaches that generally used binary hidden nodes and more restricted patterns of connection.

The authors demonstrate the new prior on benchmark tests and on weather data and neural information-flow networks. They report finding interesting structure in these settings. The significance is the ability to investigate multiple aspects of a dynamic model together, including hidden-state complexity and relationships between components. The demonstrations support its usefulness for structural discovery without establishing that every inferred structure must match a unique underlying system.
summary.tldr: The infinite dynamic Bayesian network learns hidden-state complexity and dependency structure within a flexible nonparametric temporal model.

title: Infinite Dynamic Bayesian Networks

abstract: In this paper, we analyze the performance of Lasso-TD, a modification of LSTD in which the projection operator is defined as a Lasso problem. We first show that Lasso-TD is guaranteed to have a unique fixed point and its algorithmic implementation coincides with the recently presented LARS-TD and LC-TD methods. We then derive two bounds on the prediction error of Lasso-TD in the Markov design setting, i.e., when the performance is evaluated on the same states used by the method. The first bound makes no assumption, but has a slow rate w.r.t. the number of samples. The second bound is under an assumption on the empirical Gram matrix, called the compatibility condition, but has an improved rate and directly relates the prediction error to the sparsity of the value function in the feature space at hand.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we analyze the performance of Lasso-TD, a modification of LSTD in which the projection operator is defined as a Lasso problem. We first show that Lasso-TD is guaranteed to have a unique fixed point and its algorithmic implementation coincides with the recently presented LARS-TD and LC-TD methods. We then derive two bounds on the prediction error of Lasso-TD in the Markov design setting, i.e., when the performance is evaluated on the same states used by the method. The first bound makes no assumption, but has a slow rate w.r.t. the number of samples. The second bound is under an assumption on the empirical Gram matrix, called the compatibility condition, but has an improved rate and directly relates the prediction error to the sparsity of the value function in the feature space at hand.

paragraphs: Lasso-TD modifies LSTD by defining its projection step through a Lasso problem. This paper analyzes the resulting value-prediction method with a finite number of samples. It first establishes that Lasso-TD has a unique fixed point and that its algorithmic implementation coincides with the existing LARS-TD and LC-TD methods.

The prediction-error analysis concerns the Markov design setting, where performance is evaluated on the same states used by the method. The authors provide two bounds with different strengths. The first requires no additional assumption but improves relatively slowly as the number of samples grows. It supplies a broad guarantee within that evaluation setting.

The second bound requires the empirical Gram matrix to satisfy a compatibility condition. Under that condition, the rate improves and the error bound explicitly reflects how sparsely the value function can be represented in the available features. The distinction matters: the stronger conclusion depends on a stated property of the data representation. Together, the bounds clarify both general behavior and the circumstances supporting a sharper sparsity-sensitive result.
summary.tldr: Lasso-TD has a unique fixed point and finite-sample error bounds, including a sharper sparsity-sensitive bound under a compatibility condition.

title: Finite-Sample Analysis of Lasso-TD
